#5657. MIT scientists turn immune cells into cancer killers inside the body

MIT researchers have developed a new technique that allows them to transform immune cells into cancer fighters directly inside the body, potentially making advanced treatments for cancer and autoimmune diseases much easier to produce and administer.

The method focuses on natural killer (NK) cells, a type of immune cell that can be engineered to recognize and destroy harmful cells. These include cancerous T cells and T cells that mistakenly attack healthy tissue, contributing to conditions such as lymphoma and autoimmune hepatitis.

Rather than extracting immune cells from a patient and modifying them in a laboratory, the researchers use tiny particles made of fatty molecules to deliver genetic instructions directly to NK cells. These instructions, carried by messenger RNA, tell the cells to produce specialized proteins that help them identify and eliminate diseased T cells.

The resulting cells, known as CAR NK cells, could eventually be used against several different diseases. By carrying out the engineering process inside the body, the new approach could eliminate much of the time, expense, and complexity involved in manufacturing personalized immune cell therapies.

"The manufacturing challenges with CAR NK cells are significant. The idea here is you can deliver a nanoparticle that will modify your own NK cells with a CAR construct and teach them to attack tumor cells," says Daniel Anderson, a professor in MIT's Department of Chemical Engineering and a member of MIT's Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research and Institute for Medical Engineering and Science.

Anderson is the senior author of the research, published in Nature Biotechnology. The lead authors are MIT postdoctoral researcher Yuang Chen and graduate students Julia Monkovic and Haseeb Mughal. Robert Langer, MIT's David H. Koch Institute Professor, also contributed to the study.

Why Current Cancer Immunotherapies Are So Complex

Immune cell engineering has already transformed treatment options for certain cancers. During the past decade, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved seven cancer therapies that use genetically modified T cells, known as chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells.

These treatments work by equipping T cells with specially designed receptors that recognize particular markers, or antigens, on other cells. When an engineered T cell encounters its designated target, such as a protein associated with cancer, it becomes activated and attacks the cell carrying that marker.

CAR T cell therapies have been especially effective against blood cancers arising from B cells. These include certain forms of leukemia and lymphoma, as well as multiple myeloma.

However, preparing these treatments involves several complicated steps. Doctors first collect blood from the patient and send it to a specialized facility. There, technicians separate the T cells, genetically modify them to produce the desired receptors, and grow enough engineered cells for treatment. The finished cells must then be transported back to the hospital and infused into the patient.

Natural Killer Cells Offer a Different Way to Fight Cancer

Scientists have recently been exploring whether natural killer cells could be engineered in a similar way. One important advantage is their potential to treat cancers and autoimmune conditions involving abnormal T cells.

Trying to use CAR T cells against diseased T cells creates a major problem. Because both the engineered cells and their intended targets are T cells, the modified cells may recognize and destroy one another. This unintended attack can undermine the treatment.

Natural killer cells avoid this complication because they are a different type of immune cell. They can be programmed to attack harmful T cells without triggering the same problem of engineered T cells killing each other.

"NK cells can treat these T cell malignancies -- not only T cell cancer, but also T cell autoimmune diseases," Chen says.

Producing CAR NK cells outside the body, however, still requires much of the specialized equipment, labor, and processing associated with CAR T cell manufacturing. To overcome these limitations, the MIT team investigated whether NK cells could instead be engineered "in vivo," meaning directly inside the body.

"If a patient can just get an infusion of nanoparticles, it would dramatically simplify the process and reduce costs," Anderson says.

Although researchers are actively developing CAR NK cell therapies for cancer and autoimmune disorders, none have received FDA approval.

How mRNA Nanoparticles Reprogram Immune Cells

The MIT team designed lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) capable of transporting messenger RNA into natural killer cells. The mRNA carries instructions for producing a chimeric antigen receptor that directs the modified immune cell toward a specific target.

The technology can be adapted to recognize different proteins depending on the disease being treated. For example, the researchers can provide instructions for a receptor that recognizes CD19, a protein found on B cells, or CD3, a protein present on T cells, including those responsible for autoimmune attacks.

To help the nanoparticles reach the correct immune cells, the scientists covered their surfaces with antibody fragments. These fragments recognize and attach to receptors on NK cells, helping deliver the genetic instructions where they are needed.

Once inside an NK cell, the mRNA directs the production of the new receptor, giving the immune cell the ability to recognize and attack its intended target.

The researchers then tested whether this approach could efficiently reprogram NK cells and whether the resulting cells could combat cancer and autoimmune disease in mice.

Reprogrammed Immune Cells Eliminate Tumors in Mice

The initial experiments produced encouraging results. After injecting the nanoparticles into mice, the researchers successfully modified approximately 80 percent of the NK cells they were targeting.

They next investigated whether these engineered cells could attack tumors. In mice with an aggressive form of melanoma, three of the five animals treated with nanoparticles designed to direct NK cells against the cancer experienced complete remission.

The researchers also tested the technique against T cell lymphoma using humanized mice. These animals receive transfusions of human blood cells, temporarily giving them immune systems that share certain characteristics with those of humans.

In this model, the treatment produced substantial tumor destruction. After five injections of the nanoparticles, the tumors were completely eliminated.

Importantly, these results were comparable to those achieved with CAR NK cells produced through the more traditional method of collecting NK cells, modifying them outside the body, and then returning them to the animals.

This suggests that generating CAR NK cells directly inside the body could offer similar cancer-fighting capabilities while avoiding the complicated manufacturing process required by conventional cell therapies.

A Single Injection Reverses Autoimmune Liver Damage

The researchers also wanted to determine whether their technology could help treat autoimmune diseases, in which the immune system mistakenly damages healthy tissues.

They focused on autoimmune hepatitis, a condition in which abnormal T cells attack hepatocytes, the main functional cells of the liver. By designing nanoparticles that instruct NK cells to recognize these harmful T cells, the scientists tested whether they could interrupt the autoimmune response.

The treatment successfully eliminated the autoreactive T cells in mice with the disease. Even more encouragingly, the animals' damaged liver tissue healed after the harmful immune cells were removed.

These improvements occurred after just one nanoparticle injection, demonstrating the potential of the approach beyond cancer treatment.

"This study is an excellent example of the power of nano delivery systems and their ability to potentially treat cancer and other diseases," Langer says.

A New Direction for Cancer and Autoimmune Treatments

The researchers believe that reprogramming natural killer cells inside the body could eventually provide new treatment options for a much wider range of conditions.

Among the diseases they hope to target are multiple sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis, both of which can involve harmful immune responses driven by dysfunctional T cells.

Although the findings are promising, the experiments were conducted in mice, and further research will be necessary to determine whether the technique is safe and effective in humans.

If successful, the technology could make engineered immune cell treatments considerably more accessible by replacing a lengthy laboratory manufacturing process with the direct delivery of genetic instructions through nanoparticles.

The research received funding from Sanofi, the Marble Center for Cancer Nanomedicine, and a Koch Institute Support (core) Grant from the National Cancer Institute.

Materials provided by Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Original written by Anne Trafton. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5656. Zus Health secures $33M to build the infrastructure for AI-powered clinical workflows

Zus Health secures $33M to build the infrastructure for AI-powered clinical workflows" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

As healthcare companies race to build AI copilots and agents, startup Zus Health is betting that the bigger opportunity is creating the connected patient data layer those applications need to work reliably.

Zus Health, Jonathan Bush's health tech company, picked up $33 million in series B funding to build out the data foundation for healthcare AI. Drive Capital led the series B round. Sanofi Ventures, HealthX Ventures and Alumni Ventures, as well as existing investors Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), F-Prime, Maverick Ventures and JAZZ Venture Partners also backed the round.

The financing brings Zus's total capital raised to more than $100 million, and the fresh funding will support the company's continued investment in its intelligent patient record platform, national healthcare data network and AI-powered clinical workflows.

Zus has built its platform in three layers, according to Bush. The company first focused on building a nationwide patient record, a data network that pulls information into that record, and increasingly, AI-enabled workflows that automate care tasks using a more complete view of the patient.

Electronic health record systems (EHRs) succeeded at digitizing healthcare but failed to make patient information portable across organizations, Bush, founder and CEO of Zus Health, told Fierce Healthcare. Clinicians and care teams still spend valuable time searching for records and reconciling incomplete information. For patients, that can mean repeating their medical history at every appointment or relying on memory to recall past treatments. Advances in artificial intelligence now offer an opportunity to make healthcare information not just accessible, but actionable, according to Zus Health executives.

Launched in 2021, Zus Health developed what Bush calls an "always-on, FHIR-native, API-first medical record." It offers a shared health data platform designed to accelerate healthcare data interoperability by providing easy-to-use patient data at the point of care via a standalone app, API (application programming interface), embedded components and direct EHR integration. At the center of its approach is an intelligent, continuously updated patient record that serves as a shared foundation for healthcare applications.

The company's Zus Aggregated Profile (ZAP) brings fragmented clinical information together into a unified, longitudinal patient record, supported by AI-powered clinical intelligence that makes the information easier to use across applications and workflows, according to the company. The platform also has nationwide connectivity across EHR networks, pharmacy data, care event notifications, labs and other clinical data sources that continuously updates the patient record without requiring customers to build their own connectivity infrastructure.

"We're finally on to the last and critical piece of what I think the future of medical records looks like, which is standing up workflows that automate all of the tasks of patient care in a very bespoke way," Bush told Fierce Healthcare. "[Zus Health] developed the first data-rich networked medical record platform in the industry's history. Whether Zeus wins or somebody else beats Zeus at it, all electronic medical records in the future will be national."

He added, "And now, with AI, we have an extraordinary opportunity to build workflows that actually make delivering care easier, faster and more effective."

The company is betting that the next competitive player in healthcare AI will be the data infrastructure underneath the applications.

Zus Health, a Fierce 15 of 2025 honoree, wants to use its nationwide data network and longitudinal patient record as the infrastructure on which AI-powered clinical applications can run. The company's platform enables EHRs and other applications to work from a more complete, cross-provider view of the patient. Zus Health built AI solutions and flexible integration capabilities to put connected information to work across clinical and operational use cases, while enabling healthcare organizations to build applications tailored to their needs.

Zus works with value-based care organizations, digital health companies, provider organizations, as well as diagnostics and precision medicine companies. The company claims that in August alone its nationwide network supported more than 110 million networked transactions, while its AI-native clinical platform generated 39 million evidence citations year-to-date across its solutions—demonstrating both the scale of its connectivity and how patient information is being put to work across healthcare.

Zus supports solutions spanning pre-visit preparation, transitions of care, risk adjustment, quality gap closure and population health management. Its clinical intelligence capabilities, including AI-powered generated patient summaries (GPS), turn fragmented patient records into information care teams can use more efficiently and confidently.

The company plans to use the series B funding to build out its AI-powered clinical intelligence and capabilities and broaden its healthcare data network connectivity. Zus plans to expand its solutions to automate population health and care management workflows, while enabling customers and developers to create AI-powered workflows across value-based care, specialty care and other high-value use cases.

The company is seeing rapid growth in specialty care, particularly oncology, where complex patient records are spread across multiple providers. Zeus’s continuously updated, aggregated patient data enables more comprehensive and efficient reviews of treatment eligibility, clinical trial criteria and genetic testing—tasks that traditionally required extensive manual work by nurses and analysts using fragmented legacy EHR systems, Bush noted.

"We believe healthcare is entering a new era in which AI can fundamentally change how care is delivered, but that transformation depends on having reliable, connected patient information," said Molly Bonakdarpour, general partner at Drive Capital, in a statement. "Zus has built the foundation to address that challenge at scale. Its combination of technology, market opportunity and leadership gives us conviction in the company's ability to help shape the next generation of healthcare."

#5655. CMS extends moratorium on new Medicare enrollments for hospice, home health agencies

CMS extends moratorium on new Medicare enrollments for hospice, home health agencies" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Trump administration is extending its moratorium on new Medicare enrollments from hospice and home health agencies.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said Thursday that it will extend the moratorium by six more months as part of its efforts to combat fraud, waste and abuse in the Medicare program.

CMS said that the initial moratorium window has allowed the agency "to conduct targeted investigations and deploy advanced data analytics" to identify potential cases of fraud. An extension was deemed necessary to continue that effort, as the "circumstances warranting the imposition of the moratoria have not yet abated."

The agency said that hospice and home health have long been considered high risk areas for fraud.

“We’ve made real progress over the past six months, but fraud in hospice and home health persists and our work isn’t finished,” said CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., in the announcement. “Medicare beneficiaries deserve protection from these bad actors, and American taxpayers need to know the programs they rely on aren’t being bled dry by fraudsters.”

Like the original moratorium, the extension applies nationwide. However, the extension will allow currently enrolled hospice providers or home health agencies to add new practice locations to their existing enrollment in Medicare. Providers currently enrolled in Medicare will not be impacted and can continue to provide services to beneficiaries.

The Trump administration has issued a six-month moratorium on hospice and home health agencies enrolling in Medicare as part of its efforts to combat fraud.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said in an announcement on Wednesday morning that the "data-driven" decision targets a key source of fraud activity. It follows a similar announcement made earlier this year of a moratorium on durable medical equipment, prosthetics, orthotics and supplies companies.

During the six-month window, CMS said it will focus on identifying and investigating bad actors and deploying advanced analytics that help accelerate the removal of hospice and home health providers that are likely perpetrators of fraud.

CMS added that recent action under the broader White House fraud push has suspended payments to 773 hospice providers and 23 home health agencies in the Los Angeles area, totaling about $70 million in funds.

“We’ve seen systemic and deeply troubling fraud in the hospice and home health space, with bad actors exploiting some of our most vulnerable Medicare patients and stealing money from the American taxpayer,” CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., said in the agency's press release. “Today we’re shutting the door on fraud—preventing new bad actors from entering Medicare while we aggressively identify, investigate and remove those already exploiting them."

"This is about protecting patients, restoring integrity and safeguarding taxpayer dollars," Oz said.

CMS said that the moratorium will not affect providers currently enrolled in Medicare, and they can continue to offer key services to members. It will apply, however, to new applicants for participation and "certain changes in majority ownership," which CMS said can be used to "obscure control by bad actors."

The moratoria will also prevent suspected fraudsters from evading punishment by moving across state lines, CMS said.

The announcement, the agency said, builds on a number of steps CMS has taken of late to address fraud in hospice and home healthcare, including increased oversight in states with elevated risk of fraud, such as Arizona, California, Georgia, Ohio, Nevada and Texas.

CMS is also conducting hospice site visits across the country to monitor operations and potentially identify suspicious behavior. In addition, it expanded a demonstration across several states—Florida, Illinois, Oklahoma, Ohio, North Carolina and Texas—that allowed for pre- and post-claim reviews of submissions from HHAs, which may stop improper payments before they're made.

The National Alliance for Care at Home, in a statement responding to the news, said it welcomes the administration's scrutiny and appreciates that "providers will still be able to conduct face-to-face recertification visits via telehealth during the enrollment moratorium, which will help avoid unnecessary care disruptions for patients and families." Still, it said the action raises concerns over access to care in high-demand areas and urged CMS to focus its efforts on "high-fraud markets" or actors without catching the rest of the sector in its net.

“CMS must use data-driven, risk-based program integrity measures and focus resources on boots-on-the-ground surveys and enforcement of existing oversight mechanisms that root out the blatantly bad actors without potentially limiting patient access to care or punishing high-quality providers operating in good faith," Alliance CEO Jennifer Sheets said in the statement.

#5654. Kim Kardashian’s Former Beverly Hills Tuscan Villa From Early Seasons of ‘Keeping Up With the Kardashians’ Hits the Market for $8.5 Million

Kim Kardashian’s former Beverly Hills home has hit the market, with an asking price of $8.495 million for a piece of reality television history.

The five-bedroom, five-bathroom home was featured heavily in the earliest seasons of “Keeping Up With the Kardashians.” Remember when Kris Jenner and Khloé Kardashian went out on the town, and after a few too many margaritas, decided to toilet-paper the Tuscan-style villa?

Fortunately, the defaced rose bushes have been cleaned up since that 2013 episode.

Kim purchased the 4,027-square-foot home for $3.4 million in 2010. Three years later, she sold it fully-furnished, and it went for $5.12 million after a bidding war, according to Robb Report.

Later, in 2024, Kim visited the property with Khloé and celebrity broker Josh Altman, to find that it was still nearly exactly as she’d left it. Recognizable details such as a “KK” logo on the wall of her iconic glam room and her custom bedding were still there, prompting the star to share a tour of the time capsule on her Snapchat profile.

Today, the famous family’s connection to the estate is more of an “if you know, you know” situation. It’s undergone a complete transformation by AD100 designer Sebastian Zuchowicki, and now boasts a more sleek, contemporary look.

With that said, many of the structural features that made the home a gem in the first place are still present.

The gourmet kitchen has been redone in a European country style, with custom cabinetry and a spacious center island. Charming windows line one wall, while a double-sided fireplace connects the breakfast room and lounge. New, top-of-the-line appliances have also been added.

The primary suite is certainly luxurious, with a fireside seating area, two fabulous and generously-sized walk-in closets, and a spa-inspired Italian-tiled bathroom that features double vanities, a soothing shower, and a unique soaking tub.

Additionally, the second floor also includes three more en suite bedrooms, which each have a distinct personality. From floral wallpaper to chic striped walls, these rooms manage to be neutral and statement-making at the same time.

The home is perfectly primed for entertaining, especially considering the private theater.

Indoor-outdoor living is encouraged, with a covered fireplace lounge and a fully equipped outdoor kitchen.

The resort-style pool and spa makes the backyard feel like a true getaway. There’s also a tranquil fountain, a hillside sun terrace, a dedicated bathroom, and a fire pit. A gazebo and cabana serves as a spot to watch television without being cooped up inside.

The gourmet kitchen is appointed with custom cabinetry, premium appliances, a spacious center island, and a double-sided fireplace connecting the breakfast room and lounge. A private theater provides an additional space for entertainment.

Today, Kim holds an impressive collection of properties in California and Idaho. Most notably, she’s spent years renovating her $60 million Hidden Hills home. The home has been undergoing major construction since 2024, and during a recent episode of “The Kardashians,” it was revealed that the Skims founder is creating an 8,000-square-foot closet.

Kim continues to share her real estate updates with viewers, and during the Nov. 5 episode of the family’s Hulu show, she purchased a new Palm Springs, CA, estate on what appeared to be a whim.

The Kardashian-Jenners have a series of homes in La Quinta, with hidden pathways connecting the properties. When Kim realized the house located next door to Kylie Jenner’s abode was up for grabs, she sneaked onto the property to see if she liked it better than her existing home.

Later in the episode, Khloé confirmed that her older sister had, in fact, made the purchase.

#5653. Cancer uses antioxidants to disarm the immune system, scientists discover

Free radicals have traditionally been associated with damage to the body's cells, leading to widespread interest in whether antioxidants might help prevent cancer. But new research suggests these often misunderstood molecules also play an important role in protecting us from the disease.

Scientists have discovered that certain immune cells actually need small amounts of reactive oxygen species, a group of molecules that includes free radicals, to recognize and destroy cancer cells. Even more surprisingly, tumors appear to exploit this requirement by releasing natural antioxidants that interfere with the immune system's ability to fight back.

The findings, published in the journal Science, reveal a previously unknown way that cancer evades the body's defenses. They could also point toward new strategies for making cancer immunotherapies more effective, particularly in patients whose tumors resist existing treatments.

How Cancer Uses Antioxidants to Disable Immune Cells

The immune system protects the body by identifying and eliminating threats, ranging from harmful bacteria and viruses to abnormal cells that can develop into cancer. Among its most important defenses are specialized immune cells called T cells, which can recognize and destroy tumor cells.

However, these cancer-fighting cells depend on chemical signals to activate their destructive abilities. Small amounts of reactive oxygen species provide some of those signals, helping T cells switch into attack mode.

Researchers at the University of Cambridge in the United Kingdom and Oregon Health & Science University in the United States discovered that tumors can interfere with this process. By examining the fluid surrounding cells inside tumors grown in mice, they found that cancer cells create chemical conditions that effectively prevent nearby T cells from activating.

The key is a naturally occurring antioxidant protein called Peroxiredoxin 1 (PRDX1). Cancer cells release large quantities of this protein into their surroundings, where it removes the reactive oxygen species that T cells need to function. Without those activating signals, the immune cells become less effective at destroying cancer.

In effect, tumors use antioxidants as a chemical shield, weakening the immune response that would otherwise threaten their survival.

Removing Cancer's Antioxidant Shield Slows Tumor Growth

To investigate whether this defense mechanism could be disrupted, the researchers used CRISPR gene editing to modify cancer cells in mice. The edited cells could no longer produce PRDX1, allowing the team to examine what happened when tumors lost their ability to release the antioxidant protein.

The results were encouraging. Without PRDX1, immune cells became more active, and tumor growth was reduced. This suggested that interfering with the antioxidant protein could restore some of the immune system's ability to attack cancer.

The researchers then investigated whether human cancers use the same strategy. They examined existing data on proteins released by human cancer cell lines, studied patterns of gene activity in thousands of human tumors, and analyzed fluid collected from tumors surgically removed from patients.

All three lines of evidence supported the same conclusion. Human cancers also release PRDX1 into the surrounding environment, where it can eliminate the reactive oxygen species that cancer-fighting T cells rely on.

Dr. Xan Wesolowski, one of the lead authors from the University of Cambridge's Department of Pathology, explained why the discovery challenges conventional thinking about these molecules.

"We tend to think of reactive oxygen species purely as damaging byproducts of metabolism. But we are increasingly understanding they have important functions within cells, and T cells need them to activate. Our study develops this picture, revealing that tumors can exploit this very dependency to evade elimination."

A New Strategy for Making Cancer Immunotherapy More Effective

Cancer treatment has increasingly focused on helping the immune system recognize and eliminate malignant cells. These approaches, known as immunotherapies, have produced remarkable results for some patients, but many others experience little or no benefit.

The new research identifies a possible reason certain tumors can withstand immune attacks. By releasing PRDX1, cancer cells may suppress the very T cells that immunotherapies are designed to activate.

Importantly, the researchers found that preventing cancer cells from producing this antioxidant improved their response to immunotherapy in experimental models. Some tumors that had previously resisted treatment became responsive when the antioxidant defense was disrupted.

Professor Rahul Roychoudhuri, also from Cambridge's Department of Pathology, said the findings identify a promising target for future cancer treatments.

"We've found a new way by which cancers shut down the immune system. When we block this process, tumors that don't respond to some immunotherapies start responding to treatment. That tells us this is a pathway worth targeting therapeutically, and there are several ways we might be able to achieve this."

The discovery also raises the possibility of using a different type of chemical approach to strengthen the immune response.

Dr. Robert Eil from the School of Medicine at Oregon Health & Science University said: "Our study suggests a possible way to boost T cell immunotherapies. Rather than using antioxidants, it could be that prooxidants can kickstart the T cells into action against tumor cells."

Why the Findings Raise Questions About Antioxidant Supplements

Beyond their potential implications for cancer treatment, the results may help explain a longstanding puzzle involving antioxidant supplements.

Antioxidants have frequently been promoted for their ability to neutralize reactive oxygen species and protect cells from damage. Because these molecules can contribute to processes associated with cancer development, researchers have investigated whether taking antioxidant supplements might reduce cancer risk.

However, several large randomized clinical trials have failed to demonstrate such protection. In some cases, antioxidant supplementation has even been associated with worse outcomes.

The new findings suggest one possible explanation. Although reactive oxygen species can damage cells, they also help activate the immune defenses that fight cancer. Removing too many of these molecules could unintentionally interfere with the immune system's ability to recognize and destroy tumors.

This does not establish that antioxidant supplements generally promote cancer, but it highlights the importance of understanding how these molecules behave in different biological settings.

The researchers also emphasize that their experimental findings remain preclinical. Although they identified evidence of the same antioxidant mechanism in human cancers, the potential treatment strategies have not yet been established as safe or effective in patients.

People living with cancer should therefore not change their diets, supplement use, or medical treatments based on these findings without consulting a healthcare professional.

The research was largely supported by the Medical Research Council, the European Research Council, Wellcome, and the National Institutes of Health/National Cancer Institute.

UnitedHealth releases independent audit of its medical policy development practices" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Over the past year, UnitedHealth Group has conducted a series of independent reviews of its practices as part of a broader turnaround effort at the company.

Clinical evidence comes from nationally recognized authorities, and epidemiologists play a key role in the review process, per the report.

Medical policies are built "using systematic evidence review, evidence-based tools and industry best practices," and UnitedHealthcare is transparent about posting these policies and making updates.

"We will continue to subject key practices across UnitedHealth Group to independent review, share results publicly and make changes where needed," Hemsley wrote. "This work reflects our broader commitment to transparency, accountability and continuous improvement."

While the report concluded that overall processes in place at UnitedHealth were up to snuff, the consultants did offer multiple areas of improvement for the company, too. For instance, the analysts said that the team could improve its documentation practices, including how it details criteria for policy development.

Plus, the report suggests that UnitedHealthcare review how it documents vetting criteria for internal and external subject matter experts. The company could also do more to formally document training and education for members of its governance committee.

Medical policy documents can be lengthy and complex, so the consultants recommended the insurer consider developing a template that standardizes the written format for each policy, which would make it easier to understand. For example, the template could make it easier to connect the evidence summary to the coverage rationale.

"While these gaps do not diminish the overall strength of the program, addressing them would further enhance transparency and consistency and provide opportunities for continued refinement," the analysts wrote.

#5649. Christmas Lights Are Squeezing Homeowner Budgets More Than Ever, but There’s a Way To Pay Less and Still Be Festive

Christmas lights can bring holiday cheer to your home and neighborhood, but they don’t come cheap.

The U.S. Energy Information Administration projects the national average residential electricity price at about 18 cents per kilowatt-hour in 2026—roughly 37% higher than in 2020. This translates to the highest utility bills some homeowners have ever seen, made worse during times of the year when more electricity is needed.

According to a recent study by Payless Power, running a full display throughout December costs $15.36 with LED lights and $92.03 with incandescent lights at the typical electricity rate. That’s a $76.67 difference.

Where you live can affect your electric bill, too.

Hawaii is the most expensive state for holiday lighting, at $42.53 for a full LED display and $254.84 for the incandescent version. Rhode Island ($31.85), Massachusetts ($31.47), Maine ($30.98), and New Hampshire ($26.81) also make the list of the five most expensive states for a full LED display.

Meanwhile, homeowners in North Dakota ($11.25), Nebraska ($11.49), and Missouri ($12.02) pay the least.

The good news is there are ways to lower your electric bill without sacrificing curb appeal or holiday spirit, regardless of where you live. All it takes is a bit of planning and creativity.

A variety of factors are contributing to high electric bills these days.

“The grid is outdated. Infrastructure is old, and utility companies need to replace and upgrade equipment,” says Brandon Young, CEO of Payless Power in Fort Worth, TX.

Extreme weather plays a huge role as well, as the lines and equipment can’t always handle conditions like freezing temperatures and high winds.

Increased electricity demand adds to the problem.

“Demand is growing, and the grid can’t always keep up. Data centers and industrial use are large consumers of energy, and it takes a lot to power those facilities,” Young explains.

Fuel costs also fluctuate and affect how much it costs to generate electricity.

“Prices for residential customers in 2025 went up more than twice the rate of inflation,” says Young.

These high costs are particularly noticeable during the holiday season. Young points out that many homeowners often forget that a higher utility rate doesn’t take December off.

“The higher rate is there all year, and every kilowatt-hour is more costly. The oven and lights for holiday gatherings all cost more to use,” Young adds.

Fortunately, you don’t have to forgo Christmas lights altogether.

These tips can help you enjoy them while keeping your electricity costs in check.

While you don’t get to choose your utility rates, you do get to choose your light bulbs. And LEDs are much cheaper than incandescent bulbs.

“One hundred bulb C9s cost about $19.57 in December to run, and if they're swapped with LEDs, you’ll pay $2.80,” says Young.

LED lights aren’t hard to find either. You'll notice a variety of options at just about any home improvement store.

You don’t have to keep your lights on all day, every day.

Consider displaying them only from 5 to 10 p.m., for example. You could use a timer or smart plug that allows you to turn them on or off manually when you want to.

Also, if you plan to leave town, keep them off until you return.

Lighting every bush in your yard will cost you. Instead, be selective about where you hang lights.

Highlighting your front door, roof line, and a tree in your yard can make just as big of an impact.

If you have inflatables, there’s no reason to keep them on 24/7.

“Unplugging inflatables when you go to bed saves a few dollars. The cost to leave one up for the month is about $1.68, which is a lot to pay [compared with] a 100-bulb LED light strand at 14 cents,” says Young.

In addition, you don’t have to use inflatables for your home to stand out. A light projector can do the trick at a fraction of the cost.

The study says that a projector costs only 17 cents per month to run, compared to $1.68 for an inflatable.

#5648. A 24-hour fast triggers a surprising repair response in the gut

A 24-hour fast may help prepare the intestines to recover from radiation damage, but scientists have discovered that a particular gut bacterium plays a crucial role in making this possible. New preclinical research from The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center reveals how fasting and beneficial microbes work together to activate the body's natural tissue repair mechanisms.

The findings could eventually lead to new ways to protect healthy tissue during cancer treatment. By improving the intestine's ability to recover from radiation exposure, researchers hope to reduce serious side effects and potentially make radiation therapy safer and more effective.

Published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the study was co-led by Helen Piwnica-Worms, Ph.D., professor of Experimental Radiation Oncology, and Kunal Rai, Ph.D., professor of Genomic Medicine.

"Fasting helps prepare intestinal cells to respond more quickly and effectively after injury, almost like training the cells with an emergency preparedness plan," Piwnica-Worms said. "This study helps explain how that plan is organized and identifies a key bacterium involved in coordinating the response."

Why Radiation Therapy Can Damage the Intestines

Radiation therapy is widely used to treat cancers in the abdomen, including pancreatic, colorectal, and gynecologic cancers. Although radiation can destroy cancer cells, it can also harm nearby healthy tissue. The small intestine is particularly vulnerable because its delicate lining is highly sensitive to radiation exposure.

When this protective lining becomes damaged, patients may experience nausea, diarrhea, and infections. Severe injuries can cause life-threatening complications. These risks can also restrict the amount of radiation doctors can safely administer, potentially limiting treatment options.

Previous preclinical research from the Piwnica-Worms Laboratory showed that fasting before radiation exposure helped the intestines recover afterward. However, researchers had not fully determined why going without food produced this protective effect.

The latest study provides an important piece of that puzzle by identifying a specific gut bacterium and explaining how it helps intestinal cells prepare for injury.

Researchers found that 24 hours of fasting increased the abundance of a beneficial bacterium called Akkermansia muciniphila, also known as AKK, in the small intestine. This microbe produces a substance called propionate, which helps trigger changes inside intestinal cells that make them better prepared to regenerate following radiation damage.

Propionate works alongside other metabolic changes caused by fasting to modify proteins known as histones. These proteins serve as structures around which DNA is packaged inside cells. Small chemical markers added to histones can influence which genes become active without changing the underlying DNA sequence.

These modifications make portions of DNA more accessible, allowing cells to activate genes involved in tissue regeneration. During fasting, a population of intestinal cells carrying these repair programs becomes more abundant.

In effect, fasting helps prepare these cells with the biological instructions they will need if an injury occurs. When the intestines are subsequently exposed to radiation, the prepared cells can expand and help rebuild the damaged intestinal lining.

One Gut Bacterium Proves Essential for Recovery

To determine how important AKK was to this process, the researchers selectively removed the bacterium. Without it, fasting no longer produced the same regenerative benefits.

Even more revealing, the protective response returned only when the bacterium was restored in combination with fasting. This demonstrated that neither component alone was sufficient to reproduce the full effect observed in the study.

The results suggest that fasting does more than temporarily change the gut's metabolism. Together with AKK, it alters the activity of intestinal cells before radiation exposure, placing them in a state that supports more efficient recovery after damage occurs.

By uncovering this connection between nutrition, gut bacteria, and cellular regeneration, the researchers have identified a potential new way to strengthen the body's response to tissue injury. The discovery could be especially valuable for protecting healthy organs during cancer treatment.

Could Gut Bacteria Make Cancer Treatment Safer?

Although the results are promising, the research remains preclinical. Additional studies will be needed to determine whether the same protective mechanism operates in humans and whether it can safely improve outcomes for patients receiving radiation therapy.

One possibility is that the newly discovered pathway could be used to help other healthy tissues recover from cancer treatment. Researchers are particularly interested in tissues with rapidly dividing cells, including bone marrow, which can also suffer treatment-related damage.

If further investigations support the findings, clinical trials could eventually explore whether activating this repair mechanism benefits patients undergoing abdominal radiation therapy.

Importantly, the discovery may also provide ways to achieve these effects without requiring patients to fast. Treatments involving beneficial bacteria or the molecules they produce could potentially stimulate similar repair processes while avoiding the practical difficulties of food restriction during cancer care.

"Fasting is not always practical for cancer patients, and this work supports several other potential ways to enhance recovery after treatment," Rai said. "Whether through dietary interventions, targeted microbes or their metabolites, the goal is to help repair healthy tissue more effectively while patients receive the cancer therapies they need."

The research was funded by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) within the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the Cancer Prevention and Research Institute of Texas (CPRIT).

#5646. How Agents Can Chart a Course for No Buyer Remorse

The bidding war is over. Some of the decisions made are harder to undo. As an agent or broker, is it part of your professional obligation to discuss where the buyer might be in five years financially and family-wise? Probably, even if it might occasionally put them off a purchase.

A recent survey of 1,000 U.S. property owners found that 80% had at least one regret about their home, location or buying experience. Location bothered 45%, while 58% reported regrets about the home or homeownership itself.

For homeowners who bought during the pandemic frenzy, moving on can carry an added complication: the mortgage may be more attractive than the house.

A recent study in the Journal of Banking & Finance found that for every percentage-point increase between a homeowner’s fixed mortgage rate and current market rates, the probability of selling falls 18.1%. Researchers estimate mortgage lock-in was associated with 1.72 million fewer home sales between Q2 2022 and Q2 2024.

That pressure is particularly relevant now. The average 30-year mortgage rate reached 7.28% in early October, its highest level in nearly three years.

For Nick Nastos, a real estate broker and founder of Chicago’s Property Shop, that creates an unusual form of buyer’s remorse.

“You can regret the house and still have a mortgage you’d hate to give up,” he says. “That’s what makes these decisions difficult. Someone may know the home no longer fits their life, but replacing a 3% mortgage with today’s rate can completely change the math.”

Nastos gives five reasons a pandemic purchase may feel different now.

Nastos says regret alone should not determine whether someone sells.

“Start with what you would change about the house, then price out what changing homes would actually cost,” he says. “Sometimes the answer is to move. Sometimes that low mortgage makes improving the home you already own the better option.”

Suzy Minken, a real estate advisor with Compass working out of Northern Virginia, said looking toward the future while purchasing a house today is key to avoiding buyer remorse.

“It’s not something that is talked about enough,” she says. “I’ve even had buyers speak to my architect (relationships are key) while touring the house to see if they could do an addition. The architect did a review of the property and said it could be done. The buyers submitted an offer (multiple bid situation) and bought the house. They proceeded with a two-story addition before they moved into the house.”

Minken stresses that there is a need to distinguish between buyer’s remorse and the frustration of having fewer options than originally anticipated.

“Consider the young family who purchased a starter home with the intention of moving to a larger home in five years,” she explains. “Perhaps they’ve welcomed another child and need an additional bedroom. But with higher home prices and mortgage rates, the move-up home they envisioned may no longer be financially practical.

“In many ways, today’s move-up buyer has become today’s renovation buyer. Rather than moving to a larger home, homeowners are looking for ways to make their existing homes accommodate their changing needs.”

But what happens when renovation isn’t an option either?

“When buyers fall in love with a home, I encourage them to think about whether it’s already ‘maxed out’ or has room to grow with their changing needs,” says Minken. “Is there room to expand? Could an unfinished basement become additional living space? Is there flexibility in the floor plan to accommodate a growing family?

“I also encourage buyers to look beyond the house itself. Why are the current owners selling? Did they outgrow the home after having another child? Is there something about the layout or the property that made adapting it difficult? These questions can reveal important clues about how a home might serve its next owners.”

Minken encourages buyers to think beyond what they need today and consider how their needs might change over time. That includes family circumstances, the need for additional space and even commuting considerations if their employer requires them to spend more time in the office.

“We can’t predict changes in interest rates, home prices or family circumstances,” she says. “But we can ask the right questions before they make one of the largest financial decisions of their lives. Sometimes the regret isn’t buying the wrong home. It’s discovering that the next step, whether moving to a bigger house or renovating, is no longer within reach.”

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

Billionaire Larry Ellison recently spent nearly $10 million on eight homes for his staff in a gated South Florida community—but not everyone was thrilled about his buying spree.

Ellison, 82, co-founder of technology giant Oracle, purchased the properties in spring 2023 in Palm Meadows Estates, an upscale 288-home community in Boynton Beach, FL, known for its sprawling houses, manicured lawns, and lakefront views.

But the plan hit a roadblock when the neighborhood’s homeowners association adopted a new rule limiting owners to just five properties around the same time the deals were closing.

The amendment, obtained by Realtor.com®, was signed on May 30, 2023, and recorded with Palm Beach County on June 2, 2023—during the same period Ellison's eight purchases were finalized. All eight deals were closed between May and June 2023, according to property records.

However, the amendment appears to have come too late to stop the sales from closing, and property records show that a company associated with Ellison now owns the eight homes.

All eight homes were purchased for Ellison’s household staff, which included teachers, therapists, and chefs, according to his real estate agent Kimmie Cruz, who talked to CBS12 about how some of the deals were still in the process of closing when the HOA moved to limit the number of properties a single owner could acquire.

"They tried to stop it," Cruz said. "There were also some neighbors who felt that it was going to change the dynamic of the neighborhood."

The amendment to the HOA rules also requires a year of ownership before a property can be rented out, according to the document obtained by Realtor.com.

Attorneys became involved in the dispute, and all eight purchases ultimately closed.

The HOA did not respond to a request for comment from Realtor.com.

The identity of the buyer initially remained a mystery, with an LLC listed as the buyer on property records.

But Cruz later learned the purchases were being made for Ellison, who has a roughly $200 billion fortune. A year earlier, he had bought a $173 million oceanfront estate in nearby Manalapan.

Cruz, a local real estate agent with LuxeIQ who lives in the community, previously told The Wall Street Journal that she received an urgent call in March 2023 from another real estate agent about a buyer interested in purchasing as many as 10 homes.

The agent told Cruz that it would be “worth it” to arrange the last-minute showings, she recalled. A few days later, Ellison arrived to tour the homes and that night, Cruz received the first of the signed contracts for the houses.

Cruz said the homeowners walked away with sizable profits from the sales.

“Across the homes I sold, I secured sale prices averaging 20% above market value,” she said.

One couple, Paul and Yvonne Carozza, sold their three-bedroom, roughly 2,100-square-foot home to Ellison for $1.2 million, a home they paid $567,000 for in 2019, records show.

Ellison’s purchases highlight an emerging trend among the ultrawealthy who are buying properties to house staff who manage their multimillion-dollar estates on their behalf.

Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg has been buying up a number of homes in Palo Alto, CA, to create a family compound.

Wealthy newcomers to South Florida, including billionaires, tech executives, and hedge fund managers, have poured hundreds of millions of dollars into building out new private and charter schools for their children, according to the Journal.

Some, including Zuckerberg, Elon Musk, WeWork co-founder Adam Neumann, and real estate developer Jeff Greene, have even launched schools of their own.

#5643. For decades, we were told to avoid full-fat dairy. New research says otherwise

For years, people have been encouraged to choose low-fat or fat-free dairy products to protect their hearts and manage their weight. But growing scientific evidence suggests that full-fat dairy may not carry the health risks many have come to expect.

A new Canadian study led by University of Toronto professor Harvey Anderson adds to that evidence. Researchers found that adults who consumed three servings of full-fat dairy each day for 12 weeks did not experience harmful changes in body weight, body composition, energy metabolism, or blood cholesterol levels compared with participants following a diet containing little dairy.

Even more surprisingly, participants who consumed more dairy showed improvements in blood pressure and obtained greater amounts of several important nutrients.

The findings, published in The Journal of Nutrition, raise new questions about longstanding dietary recommendations and suggest that the health effects of dairy may be more complicated than its saturated fat content alone would indicate.

For decades, nutrition guidelines in Canada and many other countries have recommended choosing low-fat or fat-free milk, yogurt, and other dairy products. The main concern has been saturated fat, which can raise levels of LDL cholesterol in the blood.

Often called "bad" cholesterol, LDL can contribute to fatty deposits in the arteries. Over time, this buildup can increase the risk of heart attacks, strokes, and other cardiovascular problems.

Because full-fat dairy contains more saturated fat than reduced-fat alternatives, health authorities have traditionally encouraged people to limit their intake.

However, research examining what happens when people actually consume full-fat dairy has produced a more complicated picture.

Anderson, a professor of nutritional sciences at the University of Toronto's Temerty Faculty of Medicine, points out that numerous studies involving humans have failed to find a clear association between full-fat dairy consumption and poor health outcomes.

Other research has even identified potential protective effects. That includes a recent study led by Temerty Medicine professor Kozeta Milliku, which found an association between whole-fat milk consumption and a lower risk of childhood obesity.

These findings have prompted scientists to investigate whether dairy foods behave differently in the body than their individual nutrients might suggest.

What Happened When Adults Ate Full-Fat Dairy Every Day?

To explore the question, Anderson and his colleagues conducted a 12-week study involving 74 adults with overweight or obesity.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of three dietary approaches. The first group followed a calorie-restricted diet containing little dairy. The second consumed three daily servings of dairy while maintaining an energy-neutral diet, meaning their calorie intake was intended to match the energy their bodies used. The third also consumed three servings of dairy each day but otherwise ate without specific calorie restrictions.

All participants received guidance based on Canada's food guide, and the researchers supplied full-fat dairy products during the study.

At the end of 12 weeks, the team compared several measures of metabolic health, including body weight, body composition, and cholesterol levels.

The results challenged expectations. Participants who consumed three servings of dairy daily did not show meaningful differences in weight gain, body composition, or blood cholesterol compared with those who ate little dairy.

The higher-dairy groups also experienced improvements in blood pressure and consumed more calcium, protein, and vitamin D. These nutrients play essential roles in maintaining healthy bones, supporting muscle function, and regulating numerous processes throughout the body.

"Those that had three servings of dairy didn't have adverse levels of blood cholesterol or lipids or evidence of insulin resistance," says Anderson.

Blood lipids are fats and fat-like substances circulating in the bloodstream, including cholesterol and triglycerides. Insulin resistance occurs when the body's cells become less responsive to insulin, making it harder to regulate blood sugar and increasing the risk of type 2 diabetes.

Although the results are encouraging, the study was relatively small and lasted only three months. Longer and larger studies are needed to determine whether the findings translate into lasting health benefits or changes in cardiovascular disease risk.

Why might full-fat dairy have different health effects than researchers would predict from its saturated fat content?

One possible explanation is the dairy matrix hypothesis, an idea that emphasizes how the physical structure of food influences the way the body processes its nutrients.

Rather than treating milk, cheese, or yogurt as simple collections of fat, protein, vitamins, and minerals, this theory considers how those components interact within the food itself.

"With dairy products, it's got two proteins -- casein and whey -- that are bound together with fat and with nutrients mixed in," says Anderson.

Casein and whey are the two major types of protein found in milk. Both provide amino acids that the body uses to build and maintain tissues, but they are digested and absorbed at different rates.

According to Anderson, the complex arrangement of proteins, fats, and other nutrients in dairy products can help regulate how quickly those nutrients are released during digestion.

This means the body's response to eating a whole dairy food may differ from its response to consuming an equivalent amount of saturated fat on its own.

The broader implication is that a food's health effects cannot always be predicted by examining a single ingredient. Its structure, nutritional composition, and interactions among nutrients may all matter.

Why the Findings Could Be Important for Older Adults

The researchers believe these results could be particularly relevant for older people, who often need to obtain sufficient protein and essential nutrients while consuming fewer calories.

As people age, their overall energy requirements frequently decrease. However, maintaining muscle mass, bone strength, and other important bodily functions still requires adequate nutrition.

That can make it difficult to meet nutritional needs, particularly for people with smaller appetites.

Anderson explains that dairy products offer a familiar, convenient source of concentrated nutrition. They provide protein, calcium, and other nutrients in foods that many older adults already enjoy and regularly consume.

The new findings suggest that including full-fat dairy in a balanced diet may help people meet these nutritional requirements without necessarily worsening cholesterol levels or markers associated with diabetes risk.

However, the study did not directly establish whether long-term consumption prevents or increases diabetes, heart disease, or other chronic conditions.

Rethinking Nutrition Advice Beyond Individual Nutrients

Beyond the debate over dairy fat, the research highlights a broader challenge in nutrition science: judging the health effects of entire foods rather than focusing exclusively on individual nutrients.

Traditional dietary advice has often emphasized reducing specific components, such as saturated fat. Although these recommendations are grounded in evidence about cardiovascular risk, researchers increasingly recognize that different foods containing the same nutrients may not have identical effects on health.

The University of Toronto findings contribute to this discussion by showing that full-fat dairy can be incorporated into certain diets without the unfavorable short-term metabolic changes that might be expected from its saturated fat content.

That does not mean saturated fat is harmless or that everyone should switch to full-fat dairy. Instead, it suggests that the overall food, its nutritional structure, and the broader dietary pattern deserve consideration.

For people trying to navigate changing nutrition recommendations and conflicting health messages, Anderson favors a practical approach rather than complicated dietary rules.

"Keep it simple, eat a variety of foods and not too much of anything."

#5642. This New Water Heater Gadget Could Turn Your Hot Showers Into Bitcoin. But Is It Worth It?

Your water heater already uses electricity to keep the showers hot and dishes clean. But what if it could also earn you a little money at the same time?

That's the idea behind Bitwater, an unusual new home appliance from technology company Heatbit that combines an electric water heater's heating element with a bitcoin mining computer.

Rather than purchasing an entirely new water heater, homeowners can install the device inside an existing electric tank, replacing a conventional heating element with one powered by computer chips that generate heat while mining cryptocurrency.

"We were actually looking for areas where electricity is turned into heat, where it's not seasonal," Alex Busarov, Heatbit's founder, told Realtor.com® in a phone interview. The company had already developed bitcoin-mining space heaters, he explained, but household water heating offered an opportunity to put the technology to work year-round.

It's an eye-catching proposition at a time when homeowners are looking for ways to offset utility bills. But can mining bitcoin really make heating water more affordable?

At first glance, Bitwater resembles an oversized heating element, the metal component inside an electric water heater that warms the water.

But instead of a traditional electrical resistance wire, it contains specialized computer chips that perform the calculations involved in bitcoin mining.

But instead of a traditional electrical resistance wire, it contains specialized computer chips that perform the calculations involved in bitcoin mining.

Those chips produce heat as they work. Bitwater transfers that heat into the surrounding water, cooling the computer hardware while heating the tank.

Unlike space heating, which is largely unnecessary during the warmer months, households need hot water throughout the year. That makes a water heater a potentially more practical home for computing equipment that generates heat.

The device replaces only the lower heating element in a conventional electric water heater. The upper element remains in place to provide additional heating when demand increases.

According to Busarov, Bitwater typically operates at approximately 400 to 600 watts, heating water more gradually than a conventional element that might draw several thousand watts for a shorter period.

Busarov said the device automatically stops mining when the water reaches its target temperature. He estimated that the mining hardware operates approximately 80% of the time, although actual utilization would depend on household demand for hot water.

Bitwater can reportedly generate up to 34 terahashes per second, a measure of the computing power used to mine bitcoin, which Busarov estimated could translate to roughly $30 per month in cryptocurrency under current mining conditions.

That would represent approximately $360 annually, although actual earnings depend on bitcoin prices, mining difficulty, operating time, and other factors.

At that rate, a roughly $900 device would require about 2.5 years to recover its purchase price, even before accounting for installation costs, mining fees, maintenance, or changes in cryptocurrency earnings.

There is an important distinction, however, between generating bitcoin revenue and saving energy. Bitwater doesn't eliminate the electricity needed to heat water. Instead, the company argues that the electricity can perform two useful jobs: powering a computer and producing household hot water.

In principle, that gives the homeowner some cryptocurrency in exchange for electricity that would otherwise have gone toward conventional resistance heating.

Busarov says the mining operation shuts down when the tank reaches its desired temperature, so the device isn't intended to consume additional electricity solely to mine bitcoin. It prioritizes heating water, with cryptocurrency mining as a secondary function.

At an illustrative electricity rate of 18 cents per kilowatt-hour, operating a 600-watt device continuously would consume about $78 in electricity each month. Bitwater is not designed to operate continuously, however, and that electricity would not necessarily represent an additional expense if the heat replaces what a conventional electric heating element would otherwise produce.

Heatbit's projected earnings are therefore not the same as guaranteed savings on a utility bill. The calculation depends on how much the device operates and how much cryptocurrency it actually generates.

Heatbit designed Bitwater as a retrofit for conventional electric tank water heaters rather than a complete replacement system.

The device is intended to fit compatible residential tanks equipped with standard screw-in heating elements.

Busarov said installation is designed to be comparable to replacing an ordinary water heater element.

"We really built it for DIY installation," he said.

That doesn't necessarily mean every homeowner should attempt it.

Working on a water heater involves electricity, pressurized water, and potential flooding hazards. Homeowners unfamiliar with those systems should use a qualified professional and check local code requirements.

Heatbit promotes several safety and maintenance features, including leak protection, overheating safeguards, and programmed high-temperature cycles intended to limit the growth of Legionella bacteria.

Busarov said protecting against leaks was a significant part of developing the physical product.

He also described a system that can periodically raise water temperatures to combat bacterial growth without maintaining those higher temperatures continuously.

The company says Bitwater also incorporates a powered anode rod designed to protect the tank against corrosion and anti-limescale technology intended to reduce mineral buildup. Both corrosion and mineral deposits can contribute to water heater maintenance problems, and Busarov saw these features as selling points even for homeowners who aren't interested in cryptocurrency.

However, homeowners should verify that the specific product they receive has the appropriate electrical and plumbing certifications, and that its temperature controls and other protective features operate as advertised.

Independent, long-term reliability data will be especially important as the technology moves beyond its initial testing phase.

For homeowners primarily interested in reducing utility bills, Bitwater faces an established competitor: the heat-pump water heater.

Unlike conventional resistance heaters, heat-pump models use electricity to move heat from the surrounding air into a water tank.

According to Energy Star, an efficient heat-pump water heater can save a four-person household approximately $550 per year compared with a standard electric water heater.

Those savings come from reducing energy consumption rather than producing a separate stream of income.

Bitwater takes a fundamentally different approach. It aims to create financial value from electricity already being used for heating.

That may appeal to homeowners who already have a functional electric water heater and don't want to replace the entire appliance.

But a homeowner considering a major water-heating upgrade should compare installation costs, electricity consumption, maintenance, and expected savings before choosing one technology over another.

For all its ingenuity, Bitwater still faces some crucial, fundamental questions—like does adding cryptocurrency mining to an everyday appliance actually save homeowners enough money to justify the investment?

Regarding the latter, Heatbit claims it tested the system in households in Miami and Rochester, NY, during January, according to Busarov. Both locations maintained adequate hot water despite their dramatically different winter climates, according to the findings.

"People didn't really notice the difference," he said.

Realtor.com asked Heatbit to arrange interviews with the homeowners who tested the devices to independently assess their experiences, but those interviews had not been arranged by publication deadline.

While the concept has generated enthusiasm among cryptocurrency enthusiasts online, others questioned whether the device's mining revenue could justify its upfront cost, particularly if its computing performance declines as the water in the tank heats up.

There is also the question of whether homeowners want to become cryptocurrency miners, even on a small scale.

Bitcoin's value can fluctuate dramatically, and mining profitability depends on competition from other miners around the world. A device generating $30 in one month might earn considerably less in another.

There are also questions about actual mining utilization. Busarov estimated the device can mine approximately 80% of the time, but that figure has not been independently verified. Because the mining operation shuts down when the water reaches its target temperature, households using less hot water may have fewer opportunities to generate cryptocurrency.

Long-term maintenance presents another uncertainty. A conventional heating element is relatively simple and inexpensive to replace, while Bitwater introduces computer chips, electronic controls, and other components into an appliance that homeowners generally expect to operate for years with little attention.

And while the company insists the early household tests suggest the product can provide adequate hot water, the item is still in pre-order phase right now with the first units slotted to ship in the first quarter, so there is no independent evidence of its performance and durability, and real-world earnings remains limited.

Taken together, those uncertainties make Bitwater an intriguing proposition, but not yet a proven way to reduce household expenses.
