#5603. Alix Earle Opens the Doors to Family’s $4.1 Million New Jersey Mansion in Season 2 of Drama-Filled Netflix Series

Social media sensation Alix Earle is preparing to once again welcome fans into her family's sprawling New Jersey mansion, this time in the second season of her hit Netflix series "Earle Meets World."

Earle, 25, initially rose to stardom on TikTok, where she amassed a legion of followers with her candid "get ready with me videos," which were filmed inside her student housing at the University of Miami.

After graduating, her career continued to go from strength to strength—while the bubbly blonde expanded her work from short-form video to podcasts, drinks brands, and numerous ad campaigns.

Then, she took her success to "next phase" by partnering with Netflix to showcase all of the most "vulnerable," "hard," and "fun" moments in her life, many of which she experiences with her family by her side in the series, which hit the streaming giant on Sept. 4.

Now, the internet star has revealed that fans will get an even closer into her life away from the camera's during the second season of the show, which Earle announced in a joint Instagram video with Netflix.

In the clip, Earle can be seen strutting into the Netflix office while on the phone with her dad.

"Okay dad, when I said, 'What's the worst that could happen?' I didn't think it would be that bad. I know they aren't talking. I'm telling you, we have to just show it all, it will be fine," she said on the call before dumping a box of football-themed items onto the floor.

"Earle Meets World is coming back for season two, I'm just making myself at home," she added while lounging in the office.

In a press release shared by Netflix, Earle revealed, “Since Season 1 aired, some s— has hit the fan. But hey, that makes for a good Season 2. I couldn't be more excited to be back and get the cameras rolling. Lots to catch up on and share with our Netflix family!”

Meanwhile, Vice President of nonfiction series, Brandon Riegg, added, “Our goal with Earle Meets World was authenticity and going deeper than social media ever could. We’re thrilled that viewers connected with that and grateful to Alix for trusting us to tell her story. We’re excited to welcome her and her family back for Season 2!”

The influencer is once again handing over control of the cameras to Netflix producers, who will continue to focus their lenses on Earle and her family, including her TikTok star sister Ashtin, her mom, Alisa, her father, Thomas "TJ," her stepmother, Ashley Dupré, and her younger half-siblings, Izabel, Penelope, and Thomas.

Those who follow Earle's content will no doubt already be familiar with many of these characters, who regularly feature in the TikTok star's videos, particularly when she returns home to Red Bank, NJ, to spend time with her loved ones.

While the online starlet has continued to reside in Miami since graduating, while also taking on a property in Los Angeles, where she regularly travels for work, her family is largely located in and around New Jersey, where TJ and Ashley live in a sprawling mansion that they share with their three youngest children.

Records show that the couple, who wed in 2013, purchased the enormous property in 2013 for $2.25 million, scoring quite the deal on the home, which had previously been listed for $3.35 million. It is currently estimated to be worth $4.1 million, according to Realtor.com®.

However, the family appears to have made numerous upgrades to the dwelling in the six years since they bought it, with Earle's videos showcasing a much more modern and elegant interior than featured in the original listing images.

Meanwhile, records show that Earle's mother, Alisa, resides in a newly-built dwelling in nearby Point Pleasant.

When they are in New Jersey, the TikTok star and her sister, Ashtin, who resides in New York City, split their time between the two dwellings and it is understood that both parents will feature heavily in the Netflix series.

Earle announced the news of the first season of the show via a joint Instagram post with Netflix, in which she was filmed on the phone with her dad—who serves as her manager—outside of the Netflix offices.

In the clip, she tells her dad that things will be "fine," adding, "Dad, it's gonna be fun! It's gonna be fine. What's the worst that can happen?"

The video was captioned, "From your FYP to your TV: Alix Earle, her family, and friends will star in an unscripted series dropping later this year on Netflix."

In a press release shared by the streaming giant, the TikTok star confessed that partnering with Netflix felt "unreal," adding that she was excited to show fans her life behind the scenes.

"It honestly feels unreal to be partnering with Netflix, and I’m so excited to be creating this show with them," she shared. "I’ve shared my life for years through my own camera, but this felt like the next phase because it’s a chance to go deeper.

"Not just the highlights, but the real moments, too. The vulnerable ones, the hard ones, and the fun, chaotic ones in between. It’s the same authenticity people know me for, but now with a different lens."

The social media mogul revealed that she was most "excited" for her fans to see her "fun" and "modern family."

"People either think we’re insane or they’re like, wait, this is exactly like my life. And honestly, both are true. I’m excited for fans to experience the full picture as it happens. The chaos, the emotional moments, the stressful parts, and all the little things in between that you don’t always see online," she added.

She admitted that the process was a "little scary," adding, "I’m so used to being in control of what I share and what I keep private, so having cameras around in moments I normally wouldn’t post is definitely an adjustment.

"But the real, human moments are what connected me to my audience in the first place. If letting people in even more makes someone feel less alone, or even just makes them laugh, then it’s worth it."

Although she is hesitant to give up power over he content, Earle noted that she finds comfort in the relationship she has with her followers.

"My relationship with my followers has always felt really personal because I’ve been sharing my life the same way I would with my best friends. With this show, I want it to feel like you’re even more in it with me, in a way that’s real and not curated.

"The goal is not to be someone different on camera. It’s to show more of who I already am, and who my family really is. The fun, the messy, the growth, while capturing the way we help each other through it all," Earle added.

The news of her family's reality TV show comes a mere month after her and Houston Texans player Braxton Berrios called it quits after two years of dating.

Earle and Berrios, 30, began dating in February 2023 but kept their romance coy on social media, with the TikTok tycoon referring to her now-ex beau simply as "NFL man," when she started discussing their relationship with her followers.

They then took things to the next level in April, when Earle revealed to her followers that she had moved out of her rented Florida condo and into her boyfriend's $2.7 million Miami home, just as former Miami Dolphins star Berrios relocated to Texas, where he now plays for the Houston Texans.

Meanwhile, Earle moved to Los Angeles temporarily earlier this year, when she landed a role on "Dancing With the Stars," ultimately finishing in second place alongside professional dance partner, Val Chmerkovskiy.

Throughout her time on the competition, Berrios failed to make a single in-person appearance in the ballroom—however, Earle insisted to fans that his absence was the result of his intense football schedule.

In December, Earle admitted to fans that they had indeed split, insisting that there was no bad blood between them.

#5602. Meritage, PulteGroup Honor Veterans With Mortgage-Free Homes

Two national home builders are honoring military veterans and their families this fall with the gift of mortgage-free homeownership.

Meritage Homes, through its partnership with Operation Homefront, welcomed U.S. Navy veteran Maggie Coleman and her family to a new home in Gulfport, Mississippi, on Veterans Day. Meanwhile, PulteGroup’s Built to Honor program and Building Homes for Heroes will present mortgage-free homes to U.S. Army veterans Carson Shaw and Ryan Heard and their families ahead of Thanksgiving.

The initiatives provide the families with greater housing stability while building on both companies’ long-standing efforts to support military families.

Meritage Homes and Operation Homefront presented Coleman and her two children with the keys to a new, mortgage-free home during a Veterans Day ceremony Nov. 11.

The approximately 2,000-square-foot, four-bedroom, three-bath home is located in Meritage’s Hidden Trails community in Gulfport, Mississippi. The donation marks the 23rd home Meritage has donated to a military family.

Coleman served 13 years in the Navy, including deployments to Italy and Kuwait. The home allows her family to put down permanent roots in her home state of Mississippi.

“I want to give my children everything I didn’t have,” Coleman said. “I want this home to be a place where my kids and I can share stories and make memories.”

“We’re proud to help welcome the Coleman family home to Gulfport,” Meritage Homes CEO Phillippe Lord said. “We recognize the service and sacrifices she and her family have made, and we’re honored to share in this special moment with them.”

The home was provided through Operation Homefront’s Permanent Homes for Veterans program, which works to help military families achieve long-term stability through mortgage-free housing and other support.

PulteGroup will continue the season of giving Nov. 18, when its Built to Honor program and Building Homes for Heroes present the keys to two mortgage-free homes at the builder’s Spencer Glen community in Riverview, Florida.

The homes will go to U.S. Army Sergeant Carson Shaw and his partner, Annalisa, and Purple Heart recipient U.S. Army Specialist Ryan Heard, his partner, Danielle, and their two children.

Shaw joined the Army in 2019 at age 18 and completed deployments to Iraq and Syria and to Africa. A line-of-duty motor vehicle accident in 2024 left him paralyzed from the waist down. He also lives with the effects of a traumatic brain injury and bilateral hearing loss.

Since his injury, Shaw has participated in six adaptive sports at the Warrior Games and plays wheelchair basketball with the Tampa Strong Dogs. His new accessible home will provide a stable foundation as he pursues a bachelor’s degree in finance and economics.

Heard enlisted in the Army in 2007 and completed two deployments to Iraq and one to Afghanistan. During his 2013 deployment to Afghanistan, an improvised explosive device detonated beneath Heard and three fellow soldiers. Despite sustaining a severe traumatic brain injury, Heard helped treat wounded soldiers and coordinate a medical evacuation before losing consciousness, according to the release.

Heard, who received a Purple Heart, also lives with PTSD, chronic migraines, hearing loss, and chronic pain. His new home will provide him and his family with a mortgage-free place to put down roots.

The two homes continue a significant milestone for PulteGroup’s Built to Honor program. Since its launch in 2013, PulteGroup has built and donated more than 100 mortgage-free homes valued at over $40 million to veterans and their families.

Building Homes for Heroes is also celebrating its 20th anniversary and expects to reach its milestone 500th home in December.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5601. Square takes Squaremates AI agent out of beta and opens up to sellers’ own AI software

Block Inc.-owned commerce platform Square today made its Squaremates artificial intelligence business agent generally available to sellers in the U.S., after the agent entered open beta in April under the name Managerbot.

For sellers who would rather stay in the AI software they already use, Square is also offering a new command-line tool and an updated Model Context Protocol server.

Running a business is “an endless string of judgment calls that are all on the owner,” said Willem Avé, global head of intelligence at Square. “We built Squaremates to help share that load,” he said.

Each seller’s agent now runs in its own secure workspace with access to cloud compute. Square said that gives it room for longer jobs. A seller could ask it to find customers who’ve lapsed over a given stretch of sales, for instance, and have it draft a discount to win them back.

A beta feature lets Squaremates build restocking orders directly on a supplier’s website, and the seller places them from there. Email access for its daily briefing is coming soon.

Fraser Thompson, who leads strategy and operations at Los Angeles-based Burgers Never Say Die LLC, put Squaremates to work on the restaurant’s house-made cheese sauce. “I dip my fries in it, I dunk my burger in it,” he said. “So I’m thinking, how are we not selling more of this stuff?”

Digging into attachment rates and customer segments showed that “our OGs, the regulars who’ve been with us since day one, love it.” The restaurant started promoting it on social media with what Thompson called “silly posts,” and he said that a few months later “we’d 12x’d our cheese sauce.”

“A lot of sellers already have an AI tool they like working in,” Avé said. The updated server, Square MCP, lets a third-party assistant answer questions about the business and make changes once the account is connected. Square CLI is aimed at sellers and developers who want to script or build on top of their accounts, and it gives their own tools and agents access to Square’s application programming interfaces.

Squaremates Apps are custom applications a seller writes with an AI coding tool and the CLI, which Square then hosts with a live connection to the seller’s business. Splitting cash tips by hours worked is one of the uses Square suggests.

Donnie McClanahan, who has four cafes around Knoxville, Tennessee, built a labor board app with the CLI and an AI coding agent. It pulls schedules and timecards from every location onto one screen. A lot of his mornings used to go to “playing catch-up just figuring out who’s where,” he said.

Sellers can try the tools at the Squaremates Tour, a run of in-person events Square kicked off recently. Apart from the features still in beta or coming soon, everything announced today is available to U.S. sellers at no additional cost. Squaremates itself is not yet available to sellers on Square’s Multi-Account Suite.

#5599. Mortgage Rates Fall for Fourth Straight Week Despite Looming Fed Hike

Mortgage rates continued their slow retreat for a fourth consecutive week, mirroring the trajectory of bond yields, although this week's hotter-than-expected inflation print suggests the relief will be short-lived.

The average rate on 30-year fixed home loans decreased to 7.11% for the week ending Nov. 12, down 7 basis points from 7.18% the week before, according to Freddie Mac. For perspective, rates averaged 6.24% one year ago.

"Mortgage rates dropped to their lowest level in seven weeks, a welcome development that gives borrowers greater flexibility as they navigate the current housing market," says Sam Khater, Freddie Mac's chief economist.

A month of falling mortgage rates comes as welcome news for homebuyers, though Realtor.com® senior economist Jiayi Xu warns that a reversal could come as soon as next week.

The stronger-than-forecast October jobs report showed the labor market holding up well, clearing the way for the Federal Reserve's next federal funds rate hike as part of its mandate to curb inflation.

Fed Gov. Christopher Waller warned this week that a larger 50-basis-point increase should be considered in December’s Federal Open Market Committee meeting if inflation remains hot.

Shortly after Waller's warning, the October consumer price index report exceeded economists' expectations, pushing the 10-year Treasury yield toward 5%.

A December hike is now essentially priced in, with odds of a 25-basis-point increase topping 93%, according to CME FedWatch. The odds of another quarter-percentage-point hike in January 2027 currently stand at 67%.

"The debate is no longer if the Fed hikes, but how far and how fast," says Xu.

Today's homebuyers find themselves squeezed by both high mortgage rates and high inflation, and Xu contends that inflation is the bigger long-term problem.

"High rates raise monthly payments and shrink the loan a buyer can qualify for, and the recent pullback in pending sales shows how sensitive buyers are," notes the economist. "But persistent high inflation is what keeps the Fed hiking and rates elevated."

Crucially, inflation also erodes households' purchasing power, especially when wages lag consumer prices.

In October, existing-home sales dropped to their lowest level since August 2010, according to the latest data  from the National Association of Realtors®.

In this economic environment, first-time buyers are hit the hardest because they have no existing equity to use as a cushion, forcing them to save toward a down payment from already stretched budgets.

"Even if rates ease, living costs rising faster than pay will keep weighing on demand for years," says Xu.

Sellers have responded to cooling buyer demand by pulling back. This week, new listing activity fell 10.3% year over year after six weeks of more incremental declines, according to the latest weekly Realtor.com housing trends report.

"Sellers are discouraged because of how disengaged buyers are," says Realtor.com senior economist Hannah Jones. "The prices buyers are open to are less appealing to sellers than they were when mortgage rates were lower."

Your credit score plays a role when you apply for a mortgage. A credit score will determine whether you qualify for a mortgage and the interest rate you'll receive. The higher the credit score, the lower the interest rate you'll qualify for.

The credit score you need will vary depending on the type of loan. A score of 620 is a "fair" rating. However, people applying for a Federal Housing Administration loan might be able to get approved with a credit score of 500, which is considered a low score.

Homebuyers with credit scores of 740 or higher are typically considered to be in very good standing and can usually qualify for better rates, which can reduce monthly payments.

#5598. ServiceNow launches AI-powered engine to accelerate migrations from CRM rivals

ServiceNow Inc. is bidding to steal business from other customer relationship management vendors with an artificial intelligence-powered engine that it says can reduce enterprise CRM implementations from months to weeks.

The new Autonomous CRM Engine uses AI to analyze existing CRM environments, recommend business process improvements and automate deployment of redesigned workflows on ServiceNow’s platform.

The offering represents a competitive challenge to established CRM providers such as Salesforce Inc. and Microsoft Corp. by potentially lowering the switching costs that help vendors retain customers. The initial rollout targets only Salesforce installations, and others are planned.

The announcement comes amid growing concern about the costs and limitations of aging CRM systems. Gartner Inc. last year warned that legacy CRM platforms can create hidden maintenance expenses, integration dependencies and security risks that impede modernization. The researcher predicts that by 2028, most enterprises will identify outdated CRM systems as an obstacle to effectively using AI.

Gartner recommends that organizations evaluate technical debt, integration dependencies, data quality and the full cost of maintaining legacy CRM systems before deciding whether to modernize or replace them.

The discovery process is one of the most time-consuming aspects of CRM modernization, said Terence Chesire, group vice president of CRM and industry workflows at ServiceNow. Organizations typically must interview employees across departments and geographies to understand how sales and service processes operate.

“We’re able to collapse that into literally days where we show them how all their sales processes occur by product line,” he said.

Autonomous CRM Engine uses metadata application programming interfaces to examine business objects, configuration settings, custom scripts and workflows. It organizes that information into a graph database and applies AI to reconstruct how activities such as sales approvals, customer escalations and service requests actually function.

ServiceNow claims the analysis can expose discrepancies between documented procedures and everyday practices, including approval steps employees routinely bypass.

Beyond transferring existing processes to a new platform, ServiceNow uses the discovery information to recommend redesigned workflows based on industry practices. Business leaders can examine proposed changes in a visual workspace and modify processes to accommodate unique business characteristics. Once approved, changes can be deployed directly into ServiceNow’s CRM environment.

Chesire acknowledged that automation doesn’t eliminate difficult organizational decisions or integration challenges. “The parts that potentially get extended are all those linkages to other systems because we always land inside a heterogeneous environment,” he said.

ServiceNow addresses those dependencies through its Workflow Data Fabric, which provides access to external information without the need to move or copy it. Its integration capabilities also extend to older applications through robotic process automation.

Gartner cautions that CRM modernization projects must account for hidden application dependencies, regulatory data-retention requirements and business processes that may rely on retired systems. It also recommends establishing clear data ownership and governance policies before making changes.

The research firm suggests measuring modernization success through operational improvements rather than retired applications. It suggests performance targets such as annual operating cost reductions of at least 20%, retention of 95% of historical data in searchable archives and a 35% reduction in duplicate or inconsistent records.

Chesire acknowledged that ServiceNow hasn’t conducted comparative productivity studies against competing CRM platforms, although the company demonstrates its technology to prospects using their own business processes and data. The firm cited several customer examples to demonstrate the potential benefits of consolidating customer operations.

Germany soccer league Bundesliga-Gruppe GmbH consolidated fan services from seven digital channels onto ServiceNow in about a month and now resolves 89% of fan inquiries on first contact, according to ServiceNow. Bell Canada connected 26 applications and 8,800 data silos to one platform to support 12,000 field employees, while Everpure Inc. eliminated 13 legacy systems and now resolves 72% of customer issues before they’re reported.

Chesire said AI adoption is increasing pressure to modernize systems whose business logic is buried in custom code. ServiceNow plans to extend Autonomous CRM Engine’s capabilities to continuously monitor configurations and eventually improve CRM operations autonomously.

The engine is available now, with additional capabilities planned for 2027.

ServiceNow said its CRM and Industry Workflows business has surpassed $2 billion in annual contract value. Its CRM net new annual contract value tripled both sequentially and year-over-year in the third quarter.

#5597. Housing Starts Pull Back, but Top Markets Hold Their Ground

Zonda’s third quarter 2026 data shows housing starts over the past four quarters declined 10% from the same period a year ago. More specifically, 22 of the top 25 housing production markets posted year-over-year declines, pointing to a broad-based slowdown. However, the national slowdown can translate into very different competitive conditions depending on geography.

Sarasota was the clear outlier, with starts rising 20% year over year to 9,691 during the four quarters through Q3 2026. Chicago also managed growth, increasing 1% year over year to 7,680 starts, while Boise was effectively flat at 7,303.

At the other end of the spectrum, Las Vegas and Provo posted the largest declines among the top 25 markets, with starts falling 22% year over year in each. Riverside/San Bernardino followed closely with a 21% decline. Washington, D.C., Nashville, Raleigh, and Jacksonville were also among the markets recording double-digit contractions.

Despite declining activity, Dallas and Houston continue to operate on a different scale from the rest of the country.

Dallas ranked first with 37,497 starts over the past four quarters, down 10% year over year. Houston followed with 34,996, down 8% year over year. The two metros operate in a league of their own, each producing more than twice as many starts as any individual market elsewhere in the top 25.

Phoenix and San Antonio were the only other markets to top 15,000 starts, at 16,770 and 15,531, respectively. The rankings also point to relative stability at the top. Every market in the top 10 retained its position from the previous quarter, even as housing production softened nationally.

For industry professionals planning for 2027, the numbers reinforce the importance of looking beyond national trends. The size and direction of the housing adjustment vary substantially by market. Production is still highly concentrated in the Sun Belt metros, but growth in markets like Sarasota and Chicago shows that opportunities remain even against a weaker national backdrop.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth research reports published in Zonda’s National Outlook subscription.

Sean Fergus, Vice President of economic research at Zonda, leads the published research team. Fergus has 20 years of expertise in economic research, market studies, and financial analysis.

#5596. Jenny McCarthy Reveals She and Donnie Wahlberg Have Disposed of ’30 Years of Clothes’ and ‘All’ of Their Furniture After Mold Poisoning Diagnosis

Jenny McCarthy is still dealing with the fallout from her mold and mycotoxin poisoning diagnosis.

The actress had recently shared that she’s been living in a tent in her yard as she continues to “detox,” and during the Nov. 10 episode of her podcast, “The Jenny McCarthy Wahlberg Show,” she revealed some of the additional steps she’s taken to work toward a solution.

McCarthy, 54, explained that she recently had to persuade her husband, Donnie Wahlberg, to say “bye-bye” to his clothing “and also furniture” after the couple went through the costly experience of remediating their home.

“We left all of our furniture behind,” she said, adding that she believes her mold poisoning came from the makeup and dressing room at her workplace. “I didn’t want to risk anything.”

The “Masked Singer” judge went on to explain that she “wound up throwing everything away” and has been purchasing inexpensive items from TikTok shop to replace her wardrobe.

McCarthy and her podcast guest, functional medicine physician Amy Myers—who has also dealt with a mold poisoning diagnosis—commiserated on how challenging it can be to spend money on clothing and household items after going through the costly process of remediating a home.

“I’m afraid to spend money on clothes anymore because I had to give everything away. And I’m like, that’s 30 years of clothes, of red carpet events, and memories,” said McCarthy.

Myers said that following her own treatment, she spent four years working with an architect, builders, and engineers to construct a “forever home” where she would “never get sick.”

The Santa Fe, NM, home was constructed using pumice-crete, steel, and glass, but after just six months, Myers discovered that it had also developed mold spores after an incorrectly installed dryer vent was affected by water condensation.

The doctor was then advised to enter another remediation process.

McCarthy has previously opened up about the “mold protocol” she embarked on in January 2025, which involved a routine of vitamins and various treatments.

“Remediation costs are so high because it takes a specialist to be able to move the mold without ruining your entire house,” she said on the Oct. 28 episode of her podcast. Following remediation, she hired contractors to “come in and rebuild” the home.

“We remediated and because I am paranoid now about basically sleeping anywhere, I live in a tent. And I’m not even joking,” she said.

Adding that she feels “a little bit crazy sometimes” and has a “paranoid” state of mind, McCarthy said the situation has been “really, really hard.” Wahlberg, 57, has not been living in the tent with her.

“Donnie is working in Canada, and he is safe inside of a building,” she said. “Does he think I’m crazy? Yes. But he completely understands it.”

After nearly two years of work to move past the diagnosis, McCarthy and Wahlberg have considered relocating.

“I am so paranoid that I’ve even talked to Donnie about moving out of the Midwest, where it’s humid, and going to a dry location like Vegas or Arizona or something, because my body just can’t detox mold very well,” she said.

While it appears that the tent McCarthy is residing in is located in California, it’s unclear whether the home she had remediated is the St. Charles, IL, residence she and Wahlberg listed for $2,799,000 in September of this year.

In a recent Instagram comment, McCarthy indicated that the couple were “going to Vegas. Not Cali.” following the listing of their longtime home.

The couple have owned the property for over a decade, purchasing it for $1.1 million in 2015.

“This isn’t an extravagant home, but there’s no greater symbol of our love for each other than this house and how much love has gone into it,” Wahlberg told People magazine of the dwelling in 2019.

The four-bedroom, 5.5-bathroom home was built in 1996. Spanning 7,236 square feet, the abode sits on 1.26 acres. Based on the contingent status on the property’s listing, it appears the couple have found a buyer.

“While rates have declined for three weeks in a row, homebuyers are still holding back,” Sturtevant said in a statement. “Higher rates, along with on-going economic uncertainty, are key reasons why housing market activity is so sluggish this fall.

She also said there is little reason to expect rates to come down further this year, and that, given this week’s inflation report, it’s more likely for rates to increase instead.

Inventory is rising but higher rates are causing sellers to pause along with buyers. “High rates raise monthly payments and shrink the loan a buyer can qualify for, and the recent pullback in pending sales shows how sensitive buyers are,” she said. “But persistent high inflation is what keeps the Fed hiking and rates elevated. Inflation also leaves households with less to put toward a home, especially when wages lag prices. First-time buyers feel it most. #5594. Clipto enables ChatGPT and Claude to search and analyze years of people’s meetings and video calls

Artificial intelligence assistants such as ChatGPT and Claude have become essential tools for millions of workers worldwide, helping them compose emails in seconds, generate complex code and draft reports by looking at whatever data that person has access to.

But there’s one thing that’s missing from those chatbots’ knowledge. Ask them what was discussed in the previous week’s team meeting or on yesterday’s call with a client, and it will be stumped.

It’s this shortcoming that a startup called Clipto Inc. is trying to solve with the launch of a new AI chatbot memory platform called Clipto Studio, which enables AI assistants to listen in on calls, presentations and meetings and search through them or analyze them upon request.

Clipto argues that this is going to be an important capability as AI becomes more pervasive in daily work. Though AI chatbots can sift through email inboxes and corporate databases in seconds, that’s not where many companies’ most valuable knowledge is actually stored. Rather, Clipto says the most important business insights are trapped in raw video and audio files.

Most of the big decisions are made during Zoom calls, customer interviews and team meetings, but the details of those discussions are stored in heavy, unstructured data formats that are incredibly expensive for AI to process. But AI can potentially provide much more meaningful help to workers if it has a way to access this knowledge.

That’s where Clipto Studio comes in. It’s a native skill set that integrates directly with ChatGPT, Claude and other AI assistants using the Model Context Protocol, powered by proprietary models that run locally on user’s Mac and Windows computers.

The software works by pre-indexing speech, individual speaker’s voices, facial expressions and other on-screen visuals before transforming the raw footage into a structured and easily searchable dataset that’s optimized for AI chatbots. Then, when the user asks a question about one of their recent conversations, or even one from two years ago, it can quickly find the answers it needs by searching through the metadata of those recordings.

Clipto founder and Chief Executive Henry Kang said AI knows basically everything that has been posted online, but has barely scratched the surface of the terabytes of audio and video data that’s sitting in people’s hard drives.

“The next generation of AI will need to understand the conversations, experiences and knowledge that never makes it into a text-based document,” he said. “That’s the future we’re building, giving AI the memory it needs to move beyond answering questions from the internet and start getting real world done with what we ourselves have seen and heard.”

Clipto Studio can be thought of as a kind of instant-replay service. For instance, a management consultant could ask ChatGPT to pinpoint the exact time when a project’s scope changed by looking at more than six month’s worth of calls and meetings, and it will surface the exact moment when that occurred. Alternatively, a researcher might prompt Claude to identify the most common problems with a particular product or service by looking at thousands of customer calls, and pull out direct quotes that illustrate the depth of those issues.

There are other use cases too. For instance, users could ask Clipto Studio to look at dozens of hours of event presentations they’ve attended and create a highlight reel that surfaces the most interesting or relevant moments from them.

Clipto Studio’s official launch is a big moment for the startup, which recently signaled its ambitions with the hiring of former Google LLC research scientist Dr. Mei Han as its new chief scientist. Han, who holds a doctorate in robotics from Carnegie Mellon University, has been tasked with leading the development of Clipto’s lightweight multimodal AI architecture.

Han said she believes in Clipto’s mission because it’s trying to help AI perceive the world in the same way as humans do, by seeing and listening to what’s going on around them.

“The challenge isn’t just recognizing speech or identifying what’s on screen,” she said. “It’s connecting that information across thousands of recordings so AI can understand the context and use it. We’re building the technology to make video and audio as accessible and as useful to AI as text, opening up an entirely new generation of applications.”

#5593. Social Security Could Have Paid Full Benefits Until 2059. What Went Wrong?

Social Security could have paid full benefits until 2059—25 years longer than currently projected—if the share of the U.S. economy subject to payroll taxes had remained at its 1983 level, according to a new analysis.

Under that scenario, the program would have collected an additional $10.8 trillion in payroll tax revenue and interest between 1984 and 2034.

The findings, from AARP's Public Policy Institute, come as Social Security's combined trust funds are projected to run dry in 2034. Without congressional intervention, incoming revenue would cover only about 83% of scheduled benefits that year.

And while much of the debate over Social Security's financial troubles has centered on declining birthrates and a growing number of retirees supported by fewer workers, the new analysis points to another major factor.

As more of the nation's income flows to high earners and investors, a shrinking share of the economy is subject to the payroll taxes that finance Social Security.

In 1983, wages subject to those taxes accounted for 41% of the nation's gross domestic product. By 2025, that share had fallen to just 34%.

To understand what changed for the trust fund, it helps to take a trip back to 1984: when "Ghostbusters" dominated the box office, Madonna broke out with "Like a Virgin," and the median household income was $61,910, compared with an average of $75,850, according to U.S. Census Bureau data adjusted to 2025 dollars.

Today, those figures have climbed to $87,460 and $126,700, respectively.

That's a 41% increase in median household income, compared with a 67% increase in the average—evidence of how income growth has become more concentrated toward the upper end of the distribution.

And that's where Social Security runs into trouble.

The program collects payroll taxes on wages, but only up to an annual limit. In 2026, workers and employers each pay 6.2% on the first $184,500 of wages. So someone earning $2 million pays the same amount in Social Security payroll taxes as someone earning $184,500.

As more wage income accumulates above that ceiling, Social Security collects nothing from those additional earnings, even as they contribute to the growth of the economy.

But the problem extends beyond how wages are distributed.

Between 1970 and 2023, labor compensation's share of GDP fell from 65% to 57%, as a larger portion of national income flowed to business owners and investors through profits and investment returns.

Unlike wages, most of that income isn't subject to Social Security payroll taxes. So as economic growth generates more profits and investment returns, Social Security doesn't necessarily collect additional revenue.

And those earnings are heavily concentrated among the wealthiest Americans.

Taxpayers earning $1 million or more represented just 1% of filers in 2023 but received 48% of all investment income, according to AARP's analysis of Internal Revenue Service data.

AARP also points to the growth of businesses whose owners can receive some of their compensation as profits rather than salaries, further reducing the amount subject to payroll taxes.

Together, these changes have allowed the U.S. economy to generate substantially more income without a corresponding increase in the share subject to Social Security taxes. As a result, the program has captured a shrinking portion of the nation's economic growth, leaving less revenue available to pay future benefits.

Millions of older Americans are already struggling to afford their homes, leaving them particularly vulnerable to any potential reductions in benefits.

In 2023, more than 12.4 million households headed by adults 65 or older spent over 30% of their income on housing, according to Harvard University's Joint Center for Housing Studies. More than half of those households—6.7 million—spent over 50% of their income on housing alone.

"Even without any insolvency-driven benefit cuts, millions of seniors already struggle to pay for food, basic healthcare, and even housing," Shannon Benton, executive director of The Senior Citizens League, said in a Nov. 10 statement.

And retirees could face those cuts sooner than the combined trust fund projection suggests.

The separate trust fund responsible for retirement and survivor benefits is projected to exhaust its reserves in 2032, two years before the hypothetical combined funds. Without congressional intervention, incoming revenue would cover only 78% of scheduled retirement and survivor benefits.

Based on the average retired worker monthly benefit of $2,089 in September 2026, a 22% reduction would amount to roughly $460 a month.

Now, advocates warn that decisions over Social Security's financing can no longer be deferred.

"The incoming class of senators face an enormous responsibility," Benton said, noting that their six-year terms will run through January 2033—past the point when Social Security's retirement and survivors trust fund is projected to exhaust its reserves.

Richard W. Johnson, vice president of financial security at AARP’s Public Policy Institute and author of the analysis, argues that strengthening Social Security requires bringing its financing into line with the modern economy.

"Strengthening Social Security does not require re-creating the economy of 1983," he said. "It just means updating Social Security's financing to reflect how Americans receive income today."

And it was a popular idea on the 2026 midterm campaign trail, too.

In October, Sherrod Brown, who won Ohio's Senate race, called for higher earners to contribute more "by raising the tax cap so we can extend the life of the program."

Troy Jackson, Maine's senator-elect, went further, calling for eliminating the cap altogether.

"Making sure that wealthier people pay the same rate that working class people do would definitely strengthen the Social Security system overall," Jackson said in a September TV interview.

The idea has also drawn bipartisan interest, with Sens. Bernie Moreno (R-OH) and Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) jointly proposing the elimination of the cap in June.

Based on Social Security actuaries' 2025 assumptions, eliminating the cap could close about 67% of the program's 75-year financing gap if higher contributions didn't generate additional future benefits—or roughly half if they did.

Other proposals would tax certain business and investment income that currently falls outside Social Security's revenue base.

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5592. Exclusive: Menlo IRIS extension gives security teams control over AI use without a new browser

Browser security company Menlo Security Inc. today launched the Menlo IRIS Browser Extension, a new offering that adds its enterprise browser security controls to the browsers employees already use with no need to switch them to separate secure ones.

Delivered as a centrally managed extension, Menlo IRIS is said to give security teams visibility into and control over generative artificial intelligence use, data movement, files and third-party extensions. Installation is claimed to take only hours, as no additional hardware is needed.

Chief Executive Bill Robbins, who took over the top job from co-founder Amir Ben-Efraim in February, said security teams have known for some time that the browser is a blind spot. Many have nonetheless held off on fixing it to avoid replacing an existing security stack, which typically means a big migration project, he added.

“Menlo IRIS removes those obstacles,” Robbins said. “Even a small team can get essential security running quickly on the browsers employees already use.”

To make its case, Menlo pointed to Verizon Communications Inc.’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report, released in May, which found regular AI use on corporate devices tripled from 15% to 45% of employees in a single year. Some 67% of people accessing AI services on corporate devices were found to be using noncorporate accounts, with more than 15% of users at the average company also running unauthorized AI browser extensions.

Among the headline capabilities is an audit of third-party browser extensions. Menlo says the audit covers every extension installed across a company, with an enterprise-wide inventory, real-time risk profiling and management controls all included. Few security teams have a count of the extensions their users have installed, according to Menlo. The company also warned that an extension’s risk profile can change at any time without notice.

Data-loss controls cover the clipboard, printing, uploads and downloads, with watermarking, read-only pages, restrictions on developer tools and screenshot deterrence also included. Web filtering steers users toward sanctioned tools, including generative AI services, with limits on what data can be entered into them offered as an alternative to banning the tools outright.

File security is part of the package as well, with inline inspection for data loss prevention violations, viruses and malware. For customers that want it, content disarm and reconstruction can be switched on to strip malicious content from files so they remain usable. Also available as an add-on is HEAT Shield AI for protection against zero-day phishing, social engineering and malvertising at the time of the click.

Deployment is through the Chrome Web Store, Microsoft Intune, Jamf or other device management tools, with support for Chrome, Edge, Safari, Firefox and Chromium-based AI browsers. Since nobody has to switch browsers, security patches from each browser’s vendor are said to keep reaching users as normal.

Most controls are enforced inside the browser session itself, which the company says removes the need for a proxy to route traffic. Menlo IRIS is intended to sit alongside existing network and endpoint tools.

The Menlo IRIS Browser Extension is available now.

Menlo Security has raised $250 million in funding, including a $100 million round in November 2020. Investors in the company include Vista Equity Partners Management, JPMorgan Chase & Co., American Express Ventures and General Catalyst Group Management.

#5591. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns following affairs scandal

Nvidia Corp.’s board of directors today announced the resignation of Jensen Huang, now former chief executive and president of the artificial intelligence chipmaker, amid a scandal, naming Colette Kress, current executive vice president and chief financial officer, as interim CEO.

The news arrives following numerous industry reports that the board intended to replace Huang as CEO after revelations of a second extramarital relationship with an executive at Nvidia, coming mere days after he admitted to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

News initially broke over the weekend that Huang had an affair with Alice Huang, no relation, an executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed International Pte. Ltd. and an alleged Chinese spy. The Information reported on Tuesday that Alice Huang facilitated $7.5 billion in chip sales to China. According to another report, Jensen Huang also had a relationship with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell, who serves as vice president of healthcare.

The New York Times reported last month that U.S. authorities concluded Alice Huang acted as a Chinese intelligence asset. Upon revelations of the affair, the Associated Press reported that President Trump announced that the Federal Bureau of Investigation was looking into the allegations, while adding, “I think that he’ll be in good shape.”

Late Wednesday, the Nvidia board met to decide whether to oust Huang and discussed a potential replacement as CEO. Huang has no obvious single successor and owns about 3.6% of Nvidia’s stock. Reportedly, the board sought counsel from an outside firm to find someone to fill the role.

With the announcement, Nvidia stock was falling more than 5% in trading today, backing off an even steeper loss at the opening. Yahoo Finance calculated that Nvidia has lost more than $600 billion in market value since the previous Thursday, likely with more shocks to come.

“Nvidia’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” said Kress. “We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead.”

Kress has served as executive vice president and CFO since joining in September 2013. Her accolades include leading the company’s finance organization and working to build the company’s dominance in the AI chip industry. Before joining Nvidia, she spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at leading technology companies, including Cisco Systems Inc. and Microsoft Corp.

The CFO was intimately involved with Nvidia’s widespread financing of AI compute providers, in particular its backing of not only AI leaders OpenAI Group PBC and Anthropic PBC — the latter set to go public as early as next week — but also neoclouds such as CoreWeave Inc. and Nebius Group NV. Those financings have been criticized by some as “circular,” meaning Nvidia essentially invested in customers so they could use the money to buy more of its graphics processing units.

The potential successors to Huang, who had 30 direct reports, include no one obvious choice and a succession plan apparently was not in place. Candidates that some have speculated about include Arm Ltd. CEO Rene Haas, who worked at Nvidia years ago, Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, and Ian Buck, Nvidia’s vice president and general manager of hyperscale and high-performance computing and creator of its CUDA software considered the real moat for its business.

“The sudden resignation of Jensen Huang is about more than succession at the world’s most important AI chipmaker,” Forrester Vice President and Group Research Director Stephanie Balaouras told SiliconANGLE in an email. “Nvidia’s leadership crisis is a stress test for the AI boom. If Nvidia stabilizes quickly under new leadership, the AI infrastructure boom will have demonstrated resilience. If its stock, financing relationships or ecosystem commitments remain under sustained pressure, that would add evidence to the fragile side of the AI bubble ledger.””

Balaouras added that “tech leaders shouldn’t overreact, but they should treat Nvidia’s CEO transition as a prompt to reassess concentration risk across their AI infrastructure, suppliers and investment plans.”

Huang is best known for co-founding Nvidia in 1993 in a San Jose Denny’s and has served as its CEO since. His departure will likely send further ripples through the AI silicon and software industry. He has been deeply involved in Nvidia’s product strategy and built longstanding customer relationships, helming the company as it became the behemoth it is today.

Nvidia commands roughly 80% of the data-center AI chip market, although industry estimates vary by methodology. Epoch Artificial Intelligence Inc. puts its share of AI computing power shipped at 63% in the second quarter of 2026. Other market carve-outs include custom chips built by cloud companies within the broader supply, including Google LLC’s tensor processing units at 25%, Amazon Inc.’s custom silicon at 5% and Advanced Micro Devices Inc.’s AI hardware accelerators at 4%.

Nvidia is expected to report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings on Nov. 17.

#5590. Sunlight, Weather and Childcare: A Year of New Data on Redfin Home Listings

In 2026, Redfin added information about sunlight, weather, childcare access and more to home listings. Here is everything you need to know about what’s new.

A home listing has always been good at telling you about a house: the square footage, the year it was built, the number of bedrooms. Historically, it has been less good at telling you what living there is actually like. Does the kitchen get morning sunlight? How hot are the summers? Is there a daycare within walking distance?

Those are the questions we set out to answer this year. Multiple new data sets arrived on Redfin in 2026, and they now sit alongside other information that was already there, including scores about a property’s walkability, transit access and climate.

Sunscore shows exactly how much sunlight a home gets

Natural light is one of the hardest things to judge from listing photos or a single showing, and it matters more than you might expect. In a recent Redfin survey, nearly 70% of people said the amount of sunlight in their home affects their satisfaction with where they live, and 11% said it is non-negotiable when searching for a home.

Sunscore is a property-level rating from 0 to 100 that shows how much sunlight a home gets. We co-created it with Shadowmap, a sunlight analysis platform, using 3D modeling that tracks how shadows fall across a home throughout the day and across the seasons. Here are the score breakdowns:

Each score accounts for the home’s 3D shape and structure, surrounding buildings, trees and terrain, the sun’s position throughout the day, and seasonal changes across the year. In other words, it catches the things you would only discover after moving in—like a neighboring building that blocks the afternoon light in winter.

And it is not only about comfort and aesthetics. A home’s sun exposure also says something about its solar potential, which can translate into real savings on energy costs over time.

Weather data helps predict precipitation and heat

Weather turns out to be one of the biggest reasons people move. In a recent Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos, 22% of Americans planning to move to another state said better weather was motivating the move—the most cited reason out of nearly 30 options, ahead of affordability, job opportunities and moving closer to family. Another 21% said concerns about climate change or natural disasters were shaping where they wanted to live.

In July, we partnered with The Weather Company, owner of The Weather Channel app and weather.com, to bring historical weather data to every for-sale listing on Redfin. As our exclusive historical weather provider, it supplies the same data hundreds of millions of people check every month.

Each listing shows ZIP code-level averages for:

Consider this information the difference between the weather on the day you tour a home and the climate you might actually live in.

Childcare data displays daycare and preschool options

For families with young children, childcare access can determine a neighborhood’s fit as much as school boundaries do. However, it’s historically been missing from the home browsing experience. Redfin is the first major real estate portal to partner with Winnie, the largest marketplace for childcare and early education in the U.S., to bring local childcare information to for-sale listings.

Nearby daycare and preschool options now appear on for-sale home listings with details that determine whether a spot is realistic for your family, such as:

Location scores capture everything from wellness access to noise

While Walk Score, Bike Score and Transit Score already existed on home listings, Redfin has expanded these location scores to capture more information about a neighborhood’s vibe using Local Logic data.

Start exploring homes on Redfin.com or the Redfin app to learn everything you’d want to know about a property. Need a place to start? Use Redfin’s conversational search to begin your homebuying journey.

#5589. What the World Series can teach real estate agents about focus

ST PETERSBURG, FLORIDA – OCT. 28: William Contreras, No. 24 of the Milwaukee Brewers, poses with the Willie Mays World Series Most Valuable Player award after defeating the Tampa Bay Rays in the 2026 World Series at Tropicana Field on Oct. 28, 2026, in St. Petersburg, Florida.

Mindfulness for real estate isn’t about calm. It’s about hearing clients under pressure. See what baseball teaches brokers about training attention.

The Milwaukee Brewers just won the World Series, and while I love baseball, I’ve been watching with a question that has very little to do with it: What happens to your attention when the outcome matters more than you can afford to think about?

Nobody at the plate can win a championship with the swing they wish they’d taken last inning. The players can only deal with the pitch (or batter) in front of them.

That sounds obvious until you notice how often we walk into a seller conversation still arguing with the deal that fell apart yesterday.

What’s interesting to me is that baseball has stopped treating this as a personality trait. Both the Rays and the Brewers have extensive mental performance training programs (as do all Major League ball clubs), but most brokerages treat mental health as a wellness issue, not a performance one.

Whatever name your office gives this kind of work, baseball has made it somebody’s job.

What makes this baseball tale useful to brokers and team leaders, though, is how much resistance the work still meets in a sport that has every reason to embrace it.

Andy McCullough’s recent reporting in The Athletic examines meditation in Major League Baseball, and I found the takeaways instructive.

For over two decades, most teams have invested in behavioral science and expanded their mental-performance staffs. It’s a sport that measures everything, with tens of millions of dollars on every roster, and it has decided the mental side is worth paying for.

What I find fascinating is that even as the evidence piles up, many players remain skeptical. Some call it “woo-woo.” One of the game’s best pitchers says he doesn’t need it. Coaches avoid the word “meditation” altogether because, as one put it, it intimidates people, and if you push it, they’ll tune you out.

My favorite part of the Athletic piece was this: The San Francisco Giants brought in a consultant, titled “Breathing Specialist,” and the players made jokes about it. The next season, the same man did the same work but with a new title: “Human Performance Coach,” and the resistance started to fall away.

By the time he left, about 15 players regularly attended his sessions (complete with Tibetan singing bowls). He concluded that the stigma had more to do with the title than the practice.

I don’t call it meditation when I train real estate teams either. But that doesn’t mean you can’t intentionally sharpen the skills involved.

When the market tightens, brokerages usually prescribe more activity: more calls, more door knocks, more open houses. We can count activity, so we reach for it. Ballplayers do the same thing when they skip the mental work and take extra swings.

The trouble is that pressure narrows attention, and narrowed attention is as poor a state for a batter with two on, two outs, behind two, in the bottom of the ninth as it is for a seasoned agent on a listing appointment, a price-reduction conversation or a buyer about to walk.

Don’t get confused. This kind of performance coaching is not about caring less about the result; it’s about letting go of the need to make it happen. A hitter can care enormously about winning the World Series and still recognize that thinking about winning doesn’t help him see the next pitch.

The same is true when a seller is deciding whether to take your advice. You need the listing, but needing it more isn’t any more effective than gripping and swinging the bat harder.

The goal isn’t calm, either. Mental-performance people who work with ballplayers talk about finding a usable level of activation for the task, since too much overwhelms you and too little leaves you flat. I’m not trying to produce agents who feel peaceful about losing business. I’m trying to help them notice when fear has taken over the conversation so that they can let it go and hear the client again.

There’s sports research worth knowing here. One study of Division I basketball players found that higher measured mindfulness predicted better free-throw percentages in games, a 5.75-point delta, to be exact. A separate training study found something more useful: under high stress, the gap between athletes who trained their attention and those who didn’t was larger than under low stress.

I won’t tell you a practice will add a specific number to your agents’ closing rates. Nobody can honestly promise that, and even baseball struggles to quantify the benefit. What I will tell you is that the moments that make or break an agent’s year are high-pressure, and training for them is a performance issue, not a wellness perk.

In each World Series game, every player must let the last pitch go before the next one arrives. Your agents face the same job on a smaller stage every week.

You don’t need agents who identify as meditators. You need agents who can hear what a client is saying while a deal they “need” is coming apart. That capacity deserves practice before the conversation, not a reminder to calm down halfway through it.

Aaron Hendon is the Managing Broker for Christine & Company with eXp and a mindfulness teacher. Connect with Aaron on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5588. Construction Site Next to Deadly Brooklyn Building Collapse Had History of Safety Issues

As authorities continue to search through the rubble of a deadly building collapse in Flatbush, Brooklyn, that killed eight, troubling details have emerged about safety concerns at a neighboring construction site.

On Wednesday afternoon, the three-story mixed-use building at 1321 Flatbush Ave. collapsed, taking the shared wall of 1323 Flatbush Ave. with it, leaving the bedrooms and closets of residents in that building exposed.

The deadly tragedy occurred next to an active construction site at 2625 Bedford Ave., where an existing structure had been demolished and excavation was underway to build a new residential building.

In a press conference at the scene of the tragedy, Mayor Zohran Mamdani vowed a full investigation into what preceded and caused the collapse, including whether the construction work underway at 2625 Bedford Ave. played any role.

"If there is anyone or any entity operating in this city that bears responsibility for what happened, we will hold them accountable," the mayor said.

The construction site at 2625 Bedford Ave. was purchased for $3.99 million by a pair of LLCs registered to Judith Swimer and Faigy Fischman in June 2024, just days after the duo purchased another property at 600 Utica Ave. in East Flatbush for $5 million, according to public records.

Public records show they initially planned to develop a three-story apartment building on the lot, but the project had been plagued with stops and starts over amendments to the building plan and safety concerns from city inspectors.

In March of this year, the Department of Buildings halted the demolition of a one-story building on the site after an inspector reported that demolition contractor N Tech Design of America had failed to take proper safety precautions, including installing netting and putting up sidewalk shields, records show.

A month later, inspectors returned to the site and found that the demolition had gone ahead anyway, in defiance of the stop-work order, according to city records. A $10,000 fine was issued.

In May, a city inspector issued additional citations and another stop-work order against the contractors for allegedly failing to ensure adequate protections of neighboring buildings and for deviating from approved construction plans. Within a week, the city lifted that stop-work order.

According to signs posted on the site, the construction and development management firm Promont is overseeing the project. Realtor.com has reached out to Promont for comment.

The alleged deviation from filed plans may have been related to a new permitting request submitted by Robert Fischman of WG Facility X LLC, amending the proposed project to a nine-story structure on the site with a ground-floor grocery store. That amended permit request has not yet been approved.

Fischman has a troubled history. In 1999, Fischman was charged in a real estate kickback scheme involving his company, M.S. Berkoff Co. Earlier this year, Berkoff Supply sent tenants of 1321 Flatbush Ave. a letter alerting them to the excavation work.

In March of this year, as a part of its survey of the property in advance of submitting the request for the revised nine-story build, Promont commissioned a pre-construction report from structural and geotechnical monitoring company Quiver Monitoring.

The report focused on the buildings surrounding 2625 Bedford Ave. and assessed the masonry on the north facade of 1321 Flatbush Ave. as being in poor condition, "with a wide range of deficiencies noted" according to the report.

Jessie Kramer is a licensed professional engineer in Colorado. She has deep experience in forensic engineering, including uncovering the causes of building collapses.

Kramer tells Realtor.com® that an older brick building adjacent to an active excavation site immediately raises red flags.

“Tons of thoughts pop up when I see something like that,” she says. "My day-to-day is looking at collapsed buildings, looking at failed buildings, and saying, 'Why did this happen? How widespread is the damage?' And often, the answer involves multiple issues."

On Thursday afternoon, Mamdani announced that the city would sweep 100 other properties associated with five entities tied to the construction site at 2625 Bedford Ave. The mayor and the city’s Department of Buildings commissioner declined to name those entities.

Isolag Realty Corp. purchased 1321 Flatbush Ave. in 2024, and Olufemi Falade signed the deed. The property consisted of four residential units and a ground-floor commercial space. A three-bedroom unit in the building rented for $3,550.

The 96-year-old building had 98 recorded violations dating to 1972, according to the city's Department of Housing, Preservation, and Development. Eleven of those violations were from this past year, including a violation for "unsafe electrical wiring" and a notice to "provide an adequate supply of water for the wet sprinkler and/or standpipe."

Falade has a tumultuous history of building ownership. In 2006, he spent 12 days in jail for failing to repair issues in numerous properties he owned. “In just 12 buildings he owns, there are more than 1,800 violations of the city’s housing and maintenance codes,” Housing Preservation and Development Commissioner Shaun Donovan told the New York Post at the time.

"I can't speak to what potential deficiencies might have been there before this happened," Kramer says. "But I can say on a building of this age, our modern codes differ a ton from what were the standards back then. So it's imperative to keep up with maintenance in these old buildings. And that's an active process. Owners have to be super on top of it.

“People obviously are wanting answers immediately, and that’s not going to happen,” Kramer adds. “This is going to be a yearslong investigation process to decide who’s at fault and what happened.”

Andrea Cavallier contributed to this report.

#5587. Realty Executives Associates Appoints New Executive Vice President of Agent Development

Realty Executives Associates (REA) has announced the appointment of J Lewis as executive vice president of Agent Development, a newly established leadership role focused on strengthening the success, productivity and long-term relationships of REA’s agents.

According to a release, prior to joining REA, Lewis served as CEO of Keller Williams for 13 years, bringing extensive experience in brokerage leadership, agent development and organizational growth.

In this new role, the company says Lewis will focus on helping existing agents increase productivity and profitability, strengthening agent relationships and retention and creating meaningful opportunities for professional development and business growth. He will work to provide agents with the resources, guidance and support they need to build sustainable businesses.

“One of the things I enjoy most is sitting down with an agent or a team, understanding what they’re trying to accomplish, and helping them figure out how to get there. That might mean looking at their production data, analyzing their financials, identifying opportunities they’re not seeing, or simply fine-tuning the way they run their business,” he says. “Every agent has different goals, and I enjoy helping them develop a plan to reach those goals and build a business that supports the life they want.”

“I’m incredibly excited to join the number one brokerage in East Tennessee,” Lewis added. “What really attracted me to REA is the opportunity to work with a company that understands the value of investing in its people. I’ve always enjoyed working alongside agents, understanding what they want to accomplish, and helping them find ways to get there. REA has created an environment where that kind of work is valued, and I’m excited to be part of it.”

“At REA, we believe our agents are our customers. Our responsibility is to create an environment where they can build successful, sustainable businesses and feel supported along the way. This position is an extension of that commitment,” said Justin Bailey, CEO and partner of Realty Executives Associates.

Bailey added: “Success isn’t simply measured by how many agents we have. It’s measured by the success of the agents who choose to call REA home. We want to be intentional about helping them become more productive, more profitable, and better positioned for the future. We have always believed that taking care of our people is what makes a great brokerage, and this is another way we are putting that belief into action.”

#5586. Computer vision startup Tristar AI pulls in $12.4M to automate quality control for manufacturers

All too often, manufacturing defects seem to slip past human eyes, with the result that high-speed production lines turn into expensive scrapheaps. Computer vision startup Tristar AI Inc. has just raised $12.4 million in early-stage funding in order to try to put an end to these costly mistakes.

Today’s Series A round was led by Isogon Ventures and saw participation from Blackhorn Ventures, Ford Street Ventures, NextView Ventures, TenOneTen and Capgemini’s ISAI Cap Venture Fund.

Tristar AI is gearing up to transform quality assurance in manufacturing at a critical moment for the industry. Manufacturers have found themselves squeezed by a combination of rising raw material costs and growing labor shortages, and these problems have been made even more acute by the U.S. government’s insistence on bringing more manufacturing back home.

According to data from the Capgemini Research Institute, 48% of U.S. companies have invested in reshoring projects this year. But 83% say they’re worried about the lack of skilled industrial workers needed to fulfill those initiatives.

One of the major challenges for manufacturers is that they’re still encumbered by inefficient inspection protocols that rely on either manual checks, or in a best-case scenario, rigid, rule-based machine vision systems. Quality control is essential for any manufacturing operation, but the inefficiency of these protocols makes it a significant roadblock too.

It forces companies to take skilled workers off production lines and sometimes even bring their entire operations screeching to a halt. Yet there are many occasions where they still miss subtle flaws in their products, resulting in wasted materials, downtime, missed deadlines and sometimes even very expensive customer claims.

Founder and Chief Executive Salem Karani is all too familiar with the inefficiency of manual inspection. He told SiliconANGLE that while growing up, he would often accompany his father to his family’s plastic film manufacturing plant in Houston, turning up at all hours of the day and night in order to troubleshoot production issues that could spring up at any moment. Because the company’s margins were so tight, any period of extended downtime could threaten its profitability, so he would spend hours with his dad frantically troubleshooting line errors.

It was this experience that ultimately inspired Karani, who studied computer vision at Harvard and MIT, to develop an automated quality inspection system that can operate continuously without slowing down production. “The problem was never that people didn’t care about quality,” Karani said. “It’s that people catch problems after the fact, once they’ve already cost time, materials and customers. Tristar gives every production line a live record so teams can act when it matters most.”

Computer vision in manufacturing operations is not a new concept, but where Tristar differs is through its use of more sophisticated artificial intelligence models that can adapt to changing conditions, materials and defect types. The startup’s platform looks at machine telemetry, the quality of the products coming off the line and the activity of human operators, allowing it to uncover issues the moment they emerge and immediately understand where the problem is, and why it occurred.

Best of all, the system can integrate with factories’ existing systems, such as cameras, sensors, programmable logic controllers, enterprise resource planning systems and so on That enables them to get up and running without an expensive overhaul.

Isagon Ventures General Partner Paco Riberas said he’s backing Tristar because manufacturers are losing far too much money to avoidable defects. “In today’s industry, precision isn’t optional, and Tristar makes it possible,” he said. “Its AI vision catches defects in real time, directly on existing production lines. Salem and his team are building the quality standard for modern manufacturing.”

Tristar’s early traction has been encouraging. Its system already monitors more than 500 production lines across North America and Europe.

Customers include global packaging giants such as Amcor, DuPont and Klöckner Pentaplast, and also some of the biggest suppliers to automakers such as Toyota, Honda and Mercedes, Karani said. Those customers report defect detection accuracy rates of between 95% and 99%, and say the platform pays for itself in an average of just four months.

Karani said the goal now is to expand Tristar’s platform into new manufacturing sectors and enhance the capabilities of its computer vision AI to try and improve its accuracy even further. Ultimately, he sees the company as the operational system of record for factory floors, giving manufacturers more visibility into everything about their production operations, from the raw materials to the finished product.

“Physical AI will play a critical role in the future of manufacturing,” said Capgemini Ventures’ Matthieu Eyriès. “Tristar combines advanced AI capabilities with a strong understanding of industrial environments, addressing concrete manufacturing challenges with measurable impact.”
