#5571. IBM Quantum and the race to make scientific advantage useful to industry

SPECIAL BREAKING ANALYSIS by Dave Vellante

QDC26 shows progress in the hardware, software and tooling around quantum computing as customers look for evidence of better outcomes.

IBM Corp.’s Quantum Developer Conference in Chicago this week marked a change in emphasis. IBM claims that researchers have demonstrated quantum advantage in 2026 by working with the classical computing community. Its public presentations showed progress in processors, error correction, scientific software and the integration of quantum with conventional computing.

The company’s quantum leader, Jay Gambetta (pictured), also set a new target. The next big milestone comes by demonstrating industry impact by 2028, conditional on collaboration across enterprise application researchers and the classical and quantum communities.

Our key takeaway is that IBM is assembling more of the full system required to turn a quantum experiment into useful scientific work. Hardware is important, but the real innovation will come from software. Importantly, the tools that help a scientist formulate a problem, run it across different computing resources, check the result and understand the economics are where much of the innovation is headed. These capabilities address several of the barriers customers described to us in our spring quantum tour of major scientific research labs; and the issues discussed with technologists on our Quantum 101 Series at theCUBE’s NYSE studio.

Despite the progress being made, the remaining gaps and challenges are many. Quantum science is advancing but impact on industries is still years away. Better software is the key to making dramatic improvements in quantum performance and a new service capability can attract researchers. But if a chemist needs to understand the deep nuances of quantum computing, it limits adoption. We believe the next phase of innovation will focus on abstracting quantum complexities and making measurable improvements in simplicity to drive further usage.

In this Special Breaking Analysis, we examine IBM’s public QDC proclamations through the prism of our spring interviews with six quantum and supercomputing experts. We add customer perspectives from our partner Qualitate, assess the implications of IBM’s foundry investments and consider what evidence would signal that progress is moving from scientific advantage to industry impact.

IBM’s progress comes into better focus when evaluating its milestones separately. IBM’s goal of demonstrating Quantum Advantage by 2026 is generally accepted as met, based on achieving particular computation superiority relative to today’s classical methods. But to truly show industry impact, IBM needs to show results make a difference to an organization. Milestones around fault-tolerant architectures will increasingly focus on the ability to sustain reliable computation in the face of errors. Progress in one category will definitely support another but it’s useful to look at milestones and proof points separately as shown below.

IBM deserves high marks for achieving that advantage but is subject to scrutiny. Gambetta’s keynote described classical researchers overtaking quantum results, claims being withdrawn as classical makes improvements, and subsequent quantum work moving the needle in favor of quantum again. This of course is how a competitive scientific ecosystem should operate. We’re eager to see the leapfrogging end and await a day where a quantum advantage becomes sustainable with clear evidence that classical computing has no chance of catching up for specified use cases.

Observers can rightly be concerned that incorrect inferences may be drawn from the term “advantage.” The phrase can sound like a statement of superiority. But if that advantage is not consistently held, then the broader industry might remain skeptical. The same applies to verifying that a customer outcome is attributable an underlying scientific model powered by quantum.

A public Allstate example is useful and illustrates the difference. IBM described underwriting-optimization results as comparable to classical optimization schemes. That can represent progress, but it does not show that quantum has delivered a superior underwriting outcome. Customers need to decide how much they are prepared to invest in learning before a measurable benefit appears. IBM, in our view, is working hard to simplify the heavy lift and broaden adoption.

The researchers we interviewed in spring 2026 for World Quantum Day were already thinking beyond the hardware. Their concerns included application selection, reliability, integration, software complexity and the ability to preserve optionality as hardware evolves. These were six independent editorial interviews conducted on theCUBE, made possible by Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co., across five institutions, offering a view of the work required to make quantum useful. The discussions were hosted by this author and Paul Gillin, managing editor at SiliconANGLE.

The following table highlights the to priority stated by each researcher at the time and our take on how IBM has responded in the past 6-9 months.

IBM is directing effort toward problems that these practitioners identified months earlier. We believe that is a strong indicator of product relevance, an even more important than hardware milestones.

It also gives us a more reasonable test of true progress. A scientist must be able to attack a meaningful problem with less setup effort, run it more reliably and compare the result with a credible classical alternative. IBM’s public announcements show capabilities intended to support that progression and the gaps identified this spring by our researcher friends. Thus far, however, they don’t show how broadly researchers can complete their tasks without specialist assistance. IBM shared additional capabilities to a small group of industry analysts under NDA, which look encouraging.

Some of the most interesting material in Chicago concerned ordinary operational friction. In the public developer sessions, IBM described experiments interrupted by sleeping laptops, dead notebook sessions, running out of memory or tokens, and lost work in process. In quantum research, as with AI YOLO training runs, they add expense and blockers to work that already requires specialized expertise.

Managed workflows address this through simplification by moving execution into a hosted environment with conventional computing resources and tools to capture and save work in process. Researchers can associate quantum jobs with the workflow and monitor consumption across both quantum and classical support infrastructure. That creates a basis for repeating experiments and understanding where resources are consumed and how to optimize the complete process.

Take the chemistry approaches discussed at the event. Researchers can divide a larger molecular problem into smaller parts, use quantum or classical computing methods for appropriate parts and combine the results. At QDC26, IBM described improvements in classical algorithms that support the processing of quantum jobs. Classical solving steps can become a major bottlenecks and represent opportunities for optimization.

The relevant focus is increasingly the complete research workflow. Here we’re referring to the preparation, the quantum work, the classical processing and the validation. This expands the opportunity for IBM and its partners because more of the work can be supported through its software and services. It also shines a light on how the economic case needs to evolve, with a focus on the cost of an outcome.

Faster quantum hardware alone is not the answer. Conversely, better classical software can make quantum experiments much more productive. Both are developments that came into focus at QDC26. Customers need enough visibility to identify the bottlenecks and implement improvements.

IBM’s pronouncements about AI are expected to address barriers raised in our spring interviews – the complexity of translating domain knowledge into a working quantum experiment. IBM must provide skills that assist with choosing methods, workflows, applying classical algorithms and the like. And validating implementations before longer, more expensive runs take place. Our developer conversations at the event underscore demand for AI assistance with calls for simpler packaging and managed services.

We believe this marks is an important near-term relationship between AI and quantum. AI can help scientists use quantum computing more effectively before quantum delivers a broadly demonstrated improvement in AI itself. The immediate opportunity is to simplify – reducing the effort required to apply specialized software and infrastructure.

This requirement has implications for how scientific software is packaged. A library contains reusable code. Increasingly, skills will supply context and guidelines for selecting and applying that code. As skills improve, we expect more of the integration work to be assisted by software. The value of a mature library will still depend on its performance and suitability for the task at hand. The public QDC releases include libraries, mapping tools and AI skills together; they hint toward an evolution in how software will be used in the future.

Another gap is accountability. For example, what happens if a workflow executes but uses invalid scientific assumptions. An AI-generated configuration can appear valid while making a poor trade-off between accuracy and cost, for example. In our view, a useful abstraction must maintain the ability to understand those AI decisions and validate them in terms that a domain expert/scientist comprehends.

This is where customer evidence must become more specific in our view. For example, can a chemist repeat useful work without a vendor team guiding them every step? Can another scientist reproduce the result? Can the organization see what exactly changed between runs? We would place considerable weight on those conditions when judging whether easier programming translates into broader scientific adoption.

Chemistry and materials are fields that provide a strong connection between our spring interviews and the public QDC discussions. Johansson at CSC emphasized the challenge of modeling interacting electrons. Beck at Oak Ridge described materials and chemistry research with potential relevance to fusion and biology. IBM’s sessions discussed tools for decomposing problems and processing results across quantum and conventional systems working in tandem.

We view these fields as particularly credible places to look for early useful applications because the scientific problems involve quantum behavior. That is a reason to prioritize research that benefits from quantum. Problem scope, accuracy and economics (or feasibility) relative to conventional methods will determine the ultimate usefulness of quantum.

IBM’s performance progress is notable, but its points of comparison are instructive. Its headline 25-fold improvement in maximum circuit throughput compares Nighthawk r2 with Heron. Several application improvements also compare newer IBM quantum systems with earlier ones. Those figures demonstrate progress within IBM’s generations but a customer still needs a comparison with the best practical classical approach to the same problem.

The mot useful metric in our view is the cost and time required to obtain a validated outcome. The calculation should include all aspects of conventional preprocessing and post-processing, the quantum work done, job completion times and the intensity of the technical skills required perform and validate the result. Importantly, an important future measure is whether the process can be consistently repeated at scale.

Customers should absolutely invest before quantum consistently wins. The key is to identify those investments as a learning experience.

Post-quantum cryptography or PQC is a topic we unpacked at theCUBE’s Quantum Readiness Day this past September. Qualitate customer survey findings add another dimension to our PQC analysis. But don’t confuse PQC spend with quantum application adoption.

A query of Qualitate’s interview data on quantum adoption focuses heavily on PQC, a tactical topic that is top of mind for enterprises today. Organizations are spending to prepare existing information systems to resist future quantum-enabled attacks. The data include customers already taking action, as well as those evaluating.

“Now is the time we’re really starting to go all in on post quantum cryptography.”

The same participant, a technology lead at a professional services company, explains the rationale in terms of future loss avoidance:

“We anticipate that this will significantly save us on dealing with enormous crises in the future.”

Today’s enterprise focus as it relates to quantum is on modernizing cryptography. This is far ahead of investing to find useful applications for a quantum computer. Today’s practitioners are consumed with deploying and securing agents and making AI trustworthy. Quantum applications, other than PQC, are not top-of-mind for most enterprise customers. Security work to protect conventional systems is tactical and there’s little evidence of interest in running workloads on quantum hardware within organizations today.

NIST released its first three finalized post-quantum cryptography standards in 2024 and encourages organizations to begin transitioning. Its guidance also explains the risk that adversaries collect encrypted information today for possible decryption later. Unlike Y2K, which had a definitive date associated wth the risk, the timing of a capable quantum attack remains uncertain. As such, migration planning is sensible now, independent of IBM’s application and hardware milestones.

The following competitive signals are seen in the Qualitate data and are almost exclusively security-related:

The opportunity for specialists also remains open. One participant states:

“The field is still not crystallized. And probably we will not necessarily rely on the hyperscalers. Probably will rely on specialists.” – Global head of analytics, financial services and insurance, large U.S. corporation (Source: Qualitate)

Our take is that technical credibility and existing relationships, combined with the ability to affect a successful migration, may all influence these purchases. IBM has many assets, but customers are still evaluating alternatives. Success in quantum-safe security strengthens its commercial position without, by itself, resolving which quantum computing architecture or application platform will prevail when quantum goes mainstream.

Quantum computing also needs to progress from building exceptional devices to producing dependable systems repeatedly. The manufacturing announcements around IBM’s roadmap deserve scrutiny in that context.

In September, IBM acquired, Anderon, finalizing a $1 billion CHIPS award supported by an additional $1 billion IBM investment. IBM has reported it has an Albany, New York-based, 300-millimeter quantum wafer foundry serving customers across the ecosystem, with initial wafers already running through the facility.

Our view is that the learning curve will be as important as any single milestone. More repeatable production can confer experience advantages to IBM (Wright’s Law), much in the same way Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. has demonstrated its leadership in semiconductor manufacturing. Serving multiple customers could help support volume across shared infrastructure. Whether those benefits emerge depends on demand, process stability, yields and the ability to protect each customer’s intellectual property. In addition, IBM can learn from Intel’s missteps and its own foundry challenges.

The industry needs to watch for manufacturing progress alongside qubit performance. Capital investments are followed by innovation. IBM’s August acquisition of HRL Laboratories adds a related strategic chess move. The rationale explained by IBM is to acquire expertise in silicon-spin qubits, sensing, materials, cryogenics, controls, packaging and interconnects. IBM describes that expertise as complementary to its superconducting work and identifies opportunities to collaborate with Anderon.

We interpret the acquisition as a way for IBM to control its destiny in a return to its vertically integrated mainframe past. At the same time, it doesn’t have the volume economics to achieve its objectives purely as a captive/integrated systems player. So it must open up its manufacturing capability to other parties, including its competitors.

Taken together, the public announcements at QDC26 suggest a broader platform ambition. IBM is connecting access to quantum hardware and software with classical computing, application functions, development tools and the like. We believe this could increase its role in the customer’s research process and create more opportunities for ecosystem partners to package specialized capabilities.

The competitive advantage will come from making useful work easier to perform and repeat. A customer that can move from a scientific experiment to a reliable result at scale, with less effort, has a reason to stay with a vendor and invest more. That advantage still has to be earned through application quality, performance, service reliability and superior economics.

There is also a customer tradeoff – the classic lock-in risk. An integrated service can reduce operational complexity while increasing dependence on the provider’s tooling and ecosystem. Open-source tools help minimize the risk, but portability also depends on whether models, workflows, validation and operational models transfer to another platform. Our spring conversations with Kranzlmüller – and his emphasis on technological independence – along with Shehata’s interest in interoperable specifications – make that point clear.

We would not declare IBM as a decisive winner from this conference. But the company has presented an impressive combination of hardware, software and infrastructure progress. Customers will determine its value through repeated use and outcomes. Competing systems from specialists and hyperscalers – as well as progress from classical methods – will continue to shape the narrative.

If Jay Gambetta’s prediction holds true, the next two years will produce a more tangible conversation around industry impact. Look for significantly more quantum POCs, more named customers solving consequential problems and a measurable change in a scientific or business decision. We would also want enough evidence for an independent team to assess the contribution; and for the customer to explain the full cost of achieving an outcome.

For enterprise leaders, the sensible approach is to separate cryptographic readiness from quantum application programs tied to specific problems and economics.

IBM has made a stronger case that the surrounding machinery for useful quantum computing is coming together. The future test is whether customers can show what changed because of quantum. A demonstrably improved scientific result or an economically superior workflow would make the 2028 ambition impressive.

That is the evidence we will be watching.

What’s on your quantum radar? Let us know.

#5570. Open Real Estate: We’re almost there, but not quite

OPINION: The Open Real Estate options give sellers just two choices: market or participant view. Darryl Davis makes the case for a third door.

Picture a homeowner at the kitchen table. She likes you. She trusts you. And she says something agents hear every week: “I want you to sell my house. Just you. I don’t want a parade of strangers walking through my bedroom with agents I have never met. But I don’t want to hide it either. Advertise it. Get the word out. I want the best price.”

That is not a strange request. Some homeowners would happily give up a few dollars on the sale price for less stress, more convenience, and the peace of working with one agent and one office. And right now, the newest system in real estate has no way to say yes to it.

On October 26, Keller Williams, AGNT (the parent of eXp and NextHome), HomeServices of America and Real REMAX Group launched Open Real Estate (ORE). Four competitors came together to stop listings from disappearing into company silos. They deserve real credit. But read the FAQ, and you will see the system gives a seller only two doors.

Now go back to our homeowner. Door one sends strangers through her bedroom. Door two gives her one agent but forbids anyone to advertise her house, the last thing she asked for. She wants one agent and full marketing. ORE makes her pick one.

That is not seller choice. That is a choice between two things she did not ask for.

Here is the option that is missing, and it is simple.

I can already hear the objection. “Darryl, isn’t this just a pocket listing with a nicer name?”

No. A pocket listing is hidden. A Coming Soon tease builds buzz while keeping other agents out, and nobody, not even the listing agent, can show it. The true exclusive is the opposite of both. The house is actively marketed to the public, and every member company knows it is available. The only thing exclusive is who walks through her front door.

Think of a restaurant that only takes reservations. Everybody sees the menu and knows where it is. You call first, and the owner decides who gets a table. Nobody calls that a secret restaurant.

Let’s say it out loud. In a true exclusive, the listing agent may well sell the house to their own buyer and get paid on both sides. For some sellers, that is exactly why they choose it. They understand that one cook in the kitchen managing the whole process beats two, especially when the second one is an untrained buyer’s agent.

ORE already has what it needs to offer this, and technology can make the fiduciary piece stronger than ever.

CCP had the right intentions. NAR wanted to stop listings from disappearing. But it was the wrong strategy, and it did the opposite. Once a listing is publicly marketed, it must go into the MLS within one business day.

Keep it quiet, though, and it falls under the office exclusive exemption. That does not tell agents to share. It tells them to stop advertising and keep the listing inside their own company. The brokerage itself became the pocket.

A rule meant to bring listings into the open pushed many further underground. As I wrote earlier this year, a Redfin analysis found pocket listings rose 67 percent after CCP passed. NAR leaves enforcement to local MLSs, and in a lot of markets, they have quietly stopped enforcing it or issuing penalties. A rule on the books but not enforced protects no one. It only confuses the agents trying to follow it.

For newer agents: Before CCP, a seller could hire one brokerage to market and show her home exclusively. But those exclusives usually stayed out of the MLS, so other agents often never knew the house existed. The true exclusive keeps what sellers liked about the old way and adds what was always missing: every agent knowing the house is for sale. That is the replacement.

Let’s give our homeowner the third door: one agent, full marketing and a way for the right buyer to find her. That is real seller choice.

Until a model like this is in place, we are still hurting buyers and sellers. Period.

The views and opinions expressed here are those of the contributor and separate from the Inman newsroom.

Darryl Davis is the CEO of Darryl Davis Seminars. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

#5569. Inside Jensen Huang’s $53 Million Property Portfolio as the Nvidia CEO Resigns After Affair with Suspected Chinese Spy

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned after having extramarital affairs with a business executive—Alice Huang, who the U.S. government has determined to be working with Chinese intelligence—and a Nvidia employee.

Finance chief Colette Kress will work as the interim CEO while the company looks for a permanent replacement, Nvidia said Thursday.

External and internal candidates will be considered as the company searches for a Jensen's successor.

“Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world," the statement read. "The board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry."

The news follows a Nov. 8 statement from Huang, who admitted to the affairs.

“I was unfaithful to my wife,” Huang stated in a previous message to the company. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

While the board of Nvidia claimed it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised,” an external counsel will be selected to investigate

The revelation, first reported by the New York Times, is expected to have an economic impact not only on Nvidia—whose stock price has already taken a hit—but on the artificial intelligence industry as a whole, given the chipmaker’s influence.

The company was the first in the world to reach a valuation of $5 trillion after seeing unprecedented growth amid the artificial intelligence bom.

According to the New York Times, Nvidia is responsible for making "the most essential and expensive component in almost every A.I. scheme," a collection of hardware designed specifically to bolster artificial intelligence.

Its ascent to the pinnacle of tech success began as something of a slow burn in 1993, when Huang, 63, launched the company alongside Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem.

At the time, Nvidia was viewed very much as a niche—and fledgling—tech startup. However, it has since grown into an industry giant, inking deals with all manner of brands and agencies, from the U.S. Department of Energy to Nokia, Samsung, and Sam Altman's company, OpenAI, the parent to ChatGPT.

Huang's own net worth has skyrocketed with that accelerated growth. He is currently one of the 10 richest men in the world with an estimated fortune of $174 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

The number of men who can claim to top him in personal fortune can be counted on two hands—and include the likes of Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg, and Larry Ellison.

Like others in the exclusive "super billionaires" club—men and women with net worths exceeding $50 billion—Huang has invested his fortune across diverse ventures and companies, while managing to remain in this elite group.

However, he has also followed in the footsteps of his fellow tech titans by pouring a sizable chunk of his fortune into real estate—amassing an incredibly impressive portfolio of homes from Hawaii to California.

Huang, who was born in Taiwan in 1963, spent his early childhood in Thailand. He moved to the U.S. after his father visited America and vowed to bring his sons, he previously told CNBC.

Ahead of his move, his mom would teach him 10 words from the dictionary each day to help him learn English, despite not knowing the language herself.

At age 9, Huang and his brother headed to America to live with their relatives. His early life in the States was starkly different from the current lavish life he lives.

When he was a child, his aunt and uncle accidentally enrolled him in a Baptist boarding school in Kentucky, thinking it was a prestigious prep school.

While there, he became a target for bullies and teasing due to his long hair and accent.

As the future of Nvidia's stock remains unclear, Realtor.com® has lifted the lid on the tech tycoon's expansive property portfolio.

In 2017, the tech tycoon splashed over $38 million for a sprawling mansion in San Francisco's Gold Coast neighborhood.

Property records seen by Realtor.com reveal that the dwelling is tied to Riva LLC, which is managed by Michael A. Chojnacki, a tax lawyer who looks after the finances of Huang and his wife, Lori.

The luxe abode in the Pacific Heights neighborhood spans 11,400 square feet and boasts a curved roof, panoramic views of the Golden Gate Bridge, and many bedrooms and bathrooms.

The limestone mansion has a large terrace, a three-car garage, two wine rooms, an outdoor kitchen, an elevator, a theater, and a gym.

Developer Bill Campbell, of Marble Management, previously told the Wall Street Journal that construction on the dwelling took nearly four years.

Of course, Huang is also neighbors with Ellison and David Sachs.

Huang previously owned two starter homes in San Jose, CA. The first one, which measured 1,500 square feet and had three bedrooms, was sold for $185,000 in 1988—just five years before he founded Nvidia.

Elsewhere in California, the tech mogul owns a lavish dwelling in Los Altos, just 15 miles west of Nvidia's headquarters, which is in Santa Clara County.

He purchased the property in 2003 for $6.9 million. It measures over 7,000 square feet and has six bedrooms.

The elegant two-story estate features lush landscaping and a resort-style pool.

To top off his property portfolio, the businessman also snapped up a home on the south side of Maui in 2004.

The dwelling is situated in the Wailea Resort, which houses 14 other properties behind a gate and spans 10.5 acres on the ocean.

The home features seven bedrooms and was built in 2008. He paid $7.8 million for the abode.

The property spans 8,000 square feet and is surrounded by lush greenery.

In 2023, Maui experienced deadly wildfires, and the Huangs "donated significantly to local relief efforts,” an Nvidia spokesperson said at the time.

She previously wrote for Daily Mail, True Urban Culture, and JMedia Corporation, where she specialized in covering celebrities, relationships, psychology, and gender issues. She has a bachelor's degree in journalism from Pace University, where she received the James Rose Award for excellence in journalism. #5568. The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

If millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right? Wrong. Just over half of millennials own their home. For the rest, housing costs have soared so much in recent years that skipping the avocado toast in their 20s wouldn’t have made a dent.

The story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing. Elder millennials who bought a home in their early 30s had it better than baby boomers did at the same age: Historically low mortgage rates and higher household incomes meant those millennials spent about 27% of their income on housing at age 30, compared with 36% for boomers. Then the pandemic changed the math. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% to nearly 7%, and home prices surged. Since rates rose above 6% in 2022, elder millennials have spent up to 35% of their income on monthly mortgage payments, compared with roughly 25% for boomers at the same age–even though millennials earn more, adjusted for inflation.

Boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day. They’d be right: Rates peaked at over 16% in 1981 and stayed in double digits for much of the decade. But prices were lower. In the 1980s, when many boomers were in their 30s, the typical U.S. home sold for about $235,000 to $265,000 in today’s dollars. When elder millennials reached the same age–prime homebuying age–in the 2010s and 2020s, typical prices ranged from about $275,000 to $455,000.

Key takeaway: Buying at the wrong time was painful for both generations, but boomers had a better chance to recover. Falling rates throughout the late 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s gave them many opportunities to refinance into lower payments. Millennials who bought before 2022 secured historically low mortgages; those who bought later—or never managed to buy—face a much less forgiving market. Of course, it’s possible the market could become more forgiving for millennials over time; rates may eventually fall significantly enough that many millennials have the opportunity to refinance into lower payments.

This is based on an analysis of Redfin and U.S. Census data. A few notes to help contextualize the numbers: All dollar figures are adjusted for inflation. Much of the data illustrates each generation’s typical experience at a given age, combining everyone in that generation who has reached that age, whenever that happened for them. Because millennials are still aging into their 40s, for example, our 40-to-44 figures only capture the oldest millennials, who hit those ages between 2021 and 2025. All boomers have been through that age range, so their figures include the whole generation. Please see the end of this report for a detailed methodology.

In their early 30s, elder millennials who bought a home spent a smaller share of their income on housing than boomers did at the same age, despite much higher home prices. Imagine a median-earning millennial born in 1984 who bought a home at age 30. They would have spent around 27% of their income to purchase the typical home, within the “don’t spend more than 30% of your income on housing costs” rule of thumb.

Two factors helped: cheap borrowing and higher household incomes. Millennials benefited from roughly a decade of historically low mortgage rates; they fell below 3% in 2021. Millennials also tend to have higher household incomes than boomers did at the same age. At age 37, the typical elder millennial household earned an average of $100,000, compared with $88,000 when boomers were that age. The discrepancy is partly because two-income households are more common today. About 78% of women participate in the U.S. workforce, up from roughly 60% in 1980. It’s also worth noting that millennials typically work similar hours for more money than baby boomers at the same life stage.

The millennial advantage didn’t last. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% in late 2021 to nearly 7% in late 2022, after home prices had surged about 40% nationwide during the pandemic homebuying frenzy. Rising rates often cool prices, but this time, prices didn’t fall. That mix of high prices and mortgage rates that had doubled from their pandemic-era low meant Americans had to spend a much higher share of their income to buy a home. Imagine that same millennial, born in 1984: If they bought a home at age 40 instead of 30, their housing costs shot up to about 35% of their income.

Rising prices and rates also priced many Americans completely out of the housing market, which is why elder millennials have a lower homeownership rate than baby boomers at the same age.

“For millennials who haven’t yet bought a home, affordability is a challenge. But it’s important to remember that you’re not trying to climb Mount Everest, you’re just trying to get back to 2018 or 2019, which was the last time the average homebuyer was spending just about 30% of their income on housing,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economic research. “Before the pandemic, younger generations actually had it easier than the ones before them. But then home prices surged during the pandemic homebuying frenzy and mortgage rates shot up, while incomes kept growing at a normal pace–and the advantage flipped. If you bought in 2020 or 2021, you’re coming out ahead, but those years were the exception, not the rule. One piece of hope for younger Americans who haven’t yet bought a home: Home prices are already falling in parts of the U.S. and they’re softening in others, which means we could be headed back to 2018 or 2019 levels sooner rather than later.”

Millennials are also contending with other major expenses; childcare costs are squeezing them particularly hard. A recent Redfin analysis found that housing and childcare consume more than half of the typical American’s household income. Student loans are another big expense; millennials have significantly more student loan debt than boomers did at the same age.

Adult Gen Zers, who are in their twenties, are tracking behind millennials at the same stage of life. Gen Zers have spent anywhere from 40% of 60% of their income to buy the typical home since they’ve reached homebuying age. That’s partly because they’re still young enough that they haven’t yet hit their earnings peak, so their current income is lower than older generations, and partly because housing costs are higher than in the past. But as Gen Zers move through their careers, their earnings are likely to grow substantially, as they have for every generation before them. Combined with a gradual normalization in housing costs, homeownership should become increasingly attainable over time.

Baby boomers faced their own affordability crisis when they were young, in the 1980s. In their early 20s, the typical boomer household who bought a home would have spent more than 60% of its income on housing costs, reflecting the era’s runaway inflation and double-digit mortgage rates.

But their housing burden fell quickly as they aged, dropping to around 40% of income by their late 20s and 26% by their late 30s. Baby boomers’ homeownership rate steadily rose from about half in 1985 to over 70% by the late 1990s, and it kept climbing after that. By their 40s and 50s, the share of homebuyers’ income spent on housing had settled into the low-to-mid 20% range, lower than millennials at the same point in their life.

Much of that relief came from the same force that had hurt them initially—mortgage rates—as rates gradually declined through the 1980s and 1990s, letting many boomers refinance into far more manageable payments even as home prices kept climbing.

Millennials haven’t had the same opportunity. Those who bought before 2022 locked in historically low rates, while those who bought later faced a costly combination of high prices and climbing rates. Would-be buyers who couldn’t afford that combination were left out altogether.

“The housing market has historically been better for baby boomers than younger generations because lower home prices and higher rates are preferable to higher home prices and lower rates,” Zhao said. “You can refinance your rate into a lower housing payment, and that’s exactly what boomers did: They refinanced for up to 40 years as rates kept falling. Then home prices soared, which is why a lot of boomers are rich in real estate.”

That dynamic shows up clearly when you ask people directly. In a recent Redfin survey, more than three-quarters (76%) of baby boomers homeowners said they can easily afford their payment, while the rest struggle. Roughly half (53%) of millennial homeowners can easily afford their payment, and the other half struggle.

The same generational squeeze shows up in the reasons people are staying put in their current home. Among people unlikely to move soon, 43% of millennials cited high home prices as a reason, compared with 31% of boomers. Three in 10 (30%) millennials pointed to high mortgage rates, versus just 18% of boomers, likely because many baby boomers have paid off their mortgage and built up substantial equity. This is from a Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos in May 2026, fielded to 4,000 U.S. residents.

Consider two hypothetical couples. Alex and Jordan are millennials born in 1984 and live on two incomes, a common setup for millennial households. Pat and Chris are baby boomers born in 1956 and got by on one, more typical for their generation. The numbers below show what it would have cost each couple to buy a home to buy a home in their early 30s and their late 30s.

This analysis uses income data from 1976 to 2025 from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS ASEC), accessed through IPUMS. The sample includes household heads aged 19 and older, and results are weighted using CPS household weights.

Each household is assigned to a generation based on the age of the household head in the survey year.

Home prices. We start with the 2025 median sale price of U.S. single-family homes from Redfin data ($456,409). Prices for earlier years are estimated by scaling that 2025 price back using the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index from 1987 onward and the FHFA All-Transactions House Price Index for years before 1987. Both indexes are averaged by year.

Monthly housing payment. For each year, we calculate the monthly payment to buy a median-priced home. It covers principal, interest, property taxes and homeowners insurance. We assume:

Income and inflation. Household income is total household income as reported in the CPS ASEC. All income and payment figures are converted to 2025 dollars using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).

Share of income spent on housing. For each generation and age, we calculate the median monthly housing payment and the median household income, and divide the payment by one-twelfth of the income.

How to read the results by age.  Much of the data in this report shows each generation’s typical experience at a given age. Because a generation spans many birth years, people born at the start of that generation turn, say, 40 in a different calendar year than people born at the end of it. For this analysis, each age point combines averages for everyone from that generation who has reached that age, in whatever year that actually was for them. For instance, millennials (born 1981 to 1996) have only had the oldest members of their generation—those born in the early-to-mid 1980s—reach their 40s so far. So when we show what the typical 40-to-44-year-old millennial paid for housing, we’re only capturing people who hit that age between 2021 and 2025. Younger millennials haven’t gotten there yet. Baby boomers (born 1946 to 1964) are fully through that age range, their 40-to-44 data point include averages from all boomers.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. #5567. Zillow Rental Market Report: Demand for Single-Family Rentals Surges

Zillow’s latest Rental Market Report shows that demand for renting single-family homes has risen, with consumers noting that they would need a $14,408 pay raise to cover the monthly costs of owning a home, even before saving for a down payment. Nationally, the typical single-family rent is $2,243 a month, compared with $2,603 a month to own a single-family home with 20% down, or $360 more each month.

“For a growing number of households, renting a house is a legitimate financial strategy,” said Kara Ng, senior economist at Zillow. “You get many of the lifestyle benefits, but it takes less income than owning and keeps more flexibility in the monthly budget. That’s the appeal for the deliberate renter.”

The size of the raise depends on the market According to Zillow, the pay raise needed to buy is now the highest since early 2025, more than double the $6,463 it took in February 2026, when mortgage rates briefly fell below 6%. The gap looks very different from market to market. It’s largest in San Jose, where the income needed to buy ($404,925) is more than double the income needed to rent ($190,561), a gap of $214,364. The next largest gap is in San Francisco ($139,353), followed by San Diego ($84,101), New York ($78,208) and Los Angeles ($78,003). The smallest annual gaps are in Pittsburgh ($2,554), Houston ($4,500) and Cincinnati ($4,774). Buffalo is the only market where buying would not require a raise.

Even with such a raise, would-be buyers still face another hurdle: saving a 20% down payment. About 30% of mortgage buyers use a gift or loan from family or friends, and 46% draw on two or more sources, including the use of down payment assistance programs, according to Zillow’s 2026 Consumer Housing Trends Report.

In addition to the monthly cost, households deciding between renting and buying should weigh the upfront costs of buying, the chance to build equity and the opportunity for renters to invest their down payment instead. Zillow’s rent vs. buy research puts the national break-even timeline—the number of years a household would need to own before buying comes out ahead—at 7.8 years with 20% down.

Rental demand keeps climbing As renting a house becomes an increasingly better value, more shoppers are turning to rentals. Rental demand is up 22.1% year over year nationwide, according to the Zillow Observed Renter Demand Index (ZORDI). Demand for single-family rentals is up 24.3%, roughly double the 12.1% rise for multifamily rentals.

Rental demand surges in the Bay Area and the Sun Belt Demand rose the most in San Jose, where ZORDI is up 78.9% from a year ago, followed by San Francisco (60.5%), Austin (59.6%), Miami (51.5%) and Jacksonville (47.9%). San Jose and San Francisco are also among the markets where buying is furthest out of reach, and where rents are rising quickly, up 8.9% and 12.2% respectively. In Austin, Miami and Jacksonville, rent growth is more moderate, at 1.1%, 2.1% and 2.6%.

Not every market is following the national trend. ZORDI is down year over year in Providence (-4.3%), Richmond (-1.9%), Baltimore (-1.7%), Hartford (-1.3%) and Washington, D.C. (-0.9%).

#5566. Google retools Kubernetes for AI agents instead of building a new stack

Agentic workloads are pushing Kubernetes into territory its creators never planned for. Agents generate untrusted code on the fly, sit idle for long stretches and churn through pods at a pace that strains the orchestrator’s control plane.

Cloud providers are now rethinking how general-purpose a cluster should be. Google LLC’s answer is to stop treating every cluster as an infinitely flexible engine and tune each one into a runtime optimized for its workload, according to Jago Macleod (pictured, right), director of engineering for Kubernetes and Google Kubernetes Engine at Google Cloud.

“There isn’t enough memory. There aren’t enough machines. So we have to get more efficient. And so one of the ways that we do that is to focus the Kubernetes cluster on the workload it’s running, and optimize it for that specific workload,” Macleod said.

Macleod and Jaana Dogan (pictured, left), principal engineer at Google Cloud, spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Google is customizing Kubernetes for agentic workloads without fragmenting the open-source ecosystem. (* Disclosure below.)

Kubernetes was built for microservices, then stretched to handle training jobs in which a single pod claims an entire node, Macleod explained. Agents are a different beast again, and some teams have resorted to building custom control planes just to cope.

“I think the agentic workloads are so different in the thrash and the churn that they represent is really not what we built Kubernetes for at all,” Macleod said. “And then agentic applications are almost the polar opposite, which is, you know, in the naive implementation, you just have as many pods as you can possibly fit, and so then the API machinery is running into limits.”

Platform teams have spent a decade making Kubernetes their compute fabric, and customers told Google they did not want agents to fragment it, Dogan explained. Google’s response is Agent Substrate, which runs AI agents in sandboxes directly on Kubernetes. The company donated the project to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation and recently released version 1.0. Because agents write their own code, that code is untrusted by default and needs sandboxing and network guardrails, according to Dogan. Customers also flagged a costly inefficiency.

“For example, our customers came to us, ‘Hey, majority of the time our agents are idle, but we have to allocate a sandbox all through the lifetime of a session,'” Dogan said. That means wasting a lot of CPU cycles, she explained.

Coding agents are also changing how engineers work, producing more prototypes and smaller, more focused teams, Dogan noted. As agentic workloads multiply, human judgment grows more valuable rather than less, according to Macleod.

“It’s not really, you know, fire off a prompt and forget it and walk away,” Macleod said. “It’s just a different level in the system where you’re applying your judgment and expertise. And that has never been more important.”

(* Disclosure: Google Cloud sponsored this segment of theCUBE. Neither Google Cloud nor other sponsors have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE.)

#5565. Zedd Parts With Hollywood Hills Home in $4 Million Sale—After Nearly a Decade of Ownership

DJ and producer Zedd has offloaded his Hollywood Hills pad for $4.25 million to a couple who plan to carry out a complete overhaul of one of the rooms.

The Grammy winner, whose real name is Anton Zaslavski, first listed the property in October 2025 for $5.5 million, before trimming the price to $4.49 million.

He snapped up the home in 2014 for $3.9 million. Now, the property has been sold in an off-market deal, as first reported by Mansion Global.

According to the outlet, the hitmaker sold the abode to a couple who reside in the area. The buyers were represented by Brandon Meneses of the Beverly Hills Estates and Janelle Meneses of The Agency.

“They’ve been looking for a long time and ultimately felt this was the right home for them,” Brandon told Mansion Global.

According to the agent, the buyers are big fans of the DJ and his in-home recording studio helped push them to snap up the property.

“They are actually huge fans of Zedd, so the music studio was an enticing factor in their decision making,” he said. They plan to transform the space into a movie theater.

The home was built in 1950, spans 3,381 square feet, and sits on just over a third of an acre.

Surrounded by lush greenery, the home features large glass doors that flood the spaces with natural light, and the chef's kitchen is equipped with state-of-the-art appliances and a glass-enclosed wine cellar.

The primary suite is the ultimate space for relaxation with its fireplace, spa-inspired bathroom, and walk-in closet.

Meanwhile, the outdoor area boasts a pool, hot tub, and fire pit—offering yet more spaces to get cozy on chilly California evenings.

#5564. Americans cling to homeownership as affordability gap widens

New ACS data shows incomes up 3.9 percent, but buyers still need $110,700 to comfortably afford a median-priced home.

Americans are clinging to the dream of homeownership — even though their incomes are barely enough to sustain it.

The U.S. Census Bureau released its 2025 American Community Survey 1-Year data on Thursday, which includes statistics on 40-plus topics, including housing. The national homeownership rate held steady at 65.3 percent, only 0.1 percentage points below the 5-year high of 65.4 percent. The majority of homeowners carry a mortgage (59 percent), with the real median mortgage payment increasing 2.4 percent year over year to $1,598.

Total housing costs, which may include expenses like homeowners association (HOA) fees, maintenance and repairs, increased 3.5 percent year over year from $2,090 to $2,163. Households now spend 21.9 percent of income on these costs, up 0.5 percentage points and just 8.1 points below the widely recognized 30 percent affordability threshold.

Median household incomes are edging up (+1.2 percent yoy after inflation), but Realtor.com Senior Economist Hannah Jones said it’s not enough to keep up with median home value growth.

“New 2025 American Community Survey data show median household income rose 3.9 percent to $84,780, with incomes up nominally in 49 of 50 states,” she said in an emailed statement. “But housing remained out of reach for many households. With a median listing price near $424,000 in 2025, mortgage rates averaging 6.6 percent, a 20 percent down payment, and taxes and insurance at roughly 1.7 percent of home value, a buyer needed about $110,700 to afford a median-priced home, roughly $26,000 more than the typical household earned.”

“Closing that gap would have required incomes to be 30.5 percent higher, prices about $99,000 lower or mortgage rates near 3.5 percent,” she added. “That affordability challenge has persisted, even as the year started with a promise.”

Jones said the market was primed in homebuyers’ favor at the beginning of the year, with sub-6 percent mortgage rates. However, macroeconomic and geopolitical conflicts have pushed mortgage rates up — now in the 7.30 percent range — leaving most homebuyers unable to take advantage of better inventory levels and falling list prices.

“Even assuming incomes have grown in line with recent wage gains of 3 percent to 4 percent since 2025, the typical household income would still be roughly $28,000 short,” she said. “Demand has cooled in response to higher rates, and pending sales fell 4.1 percent year over year in September, the steepest annual drop since March 2025, even as inventory approached pre-pandemic levels and prices softened.”

Realtor.com has released several reports on how homebuyers can attempt to make the math work, even as rates fluctuate. They can improve their credit scores, increase their down payments, shop lenders and build a budget buffer to help them absorb a 0.50 percent rate increase or decrease.

As for what lies ahead this year, homebuyers aren’t expected to receive mortgage rate relief.

The Federal Reserve held the federal funds rate steady (at 3.75 to 4 percent) at its Oct. 28 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting. The federal funds rate affects how banks and financial institutions set rates, including mortgage rates, but a change doesn’t guarantee mortgage rates will move in tandem.

The 10-Year Treasury Yield has the greatest impact on mortgage rates as lenders add a spread — or percentage markup — on top of it. The spread reflects the effects of monetary and fiscal policies, economic growth, inflation, higher origination costs and the gap between mortgage-backed securities (MBS) and Treasury yields.

“Whether the Fed hikes or holds this month, homebuyers shouldn’t expect a big change in mortgage rates,” First American Senior Economist Sam Williamson told Inman on Wednesday after the Fed’s FOMC meeting. “With another hike widely expected in December and further increases possible next year, borrowing costs are likely to remain elevated, keeping many buyers and sellers on the sidelines. But not everyone has the luxury of waiting. New jobs, growing families and other life events will keep some buyers moving forward, even as higher rates delay moves that can wait.”

Jones said mortgage rates will remain “the swing factor” and will shape next year’s American Community Survey results.

“For rates to trend lower, inflation has to cool, and the latest data shows it is moving the wrong way,” she said. “Annual inflation rose to 3.7 percent in September as energy prices surged amid the conflict in the Middle East, and core inflation edged up to 2.6 percent.”

“With the Fed focused on bringing inflation back under control while protecting the labor market, a significant drop in mortgage rates is unlikely in the near term,” she added. “For buyers on the fence, though, today’s mix of more inventory, more price cuts and more room to negotiate is the best they’ve had in years.”

#5563. 4 insights from Block Builderlab Launch Event 2026: AI agents join the team as working colleagues

At Block Builderlab Launch Event 2026, AI agents moved out of single-player chat windows and into shared workspaces. There they work beside people as named, auditable members of the team. Block Inc. built these tools to run itself as an intelligence company, and it is now offering them to other businesses, building on Buzz, its open-source workspace for humans and AI agents. Block introduced Builderlab as a set of tools for teams and AI agents to work together.

The next phase will depend less on how capable a single agent becomes than on how well agents collaborate, share an organization’s context and stay inside firm security boundaries. Block plans to spread that model with open-source code, model-agnostic design and hosted infrastructure. The company is making that push while its core business delivers a third straight guidance raise.

“If you’re talking about making the whole organization more productive, you need to break down these distinctions between what the software does and what the people do,” said Paul Gillin (pictured, right), enterprise editor of SiliconANGLE Media Inc.

Alison Kosik (left) and co-host Gillin spoke with industry experts during Block Builderlab Launch Event 2026 in San Francisco. The interviews covered Block’s open-source business model, agents with their own identities, the shift from prompting to overnight delegation and the security controls that let enterprises trust autonomous systems. (* Disclosure below.)

Here are four standout insights from the event:

Builderlab gives developers endlessly customizable agents on an open-source plug-in architecture, and the launch audience of application builders cheered the idea, according to Gillin. Agents in Buzz have names, avatars and personalities. That shifts the focus from switching among software-as-a-service applications to the work itself, and it could threaten SaaS companies. The revenue model follows the classic open-source pattern of giving the software away and charging for the convenience of a hosted cloud service, he explained. Block said little about commercialization or about Cash App, which brings in 60% of its revenue, according to Gillin.

Most AI tools are built for one person at a time, so each user becomes the bottleneck when results have to be shared with a team, noted Lucas Isaza, product lead of Buzz at Block. In Buzz, agents have their own identities, can be tagged like colleagues and leave an audit trail of every action. Plug-ins, added after the first version launched in July, let anyone reshape the interface. Nontechnical staff, such as account managers building personal dashboards, have been the heaviest users of the companion apps platform. Companies can self-host the open-source code, use a free tier or add funds for remote agents, models and extra storage, Isaza highlighted.

Builderlab sits as an interface layer above the models, so Buzz can use agents from any AI lab and switch to the newest frontier model as it arrives, emphasized Brad Axen, head of AI capabilities at Block. Remote agents run in central cloud environments that are easier to secure than laptops. People can hand them large assignments overnight and act as reviewers. Instead of soft guardrails, agents run on secure building blocks that never grant them permission for certain actions. Some teams have shipped software releases 50% to 75% faster. Axen expects agents to need much less human steering within the next year because they already sit inside the conversation.

Securing agents that act on their own does not mean starting over, because principles such as least privilege, isolated environments and egress controls still apply, shared James Nettesheim, chief information security officer and head of enterprise technology at Block. Builderlab gives every agent a full identity owned by a human, runs it in hardened cloud virtual machines and records its actions in a cryptographically signed ledger that cannot be altered. Block is also building information flow control, which tags data from sensitive sources so the security policy travels with that data and blocks leaks. AI already reviews Block’s code and sorts its security alerts. Nettesheim added that agents let defenders keep pace with attackers’ machine speed.

#5562. Nearly Half of Gen Z Admit Skipping Rent or Mortgages Just To Fund Holiday Spending

The holiday season is an exciting time, but it can also be very expensive.

If you’re careless, festive gatherings, gifts, and travel may leave you in debt well into the new year.

A new survey by Accredited Debt Relief found that 67% of Gen Z have taken on or expect to take on holiday debt this year. And nearly 15% of Americans are still paying off last year’s holiday debt.

Furthermore, 46% of Gen Z respondents have delayed or skipped rent or mortgage payments to afford holiday spending, compared with 28% of millennials, 14% of Gen X, and 3% of baby boomers.

“Holiday spending should never come at the expense of someone's financial stability, but these findings show just how difficult it can be to balance financial responsibilities with the social expectations and pressure to create a memorable holiday," said Bobbi Rebell, chief financial education adviser at Accredited Debt Relief in San Diego.

"Making tough choices around spending may feel like you’re disappointing those you care about, but protecting your financial future needs to be non-negotiable."

If you’re worried about holiday debt or keeping up with housing expenses, a bit of planning, dedication, and creativity can help you enjoy the season without putting your finances on the line.

Experts agree that your rent or mortgage and related bills should always come first, before you spend money on holiday extras.

“I’ve spent a lot of time helping people who have struggled to keep their homes. And I’ve seen how hard it can be to recover once things get out of control and they start falling behind on mortgage payments,” says Casey Yontz, bankruptcy attorney at Yontz Law, PLLC in Phoenix.

One missed mortgage payment probably isn’t going to get you into foreclosure, but it can be the beginning of a snowball of serious delinquency.

And depending on the terms of your loan, you can incur late fees on your missed payment.

Once that payment is 30 days late, it could get reported to credit bureaus and take a serious toll on your credit score. If you continue to fall behind, foreclosure is a possibility.

“It’s true that under federal mortgage-servicing rules, foreclosure generally cannot begin until you are 120 days behind. But this doesn’t mean you should treat these 120 days as extra time to spend money on something else, like holiday gifts or travel,” Yontz explains.

According to Yontz, there’s no holiday present that’s worth putting your family's home at risk.

Howard Dvorkin, chairman at Debt.com in Fort Lauderdale, FL, shares those thoughts.

“What’s worse: Someone thinking you cheaped out on their holiday gift? Or sleeping outside? Financially speaking, housing must be your top priority. I’ve yet to meet a client’s friends and family who would want you to jeopardize your housing,” says Dvorkin.

If you're still paying for the 2025 holidays, putting 2026 holiday expenses on another credit card is not the solution.

“Holiday debt is an indicator that your holiday spending is beyond your budget, and might be a little bit out of control,” says Yontz.

Stop adding to it, and be honest with yourself about the math.

Look at your actual income versus expenses and debt numbers.

Ask yourself these questions: How much do I still owe? What’s the interest rate? How much can I afford to pay each month after paying my living expenses?

“Try to prioritize higher-interest card debt first. Pay more than the minimum payments, because making minimum payments on credit cards is like throwing buckets of water on a five-alarm fire,” say Yontz.

Dvorkin also recommends seeking professional help.

“Call a certified credit counselor and receive a free, in-depth debt analysis. With that in hand, you can consider all your options and make an informed choice,” explains Dvorkin.

Depending on your situation, a debt management program may make sense. It can reduce your total credit card payments by up to half without any long-term damage to your credit score.

“It can also lower your interest rate to 10% or less—sometimes even zero. You pay a fee for a professional to set this up, but those fees are dwarfed by how much you save,” Dvorkin adds.

Holiday spending should come out of whatever disposable income you have left after paying for your necessities like housing, gas, and groceries.

These tips can help you enjoy the holiday season while still keeping your finances in check:

You'll save more if you focus on what to buy than how you buy it. That’s why a holiday budget is so important.

“Nothing evokes images of Scrooge more than sitting down with pen and paper and listing everything you'll buy. But we don't live in 'A Christmas Carol.' We have the technology to make holiday budgeting a breeze. There’s no shortage of apps that act as busy little elves and do the work for you,” say Dvorkin.

Inviting family members over for a no-cost game night will be far more memorable than buying each of them a shiny, new gadget.

“I just lost my mom this spring, and I can guarantee you that no present could ever be better than more time with her. Presents don’t matter, people do, in my opinion," Yontz explains.

You’ll notice a lot of companies that will let you buy something for the holidays and pay for it over time, especially if you’re shopping online.

Unfortunately, they’re not making your purchase any cheaper. In fact, you will probably end up paying more with interest and fees.

“They tempt you, and you pay for it. Don’t fall down the buy now, pay later chimney of misfit payments,” says Yontz.

Train your brain to dislike overspending.

Do some research on how much you’re actually paying for credit card debt if you have it. Notice how much you’re paying in interest when you buy something.

“When I started doing this, I felt like I was being taken advantage of and that was enough for me to not want to use credit cards,” Yontz explains.

At the end of the day, the holidays should be something your family remembers fondly, not something you're still paying for next Christmas.

#5560. Amid ‘tough market,’ Rocket revenues are up

Rocket’s Q3 earnings, explained: Revenue, market share, Redfin metrics and the questions agents should be asking about the integrated model.

Detroit-based Rocket Companies on Thursday announced its third-quarter 2026 earnings, and despite being in what CEO Varun Krishna said “might be the toughest mortgage market in 30 years,” revenues increased.

The company generated net revenue of $3.28 billion and adjusted revenue of $2.57 billion; net income was $709 million and adjusted net income was $419 million. The company’s Q3 adjusted EBITDA was $748 million (a 29 percent margin, up from 28 percent from last quarter).

Rocket also reported $11.4 billion in liquidity (a record), including $2.7 billion in cash and cash equivalents.

“Rocket gained market share in both purchase and refinance, quarter over quarter and year over year, and delivered our highest profitability margin in nearly five years, even as mortgage rates climbed to a three-year high,” Krishna said in a statement. “We didn’t spend the last three years waiting for rates to fall. We acquired distribution, connected real estate and mortgage, and invested heavily in technology.”

The company’s third-quarter net income compares with a $124 million loss in the same period of 2025.

“The market is literally testing every single lender,” Krishna said during the company’s earnings call Thursday. “If you have a strong business model, it’s gonna shine through, but if you have a flaw, it’s gonna get exposed.”

He pointed to Redfin as a source of new mortgage clients. “Redfin is the doorway to Rocket,” Krishna said. According to the company, the number of Redfin visitors who started a purchase mortgage from a listing rose 50 percent year over year. Cumulative unique listings displayed through Rocket’s partnership with Compass reached nearly 40,000, up from about 25,000 in the prior quarter.

Brian Brown, Rocket’s president, chief financial officer and treasurer, said the fourth quarter will come in well below the third, with refinance volume falling as much as 50 percent. Rocket expects adjusted revenue between $2.1 billion and $2.3 billion for the period. “The fourth quarter will be harder still,” Brown said. “We’re ready for it.”

In Q2 2026 earnings, Rocket Companies reported $2.78 billion in revenue for a $229 million profit, up from $34 million year over year. Company executives credited its broker partners with more than $2 billion in net rate lock volume through its Compass partnership, a three-year collaboration undertaken in February.

In March, Rocket and Redfin joined Compass International Holdings in writing an open letter to multiple listing service leaders, urging them to support phased listing distribution and stop fining agents for what they called “seller-directed marketing plans.”

Rocket Companies now encompasses Rocket Mortgage, the U.S.’s largest lender, which includes Mr. Cooper, the country’s largest mortgage servicer, acquired just over a year ago; Redfin’s brokerage and home search portal; Rocket Close, its title and closing company; and Rocket Money and Rocket Loans, its consumer finance brands.

Christy Murdock and Lucy Cohen Blatter contributed to this story.

#5559. Paris Signal Week looks to bridge crypto and institutional finance

Paris Blockchain Week is now Signal Week, a reflection of cryptocurrency’s global expansion.

The newly rebranded event is joining forces with RAISE Summit, the annual AI and networking conference, and Machina Summit, Europe’s leading physical AI event. Event organizers expect approximately 2,500 attendees, highlighting the growing profile of blockchain technology.

“The industry has changed a lot,” said Michael Amar (pictured), chairman of RAISE Summit and co-founder of Signal Week. “We really want to be the place where we bridge traditional finance and digital assets. It’s where the market is finally, and we are embracing it completely. We have the desire to go abroad to launch other conferences. So it made sense that … we join everything under the same roof, but different flows, different marketing and different ticketing.”

Amar and Charlie Meraud (pictured), chairman of RAISE Summit and co-founder of Signal Week, spoke with theCUBE host Gemma Allen, during an exclusive interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed what to expect at the 2027 event and the evolution of cryptocurrency. (* Disclosure below.)

Signal Week is designed to cover the intersection between institutional finance and digital assets. Since its founding, the crypto market has grown to $40 billion in tokenized real-world assets, or RWA, according to Meraud. The week will also encompass the CXO Summit, a private gathering of C-suite executives.

“The CXO Summit is organizing a roundtable under Chatham House rules with these … crypto-native players discussing all sophisticated topics around what they are building and how they can partner all year long,” he said. “This is the kind of activation that makes people book a flight, buy a ticket and come to Signal Week. The industry needed a room for these players to connect and start actually doing business.”

Both founders see facilitating conversations between crypto leaders and traditional finance executives as one of the primary goals of the conference. The chief executive officers of Kaiko, Morpho and Fireblocks, all leading digital asset companies, are expected to attend. European Union regulators will also be present, Amar and Meraud emphasize, which will be critical for understanding the future of AI-powered finance.

“We’re creating those moments where people can get the most out of the conference,” Amar said. “If you talk about the C-suite, people coming from traditional finance and meeting the makers of the crypto industry, we’re creating the space where they will have talks in a very small room where actually we go very much into the details of the use cases of the implementation of a digital asset solution for a bank, for example.”

Another key topic at Signal Week and RAISE Summit will be custody, the safekeeping of private keys that allow a person to prove they control an address and the cryptocurrency it holds. Security has long been a divisive issue for cryptocurrency, spurring a variety of solutions.

“When we started … self-custody was one of the promised digital assets,” Meraud said. “A lot of players have been offering different ways of custodying digital assets. And having the most sophisticated solution coming to Signal Week, explaining all the new features, they’ve been building over the years is one of the reasons financial institutions are willing to connect and network with our audience.”

#5557. Khloé Kardashian Says Lamar Odom Is ‘Dead’ to Her After His Comments About Marrying for Family’s ‘Lifestyle’—Inside Their Former Marital Mansion

Khloé Kardashian is drawing a line through her relationship with her ex-husband, Lamar Odom.

On the Nov. 11 episode of “The Kardashians,” Kardashian got candid about what the former NBA star  said regarding their marriage in the Netflix documentary "Untold: The Death and Life of Lamar Odom."

“I did watch the Lamar documentary. I’m not too thrilled about it,” she said.

The mom of two, who was involved in the making of the documentary, previously expressed her “regret” in doing so on the April 15 episode of her podcast, “Khloé in Wonder Land.”

“I’m watching the documentary, and I’m like, 'Wait, I took time out of my life to sit here and do a favor for you,'” she continued on the family’s reality show. “I’m not being paid. I’m doing this ‘cause I’m trying to be nice.”

Kardashian found “many things” Odom said in the documentary to be “really distasteful.”

“You’re saying that you weren’t really in love with me, you married me just so you could be more popular in pop culture, all these things, which is so weird,” she explained. “Even if that is your truth, why don’t you say it without me being on the other side of these interviews? I just thought that was really, really lame.”

In the documentary, Odom said he found the Kardashian family’s “lifestyle” to be enticing. The couple married in 2009 just 30 days after meeting.

According to comments Odom’s friend Anthony “Pumpkin” Booker made in the documentary, on the day of the former couple’s wedding, the basketball player said he was “doing it to try to better his future” because the family had “mad connections.”

The Good American co-founder didn’t hold back when speaking about where she stands with Odom today.

“The bridge is burned, and there’s no more rope left to throw over. So he is dead to me,” she said. “This just solidifies what liars, con artists, cheats, thieves, trolls that men are. I just don’t want to be involved. Play with yourself, don’t play with me.”

Odom and Kardashian filed for divorce in 2013, citing “irreconcilable differences.” It was not finalized until 2016, as Odom had a near-fatal overdose in October 2015, prompting Kardashian to put the legal process on pause.

“He OD’d during the divorce, and I was his next of kin, even though it was still, the divorce was still—it was on the judge’s desk,” she said during a 2019 podcast appearance. “It was like, two years, or like a year or two of us trying to get the divorce going, and then this happened.”

She explained that the pause was “not for any romantic reasons.” It was so she could continue to “help take care of him and make sure that he would be OK again.”

After the split, it was reported that Kardashian kept the couple’s marital mansion, which was located in an upscale guard-gated community called Mulholland Estates in the Los Angeles neighborhood of Tarzana.

The former couple purchased the home for $3.95 million in December 2009, about two months after their wedding day.

The six-bedroom, 8.5-bathroom, Mediterranean mansion was heavily featured on both “Keeping Up With the Kardashians” and their spinoff, “Khloé and Lamar.”

All six of the en suite bathrooms were embellished with designer wallpaper, tumbled stone, mosaic accents, and custom closets. The primary suite also had a spalike bathroom and boasted expansive views of the city.

The 8,400-square-foot estate was equipped with all of the amenities you’d expect from a home of an NBA pro and a Kardashian: a home gym, a library, an office, and a theater room, among other luxuries.

Outside, a resort-like pool included stunning water features and was accompanied by fire pits and a spa.

The home was sold for $5.49 million in January 2014, with “The Big Bang Theory” star Kaley Cuoco snapping it up for nearly $1.5 million over the asking price.

Mulholland Estates wasn’t the only place Odom and Kardashian called home during their marriage. After Odom was traded to the Dallas Mavericks in 2012, they rented a posh condo at W Dallas Victory Hotel and Residences.

The $7,500-a-month dwelling had two bedrooms and two bathrooms and featured slate flooring, a wet bar, and bathrooms tiled with mother of pearl.

The building had amenities that included two fitness centers, a spa, an entertainment room, and a zero-edge infinity pool.

Following her separation from Odom, Kardashian purchased a $7.2 million Calabasas home in June 2014. The 9,214-square-foot estate was the former home of Justin Bieber.

Today, Kardashian lives in a stunning $17 million custom-built abode in Hidden Hills, CA, with the two children she shares with ex-boyfriend Tristan Thompson. The property is located right next door to her mother, Kris Jenner.

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.
