#5539. Commission settlement accounts hold $711M as claim payouts await (EXCLUSIVE)

New disclosures show that the settlement fund accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026.

That’s how much money was held in accounts associated with the sweeping real estate commission antitrust settlements as of Sept. 30, according to newly filed federal court documents offering a fresh look at the money from the nationwide agreements.

The disclosures, filed Thursday in federal court in Missouri, show that the accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026, while roughly $5.8 million was transferred out during the same period.

The filings also come amid an ongoing court-ordered audit of settlement administrator JND Legal Administration, which reported earlier this year that it had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions.

The financial accounting follows a series of appellate rulings upholding the commission settlements, although questions remain about when eligible homesellers will receive payments.

According to a declaration signed Oct. 13 by Isaac Lim, a senior vice president and senior risk officer at Morgan Stanley Smith Barney, and filed by plaintiffs Oct. 29, the settlement accounts had a combined balance of $711,251,720.86 as of Sept. 30.

The funds were transferred from Huntington Bank to Morgan Stanley on Oct. 23, 2025, at class counsel’s direction.

Lim reported that $17,705,101.82 in interest was paid into the accounts between January and September 2026, while $5,780,467.43 was transferred out during the same period. The declaration does not identify the purpose of those transfers or establish whether any money has been distributed directly to eligible homesellers.

According to the filing, the money is invested in a BlackRock institutional money market fund yielding about 3.63 percent annually, Morgan Stanley’s preferred savings program paying 4 percent or a combination of both. The yields are estimates and subject to change.

The reported balance represents funds held in the identified Morgan Stanley accounts, rather than necessarily the full amount collected through the broader commission settlements. The declaration does not provide a complete accounting of earlier distributions, expenses or outstanding settlement contributions.

In a June declaration, Jennifer Keough, CEO of JND Legal Administration, said the company had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions. In June 2025, more than 2.5 million claims had already been submitted, while JND had invoiced approximately $32.8 million for its administrative work.

Keough said JND’s original assignment expanded into six separate notification campaigns involving more than 138 million emails and 44 million postcards. Four of those direct-mail campaigns cost about $18.7 million in postage alone, which JND characterized as a pass-through expense.

In May, Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Bough ordered JND to stop receiving payments while the court considered appointing a special master to audit the company’s past and future bills.

On July 27, the judge appointed Chris Hellums and Randall Sansom as special masters.

Hellums was tasked with overseeing the audit and helping establish future administration arrangements, while Sansom, a certified public accountant, was directed to audit JND’s billing and expenses dating back to the beginning of its work.

The order requires JND to provide detailed financial records, including employee timesheets, vendor invoices, billing records and information about rebates, credits or other financial incentives.

JND opposed the need for an independent audit, arguing in a June filing that the process would be expensive and burdensome and that its work had been performed appropriately. The company said it would cooperate if the audit proceeded, but requested confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive pricing information.

JND also said its responsibilities had expanded substantially at class counsel’s direction and that it had advanced nearly $3 million in out-of-pocket costs on behalf of the class.

The dispute escalated in August when JND sought to disqualify Hellums, alleging he had demonstrated bias against the company through his involvement in a separate antitrust settlement proceeding.

Bough denied the motion Aug. 26, finding that JND, as a nonparty, could not seek disqualification under the applicable rules. He added that even if JND could bring the challenge, it had failed to establish sufficient grounds to question Hellums’ impartiality.

The ruling also examined a question Hellums had raised in the Blue Cross Blue Shield case about potential vendor rebates and credits, which Bough said JND never answered in its email exchange with him and only partly addressed at the Aug. 20 hearing. Keough acknowledged at the hearing that separate vendor agreements govern how rebates and credits are calculated.

JND has maintained in sworn declarations that it has received no rebates, credits or other financial benefits from banks or vendors in connection with the commission settlements.

In its latest accounting, JND reported $155,932 in additional administrative invoices covering July through September, bringing the outstanding balance shown on its October invoice to $494,249.

Keough said JND continues submitting invoices and performing administrative work despite not currently receiving payments.

JND did not respond to Inman’s request for comment by the time of publication.

Despite a series of appellate rulings upholding the real estate commission settlements, it remains unclear when eligible homesellers can expect to receive payments.

On Aug. 19, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit unanimously upheld the landmark Sitzer | Burnett settlement, rejecting seven appeals challenging its scope, fairness and accompanying industry practice changes.

The court subsequently affirmed another $110.6 million in brokerage settlements in the related Gibson litigation on Sept. 1, bringing the total collected for the class to about $1.02 billion, according to the appellate opinion.

After rejecting three additional objector appeals on Sept. 15 and denying rehearing petitions from objectors Robert Friedman and Monty March on Sept. 24, the 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the main Sitzer | Burnett appeals Oct. 2, concluding those proceedings before the appeals court. Objectors may still seek review from the U.S. Supreme Court.

The 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the Gibson appeals Oct. 14.

Despite those developments, the latest financial disclosures do not establish when eligible homesellers will receive distributions or precisely how much of the $711 million held in Morgan Stanley accounts is available for payment.

Eric Dirks, an attorney with the Kansas City-based Williams Dirks Dameron, one of the plaintiffs’ co-lead counsel firms, did not respond to Inman’s request for comment regarding the account balance, interest earnings and anticipated distribution timeline.

#5537. Amazon’s AI shopping agent moves into text messages, taking orders and tracking prices

by Todd Bishop on Nov 6, 2026 at 8:07 amNovember 6, 2026 at 9:35 am

Amazon is rolling out a new feature to let customers shop by text message — sending requests to its Alexa for Shopping AI agent, which will search for products, compare options and place orders on their behalf.

The idea is to make shopping work more like messaging a personal assistant. Amazon says the agent works in the background after it gets a request or a photo, and texts back when the task is done.

It’s part throwback and part hot new thing, reflecting a broader shift in how tech companies are offering AI agents for everyday use. OpenAI added texting to Dot, its personal AI agent, last month, and DoorDash rolled out text ordering in September.

The expansion of Amazon’s AI shopping assistant comes amid a larger fight over who controls online shopping when agents do the buying. Amazon has moved to block outside agents from Meta, Perplexity, Google and OpenAI from shopping its site while building its own.

The text thread is also a new place for Amazon to sell. The company says order updates, delivery notifications and deals will eventually land in the same conversation.

Digiday reports that sponsored products can appear among the options the agent texts back, free to advertisers for now, while purchases the agent completes on its own stay ad-free. Amazon reported $68.6 billion in advertising sales in 2025.

The text feature started rolling out Friday to a small group of U.S. customers by invitation, and millions more will get access in the coming weeks, the company says.

Customers who opt in get a contact called “Alexa Shopping” and can send it requests that range from a note that they’re out of dog food to a photo of a recipe they want turned into a grocery order, according to Amazon’s examples.

The agent searches, texts back with options and completes the purchase with the customer’s approval. Customers can also turn on auto-buy to have it purchase an item automatically when the price hits their target. It can also watch for price drops, reorder past purchases and check on packages, and Amazon says a conversation started by text will carry over to the Amazon app, the website and Alexa devices.

Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping in May, merging its Rufus shopping chatbot with Alexa+, the generative AI version of its voice assistant.

#5536. Housing on the ballot: What to watch in the Nov. 3 midterms

Realtor associations in Florida, California and Massachusetts have lined up behind statewide housing measures on the Nov. 3 ballot, led by $18 million from Florida Realtors for a property tax cut.

Those are among six midterm housing ballot measures at the state level in four U.S. states, the most in a single election year since at least 2006, according to Ballotpedia, not counting property tax measures like Florida’s.

Thirty-six states will also elect governors, and candidates in California, Texas and Florida have released housing plans that range from a statewide housing emergency to ending school property taxes on homesteads.

In federal races, housing has surfaced as part of a broader argument about cost of living. Among Americans who plan to vote, 85 percent say housing affordability is at least somewhat important in choosing candidates, but 64 percent don’t know where their congressional candidates stand on housing, according to a Clever Real Estate survey.

Inman’s editorial staff will be watching California, Texas and Florida most closely next Tuesday. Each has a large real estate market and pairs a governor’s race with policy that would affect transactions, property taxes or construction.

In California, Democrat Xavier Becerra would declare a housing state of emergency on his first day, penalize cities that ignore housing element commitments, back local rent control within the statewide framework and seek disclosure of bulk investor purchases. Republican Steve Hilton would cap government fees and mandates on a new home at $50,000 and freeze new housing rules for five years.

In Texas, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott says his plan would cut the cost of a new home by more than $16,000 through faster inspections and pre-approved designs, and he wants to end school property taxes on homesteads. Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa would restrict corporate purchases of single-family homes and pursue an end to residential property taxes.

In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds wants local governments to remove zoning restraints and supports Amendment 3. Democrat David Jolly opposes the amendment and says the state’s Live Local Act has not delivered affordable housing.

Housing is also a campaign issue in governor races in Colorado, Michigan, Massachusetts and Rhode Island. In Colorado, Democrat Phil Weiser has proposed 40,000 more owner-occupied homes by 2035, and Republican Victor Marx would cut state regulations and red tape. In Michigan, Democrat Jocelyn Benson has pitched affordability proposals, and Republican John James says local codes add more than $100,000 to developers’ costs.

Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, a Democrat seeking a second term, supports Question 7, a zoning change that could lead to the construction of more single-family homes. In Rhode Island, Democrat Helena Foulkes proposes a $1 billion plan for 20,000 homes over eight years, funded by a millionaire tax; independent Ken Block says the fund would produce no more than 375 units.

Florida Realtors had contributed $18 million to the Vote Yes on 3 committee as of late September, funding the campaign in full, WLRN reported. Amendment 3 would raise the state’s homestead property tax exemption.

“Affordability is on the forefront for every Floridian, and they need meaningful relief,” Florida Realtors President Chuck Bonfiglio Jr. said in a statement.

The California Association of Realtors supports Prop. 37, which would fund second mortgages for buyers of newly built homes, and Prop. 45, which would speed permitting and shorten environmental review. The Massachusetts Association of Realtors supports Question 7.

At the federal level, NAR’s political action committee directed more candidate contributions and independent expenditures to Texas than to any other state through February, according to FEC filings Inman reporters reviewed. NAHB’s BUILD-PAC backs what the group calls pro-housing, pro-business candidates for Congress.

The National Association of Hispanic Real Estate Professionals backed the ROAD to Housing Act in a March letter to Senate leaders, citing its provisions on zoning reform and by-right development.

Florida’s Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption on non-school property taxes from about $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and lower the cap on annual assessment increases for non-homestead properties from 10 percent to 5 percent. It needs 60 percent of the vote.

California voters will decide Prop. 1, an $11.25 billion housing bond; Prop. 37, up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for second mortgages covering up to 17 percent of a new home’s price; and Prop. 45, which would set permitting deadlines and shorten environmental review.

In Massachusetts, Question 7 would require cities and towns to allow a single-family home on residentially zoned lots of at least 5,000 square feet with 50 feet of street frontage and public water and sewer.

Below the statewide level, voters will weigh more than 50 housing-related measures, according to a Shelterforce scan. Inman reporters will track the local questions most likely to touch agents’ markets, including property tax relief for older homeowners, transfer tax changes in San Francisco and Oakland and housing bonds in Charlotte and Raleigh.

Congress passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in July. None of the 12 housing bills Inman reporter AJ LaTrace is tracking have advanced since September, including a bipartisan proposal to double the capital gains exclusion on home sales.

Bills that don’t pass before the current Congressional session ends in January would need to be reintroduced. When lawmakers return after the election, they face a Dec. 11 deadline to fund federal agencies, including HUD, and to reauthorize the National Flood Insurance Program.

Inman reporters will follow how the results shape development, including data center development, which has become a campaign issue in Tennessee. The state has about 60 operating data centers and 15 to 20 more proposed, according to WSMV, and the major-party nominees for governor differ on how to handle them. Republican nominee Sen. Marsha Blackburn has said local communities should decide, and Democrat Jerri Green has called for a moratorium.

Most governors elected Nov. 3 will take office in January as state legislatures convene. That same month, the ROAD to Housing Act’s limits on large investors buying additional single-family homes take effect, and Florida’s higher homestead exemption would follow in 2027 if voters approve it.

#5535. DeFi Technologies Inc. Announces Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results with Revenue of $18.3 Million, Operating Income of $7.0 Million, and Net Income of $22.3 Million

TORONTO, Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- DeFi Technologies Inc. (the "Company" or "DeFi Technologies") (Nasdaq: DEFT) (CBOE CA: DEFI) (GR: R9B) (B3: DEFT31), a regulated capital markets platform for digital assets, today announced its financial results for the three months ended September 30, 2026. All dollar amounts in this press release are in U.S. dollars, unless otherwise stated.

Valour â AUM, Net Inflows, Management Fees, Staking and Lending Income

Cash, Treasury, Venture, and Working Capital Position

Together, total cash, USDT/USDC, STRC/RWUSD, digital asset treasury, Smart Crypto Fund and venture portfolio value stood at approximately $159 million as of September 30, 2026. The Company regularly monitors its cash and digital asset reserves on a consolidated basis and allocates a portion of its digital asset treasury reserve to support ETP market risk hedging and broader strategic capital allocation.

Comment from Johan WattenstrÃ¶m, Chief Executive Officer of DeFi Technologies

"The third quarter demonstrated how our business can respond to improving digital asset markets. We reported $18.3 million in revenue, $7.0 million in operating income, and $22.3 million in net income, with trading gains and investment revaluations contributing materially to those results.

Valour's AUM increased approximately 62%, from $397.2 million at the end of June to $643.7 million at September 30. We generated $26.1 million in positive net inflows during the quarter, bringing net inflows for the first nine months to $48.9 million. Investors continued to allocate capital to our products through difficult market conditions, and I see that demand as an important foundation for growth.

We are expanding the ways investors can access our platform and the ways we can generate revenue. Since quarter-end, Valour launched eight additional ETPs, each carrying a 1.9% management fee. During September, we also launched Valour Funds SPC and its Smart Crypto Fund SP, extending our offering into actively managed strategies for professional and qualified investors, with additional institutional offerings in development.

Stillman demonstrates the contribution our broader platform can make. It generated $7.6 million in trading commissions through the first nine months, up approximately 22% year over year. We are building on that foundation by expanding its institutional reach and client relationships.

Looking ahead, we are optimistic that the lows of this bear market may now be behind us. If that proves to be the case, we believe DeFi Technologies is entering the recovery with a broader revenue opportunity than in previous cycles. Higher AUM can increase management fees and staking income on eligible assets, while greater trading activity supports our institutional business. With much of our supporting infrastructure already in place, revenue growth can translate into meaningful operating leverage and margin expansion.

Our financial position supports our ability to pursue that opportunity. At September 30, we reported $165.8 million in total shareholders' equity and approximately $159.1 million in balance sheet holdings and investments, compared with a recent market capitalization of approximately $130 million. Considering those resources alongside Valour's asset management platform, Stillman's profitable trading business, and the new offerings we are developing, we believe our valuation materially understates the value and earnings potential of the company.

I see considerable potential in the business we have built. With a wider product range, continued investor inflows, and more ways to generate revenue, I believe we can deliver substantially stronger results in a sustained recovery than in previous bull market cycles.

Our focus now is on attracting capital, expanding distribution, and bringing our new offerings to market. I am confident in our direction and excited about what we can achieve from this position. Our responsibility is to turn that opportunity into stronger earnings and long-term value for shareholders."

#5534. Google releases Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a lower-cost model said to outscore Argon

Google LLC today released Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a lower-cost model in its Gemini 4 artificial intelligence family that it says outscores its frontier Gemini 4 Argon model on an independent intelligence ranking.

Measured on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level, Hydrogen scored 51 to Argon’s 50, according to Google. A fourth thinking level called xhigh, new with Hydrogen, takes the score to 54.

The rollout is different, too. Argon spent nearly two weeks with members of Google’s Fairwind Program, a group of vetted cybersecurity defenders, before paying developers could get at it on Oct. 13. Hydrogen skipped that stage. Anyone can use it from today, including people on the free version of the Gemini app.

Koray Kavukcuoglu, who became head of Google DeepMind in August when Demis Hassabis moved into a chairman role, wrote in the announcement that Hydrogen is “built for rapid execution.”

Orchestrator, which Google added to its Antigravity coding tool today, picks between Hydrogen and Gemini 4 Carbon as a session goes along. Google’s runs of the Terminal-Bench 4.0 coding test found Orchestrator getting close to Carbon’s success rate on an average of 24% less quota.

Gemini 3.8 Flash, which came out in September, is the yardstick for most of the other numbers in the announcement. Against it, Hydrogen finished tasks 2.5 times faster at the default setting. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, which tests work done at a command line, Hydrogen more than tripled the older model’s 18.2% with a score of 57%.

Among the early testers Google quoted, Andrew Carr, a former OpenAI scientist who is now chief scientist at 3D animation startup Cartwheel Inc., said the model caught two problems with an approach his team had been stuck on for 10 days. Discovery Loop Inc., the startup former Google Chief Scientist Jeff Dean co-founded after leaving in August, was another.

#5533. Tech Moves: Fred Hutch leader goes to AWS; Temporal, Augmodo and Neuralwatt name execs

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 6, 2026 at 10:06 amNovember 6, 2026 at 10:45 am

— Amitabha “Guppy” Gupta, a Fred Hutch Cancer Center associate director who helps researchers translate their work to broader audiences, is leaving after 14 years to join Amazon. Starting Nov. 16, he will be a strategic advisor for nonprofit research and advanced AI with AWS’ Global Nonprofit Business.

Gupta said technology was often an obstacle to scientific breakthroughs at Fred Hutch.

“It’s the infrastructure, data, and tools standing between a scientist and an answer,” he wrote on LinkedIn. In his new role, “I’ll work with researchers and research institutions on using cloud, high-performance computing, and AI to remove those barriers.”

— Microsoft board member ‌Emma Walmsley has been appointed CEO of HP, effective Jan. 4. Walmsley, who led the pharmaceutical giant GSK until December 2025, succeeds Bruce Broussard. Reuters notes that her seven years serving on the Microsoft board “are her closest brush with the tech sector” prior to taking the top job at the PC maker.

— Bas Nijholt, senior staff engineer at IonQ‘s Seattle-area facility, has resigned after three years to join an AI startup that’s still in stealth mode. At IonQ, the theoretical quantum mechanics expert built MindRoom, an open-source collaboration and knowledge-sharing platform that he calls “a company brain.”

“With this new opportunity, I get to keep building and turbocharging MindRoom with a team of people who are just as excited about AI as I am,” Nijholt said, adding that the tool will remain freely available.

Before IonQ, Nijholt spent nearly four years at Microsoft.

— Bellevue, Wash., startup Temporal, whose software keeps AI agents running reliably, has named Sean Heneghan as vice president of sales for the Americas. The company ranks No. 1 on the GeekWire 200, a list of the top Pacific Northwest startups. In September it raised $550 million, putting its valuation at $12.55 billion.

Temporal is fully remote, and Heneghan is based in the Chicago area. He joins the company from MongoDB.

— Doug Heimburger, a 26-year Amazon veteran, has changed roles, shifting from chief financial officer and vice president of Worldwide Operations to CFO/VP of Worldwide Stores. In the new position, Heimburger said he’ll help oversee efforts to improve delivery speed, reduce costs and increase growth of the Stores business. His first role at the company was data mining analyst.

— Seattle startup Augmodo has named Capri Brixey as head of retail sales. The company, which sells AI-powered wearable devices with cameras, raised $21 million in July to expand from in-store applications that let workers passively track inventory into automotive, warehouse and hospital settings. Augmodo ranks No. 122 on the GeekWire 200.

Ross Finman, founder and CEO of Augmodo, called Brixey “the right leader to accelerate our expansion” given her experience selling to both retail and warehouse operations. Her past roles include leadership positions at Coca-Cola and Kroger.

— Meaghan Davison Praznik was named vice president of marketing for Neuralwatt, a Seattle-based startup that built a tool for calculating, in real time, the carbon emissions of individual AI requests. Her former employers include Clif Bar, AllTrails and Merino Energy.

Because the carbon intensity of grid power varies throughout the day and across regions, Neuralwatt’s technology can help customers run compute-intensive operations when clean energy is more abundant.

— BuyWander, an auction-based online marketplace for returned and overstocked retail items, has named Chris Holm as senior director of product. Holm spent nine years at Amazon, leaving in 2024 after managing last-mile and same-day delivery technology and working on Amazon Fresh delivery. He has since served as a consultant for carbon removal startup Lithos Carbon and as a founder-in-residence at the startup studio Foundations.

In August, BuyWander moved its headquarters across Washington from Spokane to Kent. The company announced $21 million in new funding in September.

— T-Mobile’s Kevin Lau has joined the advisory board at the University of Washington’s College of Engineering. Lau has been with the telecom giant for 22 years over two stints and serves as VP of digital experience engineering. He holds bachelor’s, master’s and doctoral degrees in electrical engineering from the UW.

— Christian Smith, an Issaquah, Wash.-based tech leader, has been named president of revenue for Cloudflare, which provides security and speed services for websites and online applications. He will oversee worldwide go-to-market operations. Smith previously served as chief revenue officer for Splunk and Nintex.

#5532. Figure loan volume rises 135% on platform growth after Kiavi acquisition

Figure said Q3 Loan Marketplace volume rose 135% year over year to $5.8B, including $677M from Kiavi. Net revenue increased 84% to $287M, while net income was $89.3M and adjusted EBITDA rose 91% to $163.6M.  AI Summary

Figure Technology Solutions on Thursday reported a sharp increase in loan marketplace volume in the third quarter, as the blockchain-based lending platform continued expanding its marketplace business and completed its acquisition of real estate investment lender Kiavi.

The company’s Loan Marketplace volume reached $5.8 billion in the three months ending Sept. 30, up 135% from $2.5 billion a year earlier. The total included $677 million in volume contributed by Kiavi, which Figure officially acquired on Sept. 1.

Figure Connect, the company’s capital-light marketplace platform, accounted for $4.3 billion of quarterly volume, up 276% year over year. The platform represented 72% of standalone Loan Marketplace volume during the quarter.

Net revenue increased 84% year over year to $287 million, compared with $156.4 million in the third quarter of 2025.

Net income was essentially flat at $89.3 million, compared with $89.8 million a year earlier. On a quarterly basis, net income rose from its second-quarter figure of $87.4 million.

Net income margin fell to 31%, down from 57%, partly because the year-ago quarter included a one-time $31 million tax benefit related to the recognition of deferred tax assets. Adjusted EBITDA, a non-GAAP measure, rose 91% to $163.6 million. Adjusted EBITDA margin increased to 58% from 55%.

“This was a record quarter for Figure, highlighted by another consecutive quarter of over 100% volume growth and the rapid expansion of our capital-light marketplace, with Figure Connect now making up 72% of our standalone volume,” CEO Michael Tannenbaum said in a statement.

During the company’s earnings call, Tannenbaum said that Figure grew volume 107% year over year, posting a 58% EBITDA margin and maintaining a 3.7% net standalone take rate. Chief financial officer Macrina Kgil said that during the company’s Q2 2026 earnings, it guided Q3 standalone volume to a range of $4.8 billion to $5.2 billion, and that guidance proved reliable as Figure came in at $5.1 billion.

“The Kiavi acquisition … contributed approximately $670 million of volume for the one month in our results this quarter,” Kgil said. Figure Connect volume, including Kiavi, grew to 74% of overall volume, up from 65% last quarter and from 46% a year ago.”

The acquisition expands Figure’s presence in investor-focused mortgage lending, including residential transition loans (RTLs) and debt-service-coverage ratio (DSCR) loans. Figure said the deal added $8 billion in annualized volume and that it had realized $30 million in initial cost synergies since the transaction closed.

“With Kiavi, we have added residential transition loans, RTL, and debt service coverage ratio loans, DSCR, diversifying our platform beyond HELOC into a $200 billion-plus addressable market,” Tannenbaum told investors. He added that the acquisition had closed ahead of schedule and that Kiavi “also brought on a number of new full loan and securitized investors.”

The company also reported continued growth in its small- and medium-sized business lending (SMB) operation, which surpassed a $500 million annualized run rate with more than 150 active partners.

Figure said it expanded its partner network to 612 standalone partners and 894 when including Kiavi. The network includes more than 20 active depository partners.

The company also introduced an artificial intelligence-powered loan officer assistant through a partnership with Sierra. The tool has processed approximately $260 million in funded loans and increased funded dollars per loan approval by 29%, Figure said.

Separately, Figure’s $YLDS stablecoin had $504 million in circulation as of Sept. 30, compared with $328 million at the end of 2025. The company said 28 participants were using the stablecoin for marketplace transactions.

The company’s board also authorized a $200 million increase to its share repurchase program, bringing the total authorization to $400 million.

“Today, we’re announcing an expanded $400 million share buyback plan that will start tomorrow,” Tannenbaum said. “Given our profitability, cash levels, balance-sheet liquidity, and access to the capital markets, we will be opportunistic about share repurchases on an ongoing basis, including beyond this initial $400 million program. That said, we see huge organic growth and look at inorganic opportunities as well, especially those that can accelerate our marketplace reach.”

For the fourth quarter, Figure forecasts Loan Marketplace volume of $6.2 billion to $6.7 billion, along with a gross take rate of 3.1% to 3.4%.

#5531. Paytient-Greenwald Study Finds 61% of Insured Workers Have Paid for Healthcare Entirely in Cash Without Filing a Claim

In a new study of over 2,000 employer-insured workers, 68% said they would prefer predictably paying cash for a major healthcare expense through small paycheck deductions. These findings put payment experience alongside plan design as a cost and experience lever for employers and benefits advisors.

COLUMBIA, Mo., Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Employers are projecting healthcare cost increases of 11% or more without plan changes. Against that backdrop, a new national study commissioned by Paytient and conducted by Greenwald Research points to a plan design tenet that can lower premiums year over year and improve the employee experience: payability, or a person's ability to self-pay or cash-pay for care. The data shows that when employers build payability directly into plan design, they create patient-centered health plans. Those plans allow employers and employees to move to lower-cost plan designs with confidence, in a way that improves, rather than impairs, the employee experience.

Payability, Measured is the second in Paytient's Payability Papers, a four-part series examining how the out-of-pocket payment experience shapes health plan performance and the employee experience. Surveying 2,024 full-time, employer-insured workers, the study finds that two-thirds of employees prefer a $2,000 cost spread over six months to a $1,000 copay paid in full upfront to receive care. Greenwald's research is the first of its kind to reveal this behavioral preference in how consumers pay for healthcare, and it highlights real opportunities for employers and insurers to design health plans around how people prefer to pay for care.

These findings that have direct implications for employers stand out:

"Insurance was built to protect people from the financial risk of rare, catastrophically expensive care. Over time, we've stretched it to cover nearly everything, which drives up premiums and makes the system harder to navigate. This research shows that people want to pay for healthcare the way they pay for almost everything else in their lives: upfront, in-full with a clear cash price or predictably, over time to fit their household budget. A smarter plan design pairs lower-cost coverage for rare, high-cost care with the payment tools "Paytients" have told us they want for everything else. Employers already use payroll to collect premiums (and smooth the payment of taxes) over the life of employment. Using payroll to smooth out-of-pocket costs is the plan design opportunity hiding in plain sight, and it can help employers save substantially on plan costs," says Joe Gabler, Chief Operating Officer of Paytient.

The findings support that when employees have a reliable, structured way to pay for out-of-pocket costs over time, plan design can become more efficient without becoming less supportive â and that changes the calculus on deductible architecture, total cost of care, and the actual value delivered by healthcare benefit.

"What stands out in this data is how universal the preference for payability in healthcare is. It holds across income levels, from workers earning under $50,000 to those earning over $100,000.

"This isn't a low-income affordability story. It's a structural preference that cuts across the entire workforce, and can be a universal strategic advantage for employers," says Lisa Weber, Chief Research Officer and Head of Healthcare Insights at Greenwald Research.

Payability, Measured is available for download here. For more information, visit www.paytient.com. If you're attending HLTH 2026, stop by Paytient's booth (#2824).

About PaytientPaytient is the leader in innovative healthcare payment solutions. Our Healthcare Payability Platform has put over $50 billion of purchasing power into the hands of 26 million individuals across employer, ACA and Medicare plans. In doing so, Paytient is helping shape more accessible, equitable, and lower-cost health plans across commercial, individual, and regulated healthcare markets. To learn more, visit www.paytient.com and join us on LinkedIn.

#5530. How to be unemployed: Glenn Kelman on life after Redfin

by Glenn Kelman on Nov 6, 2026 at 12:47 pmNovember 6, 2026 at 12:52 pm

After 20 years at Redfin, and 10 months of unemployment, I’ve co-founded a new company. My business partner and I will announce our plans after we’ve built our product, but in the meantime GeekWire asked me to explain what I learned in the transition between Redfin and this new venture.

Many of us are in transition because society is in transition, with AI hollowing out big companies and making it easier to start new companies.

In the past, my own transitions had been harrowing, because I ran out of money or lost my sense of purpose. Leaving Redfin, I thought “here we go again.” I felt self-conscious being in the grocery store at 11 a.m. on a weekday. I was ashamed when I couldn’t come up with an idea for a company. But I made it to the other side.

To do that, I had to convince myself that I was an intrepid explorer, even if what I was exploring wasn’t Mount Everest, but instead what I could be. I wanted to feel brave about encounters I otherwise would’ve found embarrassing. Over the last year, I met people about becoming a high school teacher, a Whistler bagel shopkeeper, a candidate for the state legislature, the founder of a tree-planting nonprofit, the CEO of a pre-IPO company and a project leader for Sound Transit.

The way to prepare yourself to do one thing for a long time is first to consider everything else.

At the beginning of my exploration, a CEO recruiter told me the startup scene in Seattle was “dead” and that, for all of Seattle’s talent, more companies were forming in New York and even LA. I Googled “high-growth Seattle startups” and the list included one company that went bankrupt in 2023, and Redfin, which was acquired in 2025.

Another friend told me that she was on a Discord channel with a bunch of CTOs who were miserable trying to do “AI transformations” at businesses with legacy codebases. At least for me, the logical response to all this has been to start an AI-native company in Seattle.

“The way to prepare yourself to do one thing for a long time is first to consider everything else.”

It took me months to feel ready to do that. In January, a friend told me I wasn’t allowed to make any big decisions until September. Another said I had to wait until the frenzy of my last job had subsided. “You’ll know it has happened,” he said, “because food will start tasting better” (it never happened).

At a conference, a fashion entrepreneur who’d built and abandoned vast residences in Jackson Hole and Costa Rica, and got divorced twice in the past three years, gave me a bracelet that said “we are enough.”

Since I’d often been thinking I hadn’t done enough in the morning to deserve lunch, it was a relief to feel that I didn’t have to be creative or productive in order to justify my existence. But relieving that pressure also made it easier to be creative and productive.

On a call walking through Volunteer Park, I told a friend that the bracelet reminded me I could be happy and never start a company again. She said, “YOU JUST NEED A CO-FOUNDER.”

She told me to share flawed ideas with people who could make them better. I set up meetings with potential co-founders, and we shared our ideas before they were ready, because our meetings had become deadlines. Then we used AI to turn our ideas into products, so we could see what was good and bad about each idea. Starting a company started to feel like a natural progression, instead of Athena sprouting out of Zeus’s head.

When I confessed to a friend that everything we were working on still seemed so small, she said, “What about breakfast burritos?” She outlined her vision for a shop serving breakfast burritos all day, with a line out the door. Then she started talking about inventing a nursing home “that makes everyone happy.” Rather than running a McKinsey market-sizing analysis, she just thought about what she wanted to exist in the world.

That’s something almost anyone can do. In her living room, I suddenly felt that humanity would always have an instinct — this is a bizarre word, but it’s what popped into my head — to fructify. I remember walking home from her house with my wife and hearing the thick sound of insects humming in the night as proof of life’s rich pageant. This is what I mean by surrounding yourself with good vibes.

The last step in my process maybe should’ve come first, choosing where I wanted to make a difference. I thought about all the companies that I honestly would’ve been proud to start, and they were all in the same industry. I had no experience in that industry, but a friend said I could offset that if I were willing to give it everything I have, which is what I’m now doing. I met amazing, generous investors who gave me a good idea, and a business partner who helped me think it through.

Through all of this, I depended on my wife more than any husband ever should. She works herself to the bone treating people with cancer, but she took my calls in the middle of her workday, when I would talk in detail about what to cook for dinner and then — one more thing! — what’s the meaning of my life?

Once, she was getting into our Chevy Bolt for her morning commute while I was rounding the corner with the dog, and I saw her brighten in the way many people did back when I was Redfin’s CEO.

I found myself full of anticipation. She reached into the car, as if to grab a small gift, and heaved something at me from across the street, saying it “needs reprogramming.” Before I realized it was a garage clicker, I thought she had said I was the one who needed reprogramming. “Maybe that’s true,” I said to myself, trudging past the browned lawn, and the dirty dishes, and into a world of possibilities.

#5529. Compass pushes back on antitrust claims, says it owes StreetEasy nothing

Compass filed a motion to dismiss an amended antitrust complaint in SDNY tied to pulling rental listings from StreetEasy. Compass argues the suit conflates sales and rentals, lacks causation, and cites the FARE Act as a driver of inventory visibility.  AI Summary

Compass International Holdings is seeking to dismiss an antitrust lawsuit alleging that it created a monopoly through its acquisitions, which it used to harm consumers as well as competitors like Zillow when it decided to pull its rental listings from StreetEasy in early August.

Filed in late August, the lawsuit claims that Compass’s removal of listings from StreetEasy reduced consumer choice, while also driving up rents and brokerage fees.

In a filing on Tuesday, Compass told the court it was seeking to dismiss the amended complaint with prejudice, which would prevent the plaintiff from refilling the lawsuit.

In the filing, Compass claims that the plaintiffs have confused the residential sales market with the rental market, noting that the information cited in the complaint pertains to for-sale homes and not rental listings. The filing also notes that Compass does not own rental properties or set rental prices, claiming instead that Zillow and StreetEasy dominate the online listing-search market. The defendant also claims that the plaintiff cannot demonstrate that Compass’s alleged conduct caused his higher rent.

The filing also notes that rental inventory in New York City began to decline seven months prior to its acquisition of Anywhere and more than a year before Compass began instructing agents to pull rental listings from Street Easy. Instead, Compass points to the June 2025 implementation of New York City’s Fairness in Apartment Rental Expenses (FARE) Act, which prohibits brokers hired by landlords from charging broker fees to tenants and requires landlords to disclose applicable fees before a lease is signed, as the reason behind the drop in visible inventory.

Compass also claims that it does not have monopoly power in the rental listings market and that it has no legal obligation to share its listings with platforms like Street Easy.

According to a notice on the court docket, the plaintiff has until December 8, 2026, to respond to Compass’s motion to dismiss the suit. While the parties wait for the court to rule on the motion, Compass is also asking the court to stay discovery. The court has not yet ruled on that motion.

#5527. CNCF data shows cloud native is the on-ramp to AI, and maintainers are paying the price

The global population of cloud-native developers has topped 21 million, but the headcount tells only part of the story. Artificial intelligence is changing what those developers build and how open-source projects absorb their work.

Fresh research is putting numbers on that shift. The latest State of Cloud Native Development report from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation and SlashData Ltd. counts more than 21 million practitioners, or 41% of developers worldwide. Yet that figure likely misses many people who rely on cloud-native infrastructure without knowing it, according to Bob Killen (pictured, right), director of technical program management at CNCF.

“The big thing is it actually might be undercounting a significant amount of them,” Killen said. “Because there’s a very large amount of people that are essentially consuming cloud-native applications without even realizing it.”

Killen and Liam Bollmann-Dodd (left), principal market research consultant at SlashData, spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed the latest State of Cloud Native Development findings, AI adoption, the strain on open-source maintainers and the shift toward cost discipline. (* Disclosure below.)

The report’s most striking finding concerns AI. About 75% of cloud-native developers use AI in some form, compared with only about 55% of other developers, Bollmann-Dodd noted. The gap mirrors a broader trend of agentic AI pushing Kubernetes into a second act.

“It’s a massive difference,” Bollmann-Dodd said. “So somehow being cloud native enables you and your organization and your personal stack to do AI in all its forms.”

The same AI wave is straining the people who keep the ecosystem running. Sustainability dominated the Maintainer Summit ahead of KubeCon, as maintainers face a flood of pull requests frequently generated by agents, Killen explained.

“How do we as maintainers keep up with the flooding of PRs and issues and things like that?” Killen said. “Especially when many of them are frankly just slop. And the real frustrating part is they’ll be just good enough.”

Cost discipline is the next shift. Just as financial operations practices followed rising cloud bills, cloud-native developers will soon manage model and token spending closely, according to Bollmann-Dodd.

“I think token maxing is dead and it’s going to stay dead forever,” Bollmann-Dodd said. “And I think it’s going to become much more focused on how you spend your money and how you spend your tokens.”

The new funding supports site control, engineering, permitting, feedstock-supply and product-offtake agreements, and project-financing work. The initial assessment examined feedstock and logistics, the site-selection pathway, concept-level process engineering and permitting, supporting a recommendation to advance.

The full-campus vision would use regional forestry residuals to produce hydrogen, clean carbon coproducts and dispatchable electricity, with a next-generation AI Advanced Compute Complex alongside the energy infrastructure.

At full buildout, the current planning case targets approximately 1,000 wet metric tonnes per day of forestry residuals and a 50-megawatt advanced-compute IT load. LCH2's management target of more than 220 family-wage jobs is a project target, not an independently completed economic-impact forecast.

"Centralia's Coal Transition Grant program was created to help communities build durable economic and energy opportunities through change. LCH2's next stage brings together Lewis County's forestry strengths, emerging clean-energy technology and new industrial demand in a way that is aligned with that long-term purpose. We are pleased to see locally grounded projects continue moving from concept toward execution, supporting the region's next industrial chapter," said Chris Fralick, Executive Vice President, Generation and Chief Operating Officer of TransAlta.

"This $1 million award does more than extend a study â it funds the next substantive development stage. We have completed the first round of feedstock, site, engineering and permitting work, and now our job is execution: secure site control, advance the engineering and permits, formalize supply and offtake, and build a financeable commercial project," said Ken Cavallon, Executive Director of LCH2.

Near-term work is development workânot full-campus constructionâand future buildout remains dependent on site control, engineering validation, permits, commercial agreements and project financing.

#5524. UWM rolls out 40 bps year-end pricing bonus, expands Bilt partnership

United Wholesale Mortgage introduced “40 to the Finish,” a year-end pricing incentive that adds 40 basis points to all products for loans with 700+ FICO scores when brokers use UWM’s Underwriting+, TRAC+ or virtual closing tools through Dec. 31. At the same time, UWM expanded its partnership with Bilt to integrate Bilt Neighborhood OS into its servicing platform.   AI Summary

United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM) this week announced the launch of a year-end pricing incentive for broker loans and an expansion of its partnership with Bilt.

Effective immediately through Dec. 31, brokers who use UWM’s Underwriting+, TRAC+ or virtual closing tools will receive 40 basis points on all agency and nonagency products when the borrower has a credit score of at least 700, UWM said.

The incentive is intended to give brokers more pricing flexibility in the final weeks of 2026 while encouraging use of the lender’s underwriting and closing technology. Year-end pricing specials are common in the wholesale channel as lenders seek to pull volume into the current year, clean up pipelines and help partners hit production goals.

UWM – which was more aggressive on pricing in the past but is seeking to deleverage its balance sheet amid a deal with Oaktree Capital Management and the Ishbia family – saw its gain-on-sale margins decline to 124 basis points in the third quarter, down from 133 basis points in the second quarter.

UWM chairman, CEO and president Mat Ishbia told analysts he expects margins to be steady, adding that “people don’t use UWM because we’re the lowest rates” and arguing that competitors offering lower rates are not good partners.

Separately, UWM said it’s expanding its partnership with Bilt, a neighborhood commerce and rewards platform, to bring Bilt Neighborhood OS into its servicing ecosystem.

Bilt Neighborhood OS is designed to help businesses reach customers and build loyalty through neighborhood-level experiences. Through UWM, it links mortgage servicing with homeownership tasks and local commerce, while keeping independent brokers visible to borrowers after closing.

“The broker who helps you buy your home should be your first call when you’re ready to take the next step, whether that’s refinancing, accessing equity or buying again,” Ishbia said in a statement. “With Bilt Neighborhood OS, we’re making the servicing experience more valuable to homeowners and creating more reasons for them to stay connected to their broker between those major decisions.”

UWM already services hundreds of thousands of loans through Bilt, giving these homeowners a single place to manage their mortgage and access rewards. With Neighborhood OS added, UWM said the experience will extend into more day-to-day homeownership activities, from finding a local contractor to exploring neighborhood offers, or reconnecting with a broker about a home equity or refinance opportunity.

Bilt said it has delivered more than $1 billion in value to its 8 million members, who redeem rewards toward travel, housing payments, student loans, dining and other categories. The company also says it powers one in four U.S. rental homes, primarily through the Bilt Alliance of large owners and operators.

#5522. JPMorgan and Mastercard back Seattle startup Firmly’s bet on AI shopping agents

by Todd Bishop on Nov 7, 2026 at 10:23 amNovember 9, 2026 at 6:47 am

Firmly, a Seattle-area startup that helps online retailers sell through AI shopping assistants, raised a $15 million Series A round led by Squarepoint Capital, with participation from J.P. Morgan Payments, Mastercard, Samsung Next and others.

The company, founded in 2019, connects retailers’ existing online stores to AI assistants, marketplaces and other shopping channels, so people can buy products inside those third-party apps and services without going to retailers’ websites. Retailers keep their own payment providers and customer relationships.

“Every new AI assistant, marketplace or shopping platform is another place to sell. But connecting to each one can take serious engineering, because catalogs, inventory, payments, and checkout all have to work together,” wrote Kumar Senthil, Firmly’s co-founder and CEO, in a blog post announcing the round.

Mastercard is a commercial partner as well as an investor. Firmly handles the merchant side of Mastercard Agent Connect, a service launched in September to link merchants, AI agents and payment providers through a single integration.

Senthil told Axios Pro that Mastercard is recruiting merchants for the service, giving Firmly a route to new customers.

Firmly charges merchants $2,000 to $15,000 a month, depending on the total value of merchandise they sell, Senthil told Axios. He said connecting a merchant took four to six weeks in 2024 and now takes a day or less, including testing.

The company lists Best Buy, Furniture.com and Backcountry among its retail customers. RetailMeNot and an AI shopping app called Wizard also use its technology.

The funding comes as AI shopping agents move into the mainstream. Meta’s Muse assistant can browse retail sites and buy items with a user’s approval. Amazon has blocked Muse from its site and is suing Perplexity over a shopping agent in the startup’s Comet browser.

Firmly takes a different approach from those agents. Instead of having software click through a retailer’s web pages, it connects directly to the retailer’s systems with its permission.

The company this week also launched Ask Agent, an AI shopping assistant for retailers’ own websites. Shoppers describe what they want, get product recommendations and can check out without leaving the chat.

Other investors in the round include Alumni Ventures, ARK Invest, Benhamou Global Ventures, Granada Funds, Hike Ventures, The Mercantile Companies and Versus Ventures.

The round brings Firmly’s total funding to about $20 million. The company had raised $5.2 million when it partnered with Perplexity in March 2025 on shopping features inside the AI search app.

Senthil spent eight years at Microsoft and later led e-commerce products at Samsung. He co-founded Firmly with Damien Balsan, a co-founder of LoopPay, the mobile payments startup acquired by Samsung, and Murali Krishnamurthy, Firmly’s CTO and a former chief technical architect for Samsung’s U.S. and global e-commerce business. Firmly is based in Issaquah, Wash., and its engineering leaders work in Seattle. The company also has engineering teams in Sao Paulo, Brazil, and Chennai, India.

#5521. AI agent tooling provider LangChain secures $300M investment

LangChain Inc., a startup with a set of popular open-source tools for building artificial intelligence agents, has raised $300 million in funding.

The Wall Street Journal reported today that Alphabet Inc.’s CapitalG fund led the round. It was joined by IVP, Sapphire Ventures, GIC and DFJ Growth. LangChain is now worth $3 billion.

San Francisco-based LangChain is best known for the eponymous open-source framework it released in 2022. The software reduces the amount of work involved in building AI agents. LangChain makes it relatively simple to connect an AI agent to a large language model, integrate it with tools and add a system prompt. The framework also enables developers to customize details such as the format of prompt responses.

LangChain’s second open-source tool, LangGraph, is designed for situations where a task is too complicated to be automated by a single agent. LangGraph can link together multiple LangChain-powered agents into a single automation workflow. It can also add in other elements such as a mechanism that requires humans to approve sensitive actions.

The third component of LangChain’s open-source portfolio is Deep Agents. It extends LangChain and  LangGraph with features that make it easier for agents to perform complex work. There’s a virtual file system in which agents can keep data, a work planning tool and a subagent generation feature.

LangChain generates revenue with a suite of paid products called LangSmith. Developers can use it to not only build agents but also to maintain them once they’re in production.

An AI agent usually goes through multiple iterations before it’s released to users. LangSmith enables software teams to save those iterations in a centralized repository. If an update introduces a bug into an agent’s code base, developers can use LangSmith to quickly restore an earlier, bug-free version. Furthermore, they can compare the output quality of different agent versions to identify the one that should be deployed to production.

LangSmith also includes a set of observability features. It generates traces, logs that describe every single step of the workflow through an agent processed a prompt. LangSmith analyzes those traces to find technical issues. From there, it prioritizes them based on their severity and generates code fixes.

After its previous funding round last year, LangChain disclosed that its open-source tools were being downloaded about 90 million times per month. Its LangSmith suite, in turn, is used by Autodesk Inc., Cisco Systems Inc. and a long list of other tech firms.

LangChain reportedly plans to nearly double its headcount to 850 employees by the end of 2027. The company will hire infrastructure experts, AI engineers, salespeople and marketers.

#5520. Natura Reports Net Income of BRL 49 mn in 3Q26, Reduced Debt, and Cash Flow of BRL 268 mn Amid Operational Bottlenecks in Brazil

SÃO PAULO, Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ --Natura announced today its results for the third quarter of 2026 (3Q26). The company ended the period with consolidated net revenue of BRL 5 billion (-3% in BRL and -5.9% in constant currency). In Brazil, revenue declined by -9%, marking an improvement compared to the previous quarter but falling short of the company's expectations. The result also reflects product unavailability and a loss of productivity among beauty consultants, in addition to the decline in the relationship selling channel.

At Hispanic markets, revenue remained stable in constant currency (-0.9%). The performance reflects a slowdown in Mexico compared with the second quarter, mainly due to revenue phasing, as a sales cycle was brought forward from the third to the second quarter of this year. It also reflects Argentina's continued but still slow recovery following the integration with Avon.

Consolidated EBITDA was BRL 460 million, with a margin of 9.1% (+20 bps YoY). Excluding non-operating effects, EBITDA would have reached BRL 636 million, with a margin of 12.6%.

Net income was BRL 49 million, reversing the net loss of BRL 119 million recorded in the same period last year. One of the key highlights of 3Q26 was the company's strong cash generation of BRL 268 million, which, combined with the FIDC inflows, reduced net debt to BRL 3.4 billion. As a result, leverage fell to 1.83x, from 2.06x in 2Q26, underscoring the resilience and cash-generating capacity of the business model, even amid operational challenges.

In his message to shareholders and the market, CEO Ale Carlucci, who took the helm at Natura on October 1, shared his initial assessment of the company and outlined the key areas of focus for its return to sustainable growth. "Achieving our objectives requires strengthening and adjusting our foundational levers rather than relying on targeted short-term initiatives and superficial fixes," he said.

#5519. Newrez partners with Upgrade to add personal loans for servicing customers

Newrez is adding unsecured personal loans for eligible servicing customers through a partnership with fintech firm Upgrade, which will originate and service the loans via issuer Cross River Bank. The product gives existing Newrez borrowers a way to access cash without using their home as collateral or changing their mortgage, with no prepayment fees and soft-credit prequalification.  AI Summary

Multichannel lender Newrez partnered with financial technology firm Upgrade to offer unsecured personal loans to eligible mortgage servicing customers, giving homeowners another option to access cash without tapping home equity or refinancing.

The loans, originated and serviced by Upgrade and issued by its partner Cross River Bank, do not change the existing Newrez mortgage. Newrez funded $12.9 billion in mortgages in the third quarter and reached $878.9 billion in unpaid principal balance across its mortgage servicing rights (MSR) portfolio at the end of September.

According to the company, the loans can be funded in as little as one business day for qualified borrowers, have no prepayment fees and allow customers to see prequalified offers through a soft credit inquiry.

Newrez framed the launch as an extension of its relationships with homeowners beyond the mortgage, with loans designed for uses such as debt consolidation, home improvements and unexpected expenses.

“Our relationship with homeowners doesn’t begin and end with a mortgage,” Leslie Gillin, Newrez’s chief commercial officer, said in a statement. “Homeowners’ financial needs often extend beyond their monthly mortgage payment, and we’re proud to broaden the ways we can support them, including helping identify opportunities for savings as they navigate important financial decisions.”

The launch comes as many homeowners are struggling with revolving debt. In a June 2026 survey conducted by Morning Consult on behalf of Newrez, 51% of homeowners reported carrying credit card balances, with 59% saying the debt is negatively affecting their finances. The online survey of 2,203 U.S. adults was conducted in June 2026.

“The findings show that many homeowners are looking for ways to improve their financial position but may not know where to start,” Gillin said. “By combining education with access to responsible financing options, we can help customers make informed decisions that support their long-term financial goals.”This article was generated using HousingWire Automation and reviewed by a HousingWire editor before publication. The system helps convert company announcements and industry data into HousingWire-style news coverage.

#5518. What real estate agents should watch on Election Day, per NAHB

NAHB’s Ken Wingert on housing and the midterms, from state ballot measures and the ROAD to Housing Act to tariffs, labor and mortgage rates.

Housing may not be on many ballots by name on Nov. 3, but it’s running through nearly every race.

With the midterms set for Tuesday, candidates from both parties are pitching voters on affordability. Lawmakers are campaigning on the recently passed 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, states from California to Massachusetts are voting on measures meant to make building easier, and homebuilders are grappling with tariffs and immigration enforcement that have driven up costs and thinned out job-site crews.

Inman spoke with Ken Wingert, chief advocacy officer at the National Association of Home Builders, about the races and ballot measures NAHB is watching, whether data centers are really competing with housing for land, and what agents should keep an eye on as votes are counted.

Inman: What are two or three outcomes to the midterms you think matter most for housing — on the federal- level and state-level?

Ken Wingert: The overall theme is that this is turning out to be, once again, an affordability election, and housing is at the top of that pain point … because we don’t have enough of it. So regardless of who controls Congress or who wins the governor’s race in any given state, I think housing will be near or at the top of the agenda going into 2027. That gives us, and other groups you’re probably talking to, a lot of opportunity to advocate for more housing supply.

On specific issues, people are starting to understand that supply matters. You’re seeing ballot initiatives in a number of states aimed at making it easier for builders to build and cutting some of that red tape. Members of Congress are running on the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. Congress is still debating permitting reform that may pass in the lame-duck session or get kicked to the next Congress.

From a congressional standpoint, if Democrats win at least one chamber, there will probably be more pushback and oversight on issues like tariffs and immigration, which have made it harder for builders to build more housing, or at least more expensive.

Are there specific races that NAHB is watching closely, at the state, federal or local level?

We’re not quite NAR size, but we’re involved in a lot. At the federal level, I think we’ll see how big a wave is, if one materializes, and whether it takes out some folks who have been very helpful on housing over the years.

Financial Services Chairman French Hill will be fine, I think, but he’s in a tighter race than expected. Mike Hill, chairman of the House Financial Services Subcommittee on Housing and Insurance, faces the same challenge. In Michigan, Bill Huizenga is a former Realtor and builder. Sherrod Brown, former chair of the Banking Committee, is potentially coming back to the Senate from Ohio. A lot of folks are watching that race.

But really, at the state level: California has a couple of ballot initiatives, one in particular we’ve been involved with on changes to CEQA, the California Environmental Quality Act. The legislature had made some changes, and this would codify them in state law. In Massachusetts, we’re supporting a ballot initiative that would reduce minimum lot sizes, meaning how big your lot has to be to build on it. And there are a bunch of funding ballot initiatives around the country. All of those aim to increase supply, so we’re keyed in on those state-level races.

I’ve seen candidates from both parties campaigning on the recently passed ROAD to Housing Act. Does that kind of policy achievement resonate with voters, or does a general affordability pitch resonate more?

Both parties are campaigning on the fact that Congress passed major housing legislation with overwhelming bipartisan support. Beyond affordability, another theme in this election is that people want less divisiveness and more collaboration to solve problems. ROAD to Housing was a great example of both parties giving up a few things to get a bill they wanted.

I don’t know that the average voter is digging into a bill with 60 titles, but they understand that Congress recognized a housing supply problem and is at least trying to fix it. If I’m running for Congress, that’s something I’m going to go out and tell people.

Have you noticed more local candidates running explicitly on pro-housing or YIMBY platforms? Any examples?

Our state and local associations make their own endorsements and funding decisions, so, honestly, I’m too far removed to say whether a certain state rep in Texas is doing X.

One interesting part of this election is that the NIMBY focus has shifted from housing to data centers. The recognition that we need more housing has shifted more in the YIMBY direction. That’s a dynamic we’re not encouraging, because data centers are a separate issue, but it’s been interesting.

Talking to our locals, more folks at the city council and county level, where the rubber really meets the road on development, are talking about the need to build more affordable and workforce housing.

We’ve seen in our own polling a real desire, and real angst, from younger voters who feel they can’t afford a home, and from their parents, who are also worried their kids can’t afford a home, may be living with them for a long time, and want them to stay in their state and area and raise their families there. That underlying affordability challenge is driving a lot of the rhetoric and, quite frankly, a lot of the ads. They may not mention housing specifically, but it’s embedded in broader affordability concerns.

You mentioned data centers. I’ve written a couple of stories about data centers competing with housing development for the same land. Is that something NAHB has seen? Is it a real phenomenon?

I think it’s a little overblown, at least right now. A lot of the areas where they’re looking to build data centers aren’t necessarily areas where you would build housing. So there may be some competition over land, but it’s not as big an issue as people may think.

The larger issue is competition for labor. Residential construction always competes with commercial construction for talent and labor, whether it’s somebody building an office building or a house. That competition is real, but it also means more investment in workforce training and more attention to the trades.

We’ve seen many large tech companies announce they’ll fund apprenticeship and training programs because they also need those workers. So there may be some trickle-down help for homebuilding. But it’s still too soon to see real impact, beyond utilities and similar things.

Speaking of labor, I’ve seen quite a few stories about how immigration policy and enforcement have affected construction labor. Has NAHB seen that, what’s your stance, and how have you worked with lawmakers on it?

We’ve definitely heard a lot about it, especially in the last few months. It’s been primarily in Southern states, but not exclusively.

The big concern from members is that the way enforcement is being carried out, whether at the local level, by ICE or some combination, is scaring off all Hispanic workers, regardless of immigration status or citizenship. They’re coming onto job sites, rounding everyone up and detaining folks for hours, repeatedly showing up or pulling people over in a van on the way to a job site. That’s made it very hard to retain workers or get them to show up, because there’s a fear factor in the Hispanic community about even U.S. citizens and green card holders getting roped in with folks who may not be here legally.

That’s caused delays on job sites and made it hard to find labor, period, because there’s no immediate replacement. That’s why we’re so focused on workforce training.

I think it’ll be a factor in places like Texas and Florida, and in the electoral outcome. You’re already seeing Hispanic turnout larger than historic levels. Some polling shows that even folks who supported the president on immigration, who maybe voted for him based on closing the border and enforcement, feel the enforcement has gone too far. It’ll be interesting to see what the exit polls show.

Inman’s core audience is real estate agents. What should agents pay the most attention to in these midterms? Does it depend on their local market, or is there something general to watch?

Disclosure: I used to work for NAR, too, so I understand where they’re coming from. I don’t know if there’s one particular issue, or whether it’s about the House or Senate flipping. It’s the overall voter mindset. If Congress changes control, or a governorship flips one way or the other, does it have an immediate impact? Does it change the [Trump] administration’s course? Those are all open questions.

Ultimately, voters hope inflation can be tamed, and interest rates obviously drive much of this for agents. Resolving the situation in Iran, and maybe dialing back some tariff policies, could affect the inflation numbers driving interest rates. If we can get rates back down, certainly below 7 percent and into the mid-6s, that will unlock a lot of demand that’s still out there but has moved to the sidelines over the last six months.

It’s hard to see how those things will change, no matter the outcome. They all feel very up in the air.

Yeah, but there’s a certain psyche to it. We saw this after the 2024 election. Everyone’s so wrapped up in politics now that people go into a weird holding pattern for the last month or two before an election. They say, “I’m going to wait until after the election and see, and then make a major decision.”

Uncertainty is a factor, and depending on your political outlook, you may be much happier on Nov. 4, or you may not be. But at least it resolves one more question mark for the next two years before we start a presidential cycle.

I hope that, whatever the outcome, having the election behind us will ease angst for potential buyers and sellers, calm the overall market, and get it moving again.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

SÃO PAULO, Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ --Natura announced today its results for the third quarter of 2026 (3Q26). The company ended the period with consolidated net revenue of BRL 5 billion (-3% in BRL and -5.9% in constant currency). In Brazil, revenue declined by -9%, marking an improvement compared to the previous quarter but falling short of the company's expectations. The result also reflects product unavailability and a loss of productivity among beauty consultants, in addition to the decline in the relationship selling channel.

At Hispanic markets, revenue remained stable in constant currency (-0.9%). The performance reflects a slowdown in Mexico compared with the second quarter, mainly due to revenue phasing, as a sales cycle was brought forward from the third to the second quarter of this year. It also reflects Argentina's continued but still slow recovery following the integration with Avon.

Consolidated EBITDA was BRL 460 million, with a margin of 9.1% (+20 bps YoY). Excluding non-operating effects, EBITDA would have reached BRL 636 million, with a margin of 12.6%.

Net income was BRL 49 million, reversing the net loss of BRL 119 million recorded in the same period last year. One of the key highlights of 3Q26 was the company's strong cash generation of BRL 268 million, which, combined with the FIDC inflows, reduced net debt to BRL 3.4 billion. As a result, leverage fell to 1.83x, from 2.06x in 2Q26, underscoring the resilience and cash-generating capacity of the business model, even amid operational challenges.

"These priorities can only be delivered through a strong, focused culture, driven by collaborative teams with a sense of ownership and the ability to make tough decisions," the CEO added.
