#5503. Builders are looking for a bottom. 2027 plans can’t wait that long

Builders are balancing incentives, margins, and cash recovery as resale inventory rises and rental options improve. Key signals include a 5.5% drop in existing-home sales, 5.1 months of supply, and widespread builder discounting.  AI Summary

We’re at that agonizing moment in a housing market downturn when finding “the bottom” becomes the first next thing to hope for.

The trouble is, market bottoms tend to reveal themselves only in the 20/20 clarity of hindsight, not in any set of measures we can confidently decipher in the present.

For America’s homebuilders, residential developers and investors, this creates an uncomfortable predicament. They’re not just competing with the clock. They’re competing with other parts of the residential continuum –rentals and resales – that are also competing with the clock. They must make decisions that will determine their performance in 2027 before they know whether the worst is behind them.

Decisions, for instance, like how much to build, where to commit capital, what prices will move homes, and what sales pace will sustain profitability.

The evidence accumulating as 2026 nears year-end offers little or no assurance that the housing market has found solid footing. Weakening household demand, rising competition in the resale market, increasingly attractive rental alternatives, and persistent uncertainty about employment, incomes, and home values are making it harder to balance pricing and sales pace sustainably.

The question for builders is not whether they can predict the precise moment the market turns. It is whether they can adapt their businesses to current conditions, preserve financial and operating flexibility to withstand further weakness, and position themselves to benefit when household demand eventually stabilizes.

The latest evidence points to a market that is still losing momentum

Thursday’s report from the National Association of Realtors offered another indication of the challenges facing the housing market. Existing-home sales fell 5.5% in October to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million, down 8.8% from a year earlier and the weakest reading since August 2010.

The number of existing homes for sale increased to 1.59 million, up 4.6% from October 2025. At the current sales pace, that represented 5.1 months of supply, compared with 4.4 months a year earlier and the highest level since November 2015.

The national median existing-home price, meanwhile, rose just 0.4% from a year earlier to $416,700. That combination of declining transactions, rising months’ supply and relatively stable reported prices illustrates a housing market in which buyers and sellers have yet to agree on home values under prevailing financing and economic conditions.

Telling data points came through in this analysis, breaking out trends that speak to a softening market:

The numbers reveal a critical point of distinction. A rising months’ supply does not necessarily mean homeowners are flooding the market with listings. It can result from sales falling faster than inventory is being absorbed. Both dynamics are relevant to builders, whose homes compete with an increasing selection of existing properties for buyers.

The latest data offer little encouragement to builders expecting a quick rebound in household demand. The National Association of Home Builders reported that September new-home sales fell to a 676,000-unit annual pace, 5.3% below the year-earlier level, while the supply of new homes for sale remained elevated at 8.4 months.

The October NAHB/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index fell to 29, its lowest level since June 2012. Forty-three percent of builders reported cutting prices, while 65% continued to offer sales incentives.

Those findings point to a persistent problem for homebuilding companies: Builders continue to make meaningful concessions to stimulate sales, but households’ response remains insufficient to establish confidence in a sustained recovery.

Mortgage rates remain an important constraint, but the industry’s demand problem is increasingly difficult to explain through financing costs alone.

Cotality Chief Economist Dr. Selma Hepp points to the cumulative financial pressures facing prospective buyers. Elevated mortgage payments, tariff-related construction costs, insurance premiums, property taxes, utilities, and everyday household expenses are affecting households’ ability and willingness to take on the obligations of ownership.

“For housing, the key question is not simply whether mortgage rates decline, but whether they fall enough to meaningfully improve purchasing power and bring more buyers and sellers back to the market,” Hepp says.

Her observation highlights a sharp difference between qualifying for a mortgage and deciding that buying a home makes financial sense.

A household may technically qualify for a mortgage yet still find that the monthly payment, down payment, and ongoing ownership costs leave too little room for savings, unexpected expenses, or other financial commitments. For households concerned about job security or declining home values, waiting may seem increasingly prudent.

The broader economy complicates that calculation. Higher-income households with substantial savings, accumulated home equity, or financial assets may be able to absorb elevated housing costs, whereas entry-level and middle-income households have far less flexibility.

That unevenness helps explain why a national decline in mortgage rates might boost sales only modestly. Some prospective buyers need lower monthly payments. Others need greater confidence that their incomes will remain secure, that their other living expenses will stabilize, and that the home they purchase will retain its value. These concerns are not necessarily resolved by a builder’s offer of a temporary mortgage-rate buydown.

The Federal Reserve’s latest Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey underscores the demand problem. Banks reported weaker demand across all residential mortgage categories in the third quarter, even as lending standards remained largely unchanged for most mortgage products. Banks also reported weaker demand and tighter lending standards for construction and land development loans.

The implications extend beyond individual homebuyers. When expected sales absorption weakens, the financial justification for developing additional lots, opening communities, and committing construction capital becomes more difficult.

One of the most important changes in homebuilding’s competitive environment has been the reversal of several conditions that supported new-home demand during the pandemic and its aftermath.

During that period, builders benefited from an unusually tight existing-home market. Homeowners who had secured historically low mortgage rates had little incentive to sell, limiting resale inventory and directing prospective buyers toward new construction.

At the same time, elevated rents in many markets made homeownership relatively more attractive. Builders with available lots, construction capacity, and mortgage financing relationships were positioned to capture buyers with fewer alternatives.

The appeal of renting is not limited to households that cannot afford to buy. For some households, renting lets them keep their savings, preserve geographic flexibility, and avoid the risk of buying a home before local prices have stabilized.

Existing homes are also becoming more formidable competitors. In markets where resale listings have increased and homes are taking longer to sell, prospective buyers can compare new construction with a wider selection of existing properties. Sellers who need to relocate, settle estates, or complete other transactions may be increasingly willing to negotiate.

Builders therefore face a three-way competitive challenge that was less pronounced during the pandemic-era housing boom. They must compete against other builders, existing-home sellers and rental operators, each offering a different mix of price, location, amenities, monthly cost and financial commitment.

This competition is especially intense in markets where builders have substantial inventories of completed homes and developed lots. A resale seller may have the financial flexibility to postpone a transaction, whereas a builder must continue to carry land, construction, financing and overhead costs until inventory converts to cash.

This pressure can prompt builders to adjust their effective prices sooner than many existing-home sellers. Yet lower new-home prices can also influence resale sellers’ expectations, triggering another round of competitive adjustments. The process may continue for some time before either market reaches a sustainable balance.

For builders, the most immediate challenge is determining how much pricing flexibility is needed to maintain sales velocity without sacrificing the profitability required to sustain their businesses. Reducing prices and offering incentives may increase orders, but those measures can also erode gross margins and reduce returns on capital already committed to land and construction. Maintaining prices may protect reported margins on individual transactions, but it can leave completed homes on the market longer, increase carrying costs, and delay the recovery of invested capital.

Neither approach necessarily produces a better outcome without understanding the relationships among sales pace, effective pricing, inventory costs and cash generation.

The problem becomes more difficult when household demand continues to weaken. Pricing decisions that seem sufficient to generate sales in one month may need to be reconsidered the next as competing builders adjust incentives, resale sellers lower expectations, or rental operators offer more attractive terms.

The industry’s challenge is therefore to find a lower price at which buyers will purchase homes and to determine whether homes can be produced, marketed, and sold at that price while still generating acceptable returns. Not one or the other, both. That distinction directly impacts 2027 budgets.

A community that achieves an acceptable gross margin with three sales per month may generate inadequate returns if absorption drops to one or two sales. Conversely, a lower-margin community that turns inventory quickly and requires less capital may outperform one with stronger nominal margins but slower cash recovery.

These tradeoffs will vary by market, product type, land basis, construction costs, and financing structure. A single national assumption about mortgage rates or home-price appreciation cannot resolve them.

The industry’s search for a bottom should not become a reason to postpone decisions about how businesses will operate if demand remains weak. Instead, the uncertainty should drive builders to test their 2027 plans against a broader range of outcomes, including scenarios in which conditions deteriorate further before improving.

The first priority is a more precise understanding of household purchasing power and competing housing alternatives in each community’s trade area.

Builders need to know not only which prospective customers qualify to purchase, but also what they are willing to pay when comparing a new home with available resales and rental properties. That analysis should include the full monthly cost of ownership, the incentives required to attract buyers, and the potential impact of additional competing supply.

The second priority is reassessing land commitments, community-opening schedules, and construction starts.

Projects approved under stronger demand assumptions may no longer meet their original return requirements. Builders should evaluate whether development schedules can be phased, whether lot deliveries can be adjusted, and whether to defer capital commitments until sales absorption justifies additional investment.

The third priority is to maintain the financial and operational flexibility to respond when conditions change.

That means closely monitoring completed-home inventory, construction cycle times, cancellation rates, financing costs, and cash recovery. It also means identifying opportunities to reduce product and construction costs rather than relying indefinitely on incentives to bridge the gap between household purchasing power and home prices.

These are practical operational decisions, not substitutes for a stronger housing market. They can, however, determine how much financial strain a builder faces while waiting for demand to stabilize. They may also determine which companies are positioned to invest as better opportunities emerge.

Hepp identifies the upcoming spring selling season as an important test of whether housing activity can begin to recover.

“Until then, I expect activity to remain relatively subdued, making the spring homebuying season an increasingly important test of whether the market can finally turn a corner,” she says.

Homebuilders cannot control when household demand stabilizes. They can control how quickly they recognize market changes, how effectively they adjust their cost structures and capital commitments, and how well they prepare their businesses for conditions that may remain difficult longer than expected.

The bottom will become clear in hindsight. The work of getting through it – and of emerging stronger – waits for no one.

#5502. Hollyland Named Official Sponsor of APEC 2026 Shenzhen Meetings

SHENZHEN, China, Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting will take place in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19, following the APEC CEO Summit and concluding a series of APEC ministerial and senior officials' meetings. The meetings will mark China's third time hosting APEC and Shenzhen's debut as an APEC host city.

Hollyland, a Shenzhen-founded provider of wireless audio and video transmission solutions, has been named an official sponsor of APEC 2026. The company will support media operations throughout the meetings with professional audio, intercom, and video transmission technologies, helping facilitate communication and coverage at one of the region's most important international gatherings.

"Shenzhen's manufacturing depth and engineering talent have played an important role in shaping Hollyland," said Lima Wen, CEO of Hollyland. "We are honored to support APEC Shenzhen 2026. As Shenzhen is the city where Hollyland was founded, witnessing it host the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting for the first time makes this occasion especially meaningful."

Hollyland will provide LARK M2S wireless microphones at a designated service desk in the APEC Media Center, where participating media can access the equipment and technical support for their reporting needs. The ultra-mini system is designed to stay unobtrusive on camera while capturing clear speech in crowded, fast-moving reporting conditions, from corridor scrums to stand-ups on the exhibition floor.

Hollyland will also equip the APEC Media Center's on-site studio with its Solidcom series wireless intercom systems, enabling seamless communication among production personnel throughout live operations. Complementing this setup, the company's Pyro series solutions will power wireless camera signal transmission, reception and real-time monitoring, delivering stable video feeds to support the production team's workflow and on-site decision-making.

The deployment builds on Hollyland's extensive experience supporting high-pressure production environments. Its solutions are widely used across film and television productions, major sporting events and live stage productions, where seamless coordination between camera, audio, lighting and directing teams relies on stable and reliable wireless communication.

Hollyland is a leading provider of wireless products, specializing in wireless intercom systems, video transmission systems, monitors, wireless microphones, and live streaming cameras. Since 2013, Hollyland has been serving millions of users around the world in various sectors, including filmmaking, telecasting, video production, live events, exhibitions, theaters, houses of worship, and individual content creators. It has built a sales network covering approximately 160 countries and regions, supported by regional teams and offices worldwide. For more information, please visit https://www.hollyland.com/, Hollyland Facebook, and Hollyland Instagram.

#5501. Jeff Glover goes indie after 17 years with Keller Williams (EXCLUSIVE)

Jeff Glover, founder of Live Unreal Companies |

Jeff Glover takes Glover Agency independent after 17 years with Keller Williams, telling Inman the move is about keeping Glover U broker-agnostic.

Glover Agency, the Michigan team Jeff Glover founded in 2008, became fully independent on Nov. 1, ending a 17-year run with Keller Williams. The move comes roughly three months after Glover sold his three Keller Williams market centers.

The team says it has been Michigan’s top homeselling team across all brands in 11 of the past 13 years and has sold more than 10,000 homes. It operates out of four offices in Birmingham, Plymouth, Fenton and Grand Rapids.

Glover Agency will now operate only in Michigan and isn’t affiliated with any franchise or national brand.

With Glover Agency out of the franchise system, none of Glover’s Live Unreal Companies are tied to a single brand, which Glover says frees Glover U to work with agents and leaders at every brokerage in the U.S. and Canada.

In an exclusive interview with Inman, Glover said the decision had a lot to do with Glover U, the coaching and training company where he now spends most of his time. Glover U has long pitched itself as broker-agnostic, but Glover said his KW ties kept closing doors, even after the market center sale.

In August, Glover sold his ownership stakes in three Keller Williams market centers across Michigan, where he served as majority owner and operating principal. He said the sale supported Glover U’s broker-agnostic approach to serving agents across the U.S. and Canada. The three market centers combined closed nearly $1 billion in sales volume in 2025.

“Most of [the potential Glover U clients], if they don’t know me and their agents don’t know me, they’re not going to return my call,” Glover said of leaders at rival brands. “I had leaders of large companies — I mean, the largest that exist today — say, ‘Hey, Jeff, that’s great you sold your franchises, and we’re definitely open to you helping our agents, but I’m sorry, I can’t put a Keller Williams guy on our stage.'”

Joining another brand would have recreated the same problem. Going independent, Glover says, removes it.

“This move furthers the brand-agnostic approach we’ve been working toward, and now there should be little to no objection to somebody trusting me with their agents, because I don’t have a dog in the fight,” Glover said. “They don’t have to worry about me pushing their agents to go to any one company when I’m independent.”

The second driver is marketing. Glover Agency has advertised under its own name for years on TV, radio and billboards, and Glover said most Michigan consumers already assumed the team was independent.

Franchise rules on how the team could advertise, down to how large its name could appear, made it harder for individual agents to build their own brands.

“It’s very hard for them to create a brand within a brand within a brand,” Glover said. “It’s confusing to consumers. It’s confusing to other agents and other companies.”

Glover said top teams that understand marketing already know where consumer loyalty sits.

“The everyday seller and everyday buyer generally doesn’t say, ‘ We’re listing our home with Keller Williams or with Coldwell Banker,'” Glover said. “They say, ‘We’re listing our home with ‘Joe Smith’ or ‘Amy Duncan.'”

For the consumer, Glover said that the brand is “just the gravy on top.” “The brand helps, but today’s consumer resonates more with an agent’s or a team’s brand than with the company’s brand,” he said.

Day-to-day operations at Glover Agency are run by CEO Taylor Kerrigan. Glover remains involved and still lists and sells. He said he was prospecting in front of the team’s agents just before speaking with Inman on Friday.

“For our clients, nothing changes about how we serve them, other than a more personalized approach,” Kerrigan said in a statement. “What does change is that the name on the door is entirely ours.”

Glover joined Keller Williams in 2009, and the company says the team climbed as high as No. 3 nationally among all groups and No. 1 among expansion teams for homes sold. Asked what would be hardest about leaving, Glover didn’t hesitate.

“Without question, my relationship with Gary Keller,” he said, pointing to Keller’s early top 100 mastermind and a smaller circle of about a dozen agents, the Pirate Group, who got regular access to the KW co-founder. “I wouldn’t be where I am today if it weren’t for him.”

Glover said he still considers Keller a mentor and expects to keep speaking at KW events “so long as I’m welcome.”

The timing puts Glover on the opposite side of an industry trend. Consolidation has dominated brokerage headlines this year, including Compass–Anywhere and Real–REMAX, and independents face growing pressure to align with a larger platform.

Glover doesn’t think independence is right for everyone. He said it works for owners who know what agents need today, such as database growth, leverage and help building personal brands, and who have the energy to deliver it.

“For the person who somewhat wants the easy button, and maybe they’re at a point in their life where they don’t have the energy or time to pour into their company,” he said, joining a franchise or a company like Real, eXp or LPT “makes a lot of sense for that individual.”

For Glover, the bigger bet is on Glover U.

“The biggest thing is neutralizing Glover U so that it will be the No. 1 training and coaching company on the planet for real estate agents at the rate we’re growing,” he told Inman. “And I can’t do that if I’m affiliated with any one brand. So that’s a big part of it. The other part is the freedom and flexibility this gives us to help our agents grow their brands even bigger.”

#5500. Cisco beats expectations, lifts guidance and forecasts AI infrastructure revenue to double in fiscal 2027

Shares of Cisco Systems Inc. were flat in late trading today after the networking infrastructure giant reported first-quarter earnings and revenue that came in ahead of Wall Street’s expectations.

The company also raised its guidance for fiscal 2027, citing strong demand for artificial intelligence network infrastructure.

Cisco reported earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $1.40 per share, comfortably beating the Street’s target of $1.33 per share. Revenue for the quarter jumped 24% from the same period one year earlier, to $18.5 billion, ahead of the $18.1 billion analyst consensus estimate. All told, Cisco’s net income rose to $4.6 billion, up from just $2.9 billion a year ago.

Although the stock was flat in extended trading, it’s still up 32% in the year to date, way ahead of the broader Nasdaq index, which has gained just 9% over the same stretch.

Cisco has been pushing to gain a foothold in the AI infrastructure buildout that’s dominating the technology industry these days after failing to capitalize on the generative AI boom in the early days. However, its push has come at a critical juncture, as investors have become increasingly concerned over the prospects of a slowdown in data center building following the Democratic party’s sweeping victory in the U.S. midterm elections. Additionally, there are growing fears about the impact rising borrowing costs will have on debt-fueled data center construction projects.

Still, Cisco Chief Executive Chuck Robbins (pictured) expressed confidence in the company’s ability to maintain its momentum. He told analysts on a conference call that we’re still in the “very early stages of a multiyear network supercycle.” He said he’s confident Cisco’s AI networking technology is strong enough to continue to capture a portion of the multibillion-dollar opportunity that presents.

“Organizations are turning to Cisco for our trusted, market-defining technology and our expertise to help them scale, secure and optimize their environments for the agentic AI era,” Robbins added.

Cisco is also building out its software portfolio with new tools that can help businesses to build armies of autonomous AI agents that can perform work on behalf of humans. It also sells the security software necessary to protect those agents and their underlying infrastructure against cyberattacks.

The company said it’s increasing its AI infrastructure revenue forecast for the fiscal year to $9 billion, which would be more than double what it earned in fiscal 2026. According to Chief Financial Officer Mark Patterson, the company is “unlocking significant operating leverage,” and this is what’s enabling it to grow its earnings “much faster” than its revenue.

Investors may still be worried about Cisco’s gross margins, though. This has been a concern for many companies, as the global shortage of memory chips has steadily increased the cost of the components that hardware makers need to build their data center infrastructure products.  Cisco’s gross margin of 65.6% in the quarter was in-line with the Street’s estimates, but down from 68.1% in the year-ago period.

TECHnalysis Research analyst Bob O’Donnell told Reuters that the decline was unlikely to worry too many people, though. “A small dip in gross margin is not a major concern given higher memory and component costs,” he said. He added that the company’s raised forecast and strong earnings and revenue was the main thing the market wanted to see.

For the current quarter, Cisco said it’s looking for earnings of between $1.34 and $1.36 per share on sales of $18 billion to $18.2 billion. That’s a strong forecast, with the Street looking for earnings of just $1.23 per share on revenue of $17.88 billion.

#5499. Exclusive: ARA forms AI Task Force to back licensee-in-the-loop laws

The American Real Estate Association launched an AI Task Force, chaired by Dmitriy Kruglyak, to advocate licensee-in-the-loop rules. The group plans white papers and state-by-state outreach to require licensed supervision of AI actions in real estate transactions.  AI Summary

The American Real Estate Association (ARA) has launched an AI Task Force focused on advocating for and advancing “Licensee-in-the-Loop” legislation in all 50 states.

Jason Haber, a co-founder of ARA along with The Agency’s Mauricio Umansky, said the legislative effort was inspired by a contributor article published on HousingWire by Dmitriy Kruglyak, a self-described software engineer turned real estate broker. In the piece, Kruglyak argues that the growing use of agentic AI in real estate could put consumers at risk by allowing unlicensed automated systems to perform tasks traditionally handled by licensed agents, including negotiating contracts and guiding transactions.

“I think this could be the defining issue for our industry in 2027,” Haber told HousingWire. “I read Dmitry’s oped and I was glued. I immediately understood the implications of what he was writing about. It struck me as a gigantic red flag in our industry and no one was talking about it.”

Haber said Kruglyak is now chairing ARA’s AI Task Force, which will be meeting for the first time in the coming weeks. The group will work on white papers focused on the issue, along with AI policy analysis and advocacy, with “licensee-in-the-loop” being the first issue the group will focus on.

“AI has no fiduciary, it holds no license, it has no errors and omission insurance and when something goes wrong, there is no real estate board to file an ethics complaint with,” Haber said. “So what happens is you have a consumer that has no idea how the AI model has been trained. For example, maybe it has been trained to benefit the seller and not the buyer so it convinces a buyer to make a higher offer.”

However, if a real estate licensee is involved, the whole situation changes, Haber said. ARA views “licensee-in-the-loop legislation as a guarantee that anyone who buys, sells or rents a home has a licensed, accountable real estate professional standing behind the transaction.

“We’re saying, if you have an act performed by an automated system on behalf of the consumer for a real estate transaction, it has to be supervised by a responsible licensee that’s identifiable to the consumer with a name and license. And, before any offer goes in or counter offers are transmitted, it’s really reviewed by someone who holds a license and that the autonomous system is backed by the licensees fiduciary responsibilities to a client,” Haber said.

He said ARA views this as the responsible way to embrace AI technology, as it enables consumers to hold someone accountable if something goes wrong in their transaction. Although the share of consumers buying or selling their home solely with the help of an AI model or an AI real estate agent product is still the minority, Haber said he believes the industry will see more of these AI real estate agent platforms popping up in the next year, which is why he feels it is important for ARA to get ahead of the issue.

“We are looking to future proof for the consumer in the industry,” he said. “We see this coming and we want to have regulatory and statutory framework in place so that we don’t have to react after the consumer has been harmed. So, we think by moving now we are in a better position.”

Haber also noted that these efforts take time, especially because there are no federal real estate licensing laws. Due to this, Haber said ARA is going state-by-state talking to legislators regarding this issue in hopes that they will be willing to introduce this legislation in their state.

“We are tapping our state association chairs and working with our federal lobbyist to connect us with elected officials around the country,” Haber said. “It is going to take some time and just getting one bill through one state is Herculean enough, but now we are trying to take this already very challenging thing and do it 50 times.”

While Haber acknowledges that this will be a tall order, he believes it is a great opportunity for ARA to show what it is doing to help agents and American consumers at a national level.

“I think it is going to be interesting to see how it plays out, it is a long process, but we think we will have legislation introduced as early as the end of the year or early January in some states,” Haber said.

#5498. Amazon’s Ring tries again with a $250 flying home security drone and a $1,000 patrol robot

by Todd Bishop on Nov 10, 2026 at 5:30 amNovember 10, 2026 at 5:42 am

Amazon’s Ring unveiled a $249.99 flying indoor security drone and a $999.99 mobile patrol robot for businesses, bringing back two ideas that stalled in earlier incarnations.

The Ring Drone Cam and Ring Rover Cam, announced Tuesday, are the first products under the Ring Robotics name, which the company calls “a new category of autonomous, mobile security.” Both devices use a system Ring calls AI Pilot to map a home or business, suggest spots worth checking, and find their own way around obstacles such as furniture and shelving.

The drone stays docked with its camera off until it’s sent out on a schedule, on demand, or automatically when another Ring device is triggered. The Rover patrols stores and offices, using a periscope camera to see over counters and shelving.

The Rover is available for preorder in the U.S. and is scheduled to ship Dec. 16. The Drone Cam is slated for Jan. 27, 2027, but Ring is only taking email sign-ups for now. The fine print notes that the drone hasn’t yet received the required authorization from the Federal Communications Commission.

Scheduled flights and patrols, and reviewing the Rover’s recorded video, require a Ring Protect subscription plan. Ring didn’t say which plans qualify.

Ring says customers wanted to see spots a fixed camera can’t reach, and rooms where they wouldn’t want one mounted.

“The honest answer wasn’t more cameras; it meant reimagining what a security device could be,” said Jamie Siminoff, Ring’s founder and chief inventor, in a statement. “That kind of invention is hard, and it takes time.”

Ring unveiled a flying indoor camera called the Always Home Cam in 2020, also priced at $249.99. The company later opened an invitation list, but the device never went on general sale.

The original drone flew only along paths that owners mapped out with it in advance. Ring says the new one builds a floor plan as the owner carries it through the house, suggests spots to check, and plans its own routes.

The Rover Cam traces back to Astro for Business, a rolling security robot that Amazon launched in November 2023 at a starting price of $2,350. Amazon discontinued it less than a year later, refunding customers and shutting the robots off.

Astro for Business was a spinoff of Amazon’s Astro home robot, an Alexa-powered device on wheels that debuted in 2021 and can patrol the house on its own.

Ring says the new robot was inspired by Astro customers who said roving security was their favorite feature. The Ring team “leveraged the best of Astro” to build it, the company says. Ring is pitching the Rover as “not a home robot that also does security, but a purpose-built security robot.”

The original Astro for the home remains an invite-only product. Amazon has redeployed much of the Astro team to work on a new home robot, CNBC reported Sunday. In March, Amazon acquired Fauna Robotics, a New York humanoid robot startup, saying it would become part of a new Personal Robotics Group. Ring’s announcement doesn’t mention either effort.

The Rover also extends Ring’s push into commercial security, following a $5,000 surveillance trailer for parking lots that it unveiled in January. In security robots, it competes with companies such as Knightscope, which rents its robots through a subscription, and Cobalt AI. At $999.99, the Rover costs less than half what Astro for Business did.

On the security drone front, Indoor Robotics makes a ceiling-docking drone that patrols offices and warehouses, but flying security cameras for the home remain rare.

Siminoff, who launched Ring’s predecessor, Doorbot, in 2012 and sold Ring to Amazon in 2018, left the company in 2023 and returned last year to lead Ring and Amazon’s related home security businesses. Last month, Ring unveiled its first smart lock, a $249 deadbolt with no keyhole and a dial that recharges a dead battery by hand.

#5496. California cities get firm notice: follow new housing laws, or else

California housing fights are increasingly happening before a vote, with nonprofits sending letters that cite HAA, density bonus law, and CEQA reforms. The goal is to warn officials and create a record that can be used if a city rejects or reduces a project.  AI Summary

A 135-townhome project cleared the Rancho Cucamonga Planning Commission on Tuesday on the planning department’s recommendation.

That is the outcome state reforms are meant to produce: more housing, including affordable units. Warmington Residential Homes’ project includes seven for very-low-income households. Still, the meeting showed how these disputes now run. Before a decision, a pro-housing nonprofit reminds the city to follow the law, creating a record it can cite if officials ignore the warning.

In Rancho Cucamonga, the California Housing Defense Fund sent a three-page letter citing the Housing Accountability Act, the state Density Bonus Law and last year’s California Environmental Quality Act reform. Rejecting the project or cutting its size, it warned, would require written findings of a specific health or safety hazard.

The Rancho Cucamonga letter was one of at least five CalHDF sent that day, along with letters to Santa Clarita, Whittier, Escondido and Twentynine Palms. Four concerned projects of 17 to 146 units. One addressed an ADU ordinance.

Those letters are a fraction of the total. James Lloyd, the organization’s director of planning and investigations, told HousingWire the number reaches about 100 a year.

They serve as a first step toward making sure cities implement state housing reforms properly, according to the organization.

Broadly, the letters pair legal warnings with a pitch to local officials: new housing helps a city’s finances and existing residents while meeting the state’s need for more homes.

“While no one project will solve the statewide housing crisis, the proposed development is a step in the right direction,” the organization writes.

Lawmakers have spent years trying to speed housing construction to improve affordability. Gov. Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill 130 to reform CEQA and SB 131 in 2025, exempting qualifying infill housing from environmental review and narrowing review for projects that nearly qualify. Legislators also tightened the Housing Accountability Act, which limits when cities can deny or shrink projects that meet zoning.

Neighbor suits have not disappeared. They have shifted to different arguments. Attorneys at the legal publisher CEB expect litigation to focus on whether a project qualifies for a CEQA exemption at all, rather than on the adequacy of an environmental report.

Builders and advocates pose a growing risk for cities that resist state law. Cities frequently lose when they test the rules in court, and the losses can be costly. Under Senate Bill 1037, penalties can reach $50,000 per unit for willful Housing Accountability Act violations.

La Cañada Flintridge refused to process a builder’s remedy project. A judge ruled against the city in March 2024, and the city dropped its appeal a year later rather than post a $14 million bond. It paid CalHDF $1,262,500 in fees and costs last year.

A small project in Pacifica shows the stakes. Neighbors sued over an eight-townhome project, arguing it needed a full environmental impact report instead of the lighter review the city used.

A trial court sided with them, rescinded the approvals and awarded nearly $1.3 million in attorney’s fees. In December 2025, an appeals court vacated the fee award, saying the judge had wrongly discounted the project’s housing value. It sent the question back to the trial court.

But when it came to a recommendation, staff tracked the laws CalHDF cited. They wrote in their staff report that the project qualified for waivers under the state density bonus law, which limits when a city can deny them. Staff also noted the project was exempt from environmental review under CEQA guidelines.

#5495. Applied Materials posts impressive 53% jump in revenue as it beats expectations again

Semiconductor industry giant Applied Materials Inc. chalked up another strong quarter as it continued to cash in on the artificial intelligence boom, delivering fourth-quarter results that surpassed Wall Street’s expectations on earnings and revenue.

The company reported adjusted earnings of $4.16 per share on revenue of $10.41 billion, up by an impressive 53% from a year earlier. The results were impressive, with analysts modeling earnings of just $4.06 per share on sales of $10.3 billion. Net income rose to $2.71 billion, up from $1.89 billion in the same period one year ago.

Applied Materials is the world’s biggest supplier of the equipment used by semiconductor manufacturers such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Ltd., Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. and Micron Technology Inc., so its results are widely seen as a bellwether for the broader chipmaking industry. If Applied is growing, it means chipmakers are investing in their factories and presumably expecting to churn out more chips, driving growth in the industry. The company manufactures all sorts of machines to support different semiconductor manufacturing processes, catering to the most advanced silicon for AI workloads.

Chief Executive Gary Dickerson (pictured) said the company delivered record-breaking results in fiscal 2026, with full-year sales rising 21% from the prior year, to $34.31 billion. He also said the semiconductor systems business unit is on track to grow more than 40% in calendar 2026. “AI continues to fuel strong incremental demand for semiconductors and Applied has the most-enabling portfolio to advance the AI computing roadmap, putting us in a great position for multiyear revenue and profit growth,” he added.

Applied’s stock was under pressure earlier in the day following the news of Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation, which came after he admitted to having an affair with a woman who is believed to be working for China’s intelligence services. Some investors worry that instability at Nvidia, which is the world’s most dominant AI chip supplier, could have a knock-on effect on the broader chipmaking industry.

However, the strong results brought Applied’s daytime slide to a halt, and the stock gained more than 2.5% in late trading. In the year to date, its stock is up 48%.

Applied’s main business, the semiconductor systems unit, saw revenue jump from $4.88 billion in the year-ago period to $7.99 billion. Meanwhile, sales from the smaller applied global services segment rose from $1.5 billion a year earlier, to $1.89 billion.

For the current quarter, Applied said it’s looking for earnings of $4.35 per share at the midpoint of its guidance range, with revenue coming to $11.1 billion. Those numbers were better than expected too, with the Street modeling first quarter earnings of just $4.24 per share on sales of $10.85 billion.

During the quarter, Applied made a big splash when it said it’s going to invest $5 billion in a new chip research and development facility located in Silicon Valley. It’s called the EPIC Center, and it will act as a shared R&D center for chipmakers to collaborate on new process manufacturing technologies.

Initial partners include Intel Corp., which is working with Applied and other companies on the development of next-generation transistors, interconnects and advanced packaging technologies. Other founding partners include Kioxia Corp., BE Semiconductor Industries N.V. and the UCLA Samueli School of Engineering.

#5494. SEMIFIVE Secures KRW 178.4 Billion in Q3 New Orders, Up 437% YoY, Driving Order Backlog to Record High

SEOUL, South Korea, Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- SEMIFIVE, a leading global provider of custom AI semiconductor (ASIC) solutions, today announced record-breaking order performance for the third quarter of 2026, securing KRW 178.4 billion in new orders and driving its order backlog to an all-time high of KRW 245.5 billion on a consolidated basis.

SEMIFIVE achieved a remarkable 437% year-over-year (YoY) surge in third-quarter new orders, up from KRW 33.2 billion in the same period last year. The quarterly total was approximately 2.8 times the KRW 63.3 billion recorded in the previous quarter, representing a 182% quarter-over-quarter (QoQ) increase, and 1.5 times the company's total new orders of KRW 118.9 billion for the first half of 2026. Capitalizing on surging global demand for custom ASIC solutions, SEMIFIVE accelerated its expansion into key international markets, including North America and Japan, fueling exceptional order growth.

The company pushed its order backlog to a record KRW 245.5 billion, a 75% increase from KRW 140.3 billion in the previous quarter. As these orders progressively convert into revenue, the expanding backlog is expected to serve as a powerful engine for sustained mid- to long-term growth.

SEMIFIVE generated order growth across all business segments, including ASIC development, mass production, and intellectual property (IP), with its ASIC Service business spearheading overall performance.

SEMIFIVE drove strong growth in its ASIC Service business by securing high-margin advanced-node turnkey projects. Third-quarter new orders in this segment soared 705% YoY to KRW 136.9 billion, compared with KRW 17.0 billion in the same period last year. A major high-performance computing (HPC) project win in North America reinforced the company's position as a trusted provider of advanced-node turnkey solutions for large global customers. SEMIFIVE has also gained strong traction in the sovereign AI markets of South Korea and Japan, delivering tangible revenue growth.

SEMIFIVE leveraged the maturity of the 4nm process and its proven mass production track record to sharpen its competitive edge. As demand accelerates for AI inference chips built on the cost-effective, high-performance 4nm process, the company is actively capturing new opportunities through its established 4nm design and mass production capabilities.

In mass production, SEMIFIVE continued to secure a steady flow of purchase orders (POs) while accelerating the diversification and advancement of its product portfolio. The company is shifting its portfolio from smaller chips built on legacy process nodes for domestic customers toward advanced-node AI devices and dedicated AI HPC chips. Backed by exclusive mask production rights, stable shipments and an expanding AI mass production portfolio are expected to drive revenue growth beginning in 2027.

SEMIFIVE sustained steady growth in its IP business by securing additional orders for its off-the-shelf, silicon-validated IP offerings. The company supplies silicon-validated IP, originally developed for specific customers, to additional customers, maximizing the value of its proven IP assets. SEMIFIVE is also expanding into leading-edge 2nm and 3nm process technologies and HPC applications. By strengthening its IP portfolio based on Samsung Foundry's 2nm and 3nm processes, the company aims to unlock additional order opportunities in the high-performance AI semiconductor market.

For the first nine months of 2026, SEMIFIVE recorded cumulative revenue of KRW 146.1 billion, up 62% YoY. Notably, as shipments of high-value AI chips gained momentum, product revenue surged 167% QoQ to KRW 12 billion, up from KRW 4.5 billion in the previous quarter, marking the beginning of a new growth phase. The company also continued to improve profitability, achieving a cumulative gross profit margin of 28%, up 11 percentage points YoY, and improving its operating margin to -14%, up 25 percentage points YoY. Looking ahead, SEMIFIVE expects to accelerate its financial performance in the fourth quarter as its KRW 245.5 billion order backlog begins converting into revenue at a faster pace, supported by increasing mass production volumes.

"Our latest performance proves that SEMIFIVE has entered a new phase of accelerated growth in the global AI ASIC market," said Brandon Cho, CEO and Co-Founder of SEMIFIVE. "With our record-high order backlog and high-value mass production pipeline serving as powerful turbo engines, we are poised to further accelerate our growth."

#5493. PitchBook to give early-stage startups free access, using their data to feed a new tool for VCs

by Todd Bishop on Nov 10, 2026 at 7:23 amNovember 10, 2026 at 7:25 am

PitchBook announced a new program to give early-stage startups free use of its private-market data, if they share their financials and other company details.

The Seattle-based company says the new program, dubbed PitchBook for Startups, will feed PitchBook Origin, a new deal-sourcing product that helps venture capitalists and other investors find startups before they raise their first institutional round.

PitchBook announced both offerings Tuesday morning at Web Summit in Lisbon. Owned by Morningstar since 2016, the company has more than 3,000 employees and sells subscriptions to venture firms, private equity investors and dealmakers.

The launches come as first-time startup financings hit a record. There were an estimated 8,625 such deals in the U.S. through the third quarter, already more than the 8,507 in all of 2021, according to the PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor. PitchBook attributes part of the surge to AI, which it says is making it easier to start companies.

The startup program is open to pre-seed and bootstrapped companies that haven’t taken money from a venture firm or other institutional investor, or raised a priced round, the type of funding round that sets a valuation.

Founders can use PitchBook to find investors who are active in their sector and stage, and to compare their valuation and growth against similar companies.

To keep their free access, startups must update their company information every quarter. PitchBook says that information can include financials, team growth and product milestones. Only “select portions” of that data will go into Origin, the company said, without saying which.

Origin covers about 25 million companies, including stealth, pre-funding and bootstrapped companies. About 15 million of them are new to PitchBook. It scores companies on how well they match an investor’s criteria and sends alerts when they show new activity.

“What’s been missing is visibility into the stage before a company raises, when the most important signals are the hardest to see,” said Paul Santarelli, PitchBook’s chief solutions officer, in a statement announcing the products.

PitchBook didn’t disclose pricing for Origin, and the product’s web page currently asks investors to join a waitlist.

#5492. Compass sues 15 MLSs over office exclusive rules

Compass filed 15 lawsuits against MLSs alleging they punish agents for publicly marketing office exclusive listings at a seller’s request. The claims track Compass’ earlier CRMLS suit and focus on rules requiring MLS submission for cooperation.  AI Summary

Compass International Holdings is taking its fight with MLSs over their cooperation and listing submission rules to the next level. On Thursday evening, the real estate brokerage conglomerate fielded 15 lawsuits against 15 MLS.

The lawsuits all claim that these MLSs fine and punish agents who publicly market office exclusive listings at the request of the home seller.

Defendant in these lawsuits include bridgeMLS, Bay East MLS, Contra Costa MLS, MLSListings, The MLS-CLAW, San Diego MLS, Canopy MLS, Hive MLS, Doorify MLS, Arizona Regional MLS, Recolorado, NorthstarMLS, Houston Association of Realtors, Stellar MLS and OneKey MLS.

Compass also contends that MLS boards consist of Compass’s competitors who are dictating how Compass and its agents can and cannot compete in the marketplace. Compass has recently announced that it is banning all employees from serving in Realtor association leadership roles. The firm has not clarified if this also extends to non-Realtor affiliated MLSs or if it pertains to brokers and agents affiliated with Compass, as many Compass International Holdings agents and brokers serve on MLS and Realtor association boards.

“Only the law and the homeowner should tell agents how to market a home, and the MLS is neither the law nor the homeowner. Agents should be free to compete on the marketing strategies they offer,” a Compass spokesperson told HousingWire. “It’s almost as if these MLSs are asking people to ignore the evidence that proves their claims aren’t true. For years, seven of the top 25 MLSs, covering 340,000 agents across 12 states, have allowed agents to publicly market ‘office exclusives’ without fines, and none of the problems they warn about have happened. If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30% of the country?”

These lawsuits come after Compass International Holdings sent letters to MLSs in early September demanding that they stop enforcing rules governing when publicly marketed listings must be submitted to the MLS for cooperation. On stage at the Council of MLSs (CMLS) Open House conference in late September, Compass CEO Robert Reffkin  threatened to sue any MLS that refused to change their rules in response to his firm’s demands.

In response to these threats, CRMLS, ARMLS, OneKey MLS, MLSListings, Bridge MLS, Canopy MLS, Recolorado, Hive MLS and Doorify MLS have filed two separate lawsuits against Compass International Holdings in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York seeking a declaratory judgement from the court allowing them to continue enforcing their cooperation rules and policies without violating antitrust law.

The MLS defendants have not immediately returned HousingWire’s request for comment.

The Compass brokerage brand has recently announced a new broker-to-broker cooperation policy, which requires all Compass agents to cooperate with other brokers and agents, including for listings in Private Exclusive or Coming Soon marketing phases, unless otherwise instructed by the client in writing.

#5491. Allen Family Philanthropies gives $10M to hundreds of small arts groups across Washington state

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 10, 2026 at 7:30 amNovember 9, 2026 at 2:56 pm

Allen Family Philanthropies and Seattle nonprofit ArtsFund awarded $10 million to 745 small arts and culture organizations across Washington state, and renewed the grant program for another $10 million next year.

The latest Community Accelerator Grant awards range from $2,500 to $25,000 and reach organizations in 37 of the state’s 39 counties. The 2027 renewal brings the program’s total to $50 million over five years.

For 2026, the program focused on groups with annual budgets under $1 million, which raised the average award by about 25%, from $10,753 last year to $13,423.

The change followed a sector analysis by Allen Family Philanthropies and SMU DataArts. It found that smaller arts groups lost an average of one staff position between 2023 and 2024, while organizations with budgets over $1 million added an average of five.

“The incredible reach of this program across our state, along with the significant findings from our report, show just how much this type of flexible support is needed to bolster Washington’s rich and diverse arts and culture sector,” said Lara Littlefield, executive director of Allen Family Philanthropies.

Of this year’s grantees, 496 are in Northwest Washington, 132 in Southwest, 67 in Eastern and 50 in Central Washington. Recipients include 12 of the state’s 29 federally recognized tribes, and more than 22% are in rural counties.

A handful of the organizations blend art and technology, including Tacoma’s Fablab Nonprofit ($25,000), Seattle-based Simulated Immersive Experimental Realities ($15,000) and Bellingham Makerspace ($2,500).

The Old Hotel Art Gallery in Othello, in Adams County, has received a $25,000 grant each year since 2024. The gallery used the money to pay staff a living wage, to keep operating until its annual fundraiser, and to renovate its historic building, which now brings in rental income.

Gallery director Samantha Copas said the 2025 award “truly kept our doors open.”

Allen Family Philanthropies, formerly known as the Paul G. Allen Family Foundation, was founded in 1988 by the late Microsoft co-founder and his sister, Jody Allen. Arts and culture is one of its core program areas, along with youth and the environment. Last year the foundation committed nearly $7 million to eight Seattle Center nonprofits, including KEXP and the Museum of Pop Culture, to expand youth access to the arts.

ArtsFund will hold a virtual webinar in the spring for organizations interested in applying for 2027 grants. Details will be posted here.

#5490. Five thoughts from Cisco’s first quarter of fiscal 2027

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

Cisco Systems Inc. opened fiscal 2027 with a quarter that should put any question about whether artificial intelligence will act as a massive tailwind for it to rest. Revenue and earnings hit records, growth rates were the best Cisco has posted in more than 15 years, and management raised its full-year outlook and AI infrastructure revenue target.

While Cisco has delivered a string of solid quarters, some investors are concerned about the durability of the growth. After listening to the analyst call, I maintain that accelerated growth is what Cisco watchers should expect, as AI will act as a catalyst for several years. Here are my five thoughts, plus the one metric I think investors should care about most:

Asked why this isn’t simply the top of a hyperscaler spending cycle, Chief Executive Chuck Robbins (pictured) cited five growth drivers: hyperscale AI, the campus refresh, the “post-Mythos” security upgrade cycle, sovereign infrastructure and enterprise hybrid data centers. “All five of these are multiyear, multibillion,” he said. “And they’re all in relatively early stages.” In particular, the enterprise opportunity is in its infancy. Using the baseball analogy for “what inning” we’re in, the pitchers are still warming up, and enterprise is what Cisco does best.

Though hyperscalers have been driving AI growth across the industry, only one of the five trends Robbins highlighted was related to that group of companies. Chief Financial Officer Mark Patterson reinforced the point by breaking down the guidance raise, noting that a large share came from Cisco’s core, non-hyperscale business. “It’s not just campus,” he said. “It’s broad-based, and the core continues to do quite well.”

The market still views the enterprise as a slow-refresh business. The call made a strong case that it’s about to become the bigger part of Cisco’s AI story.

During the investor Q&A, a data point was worth highlighting. Robbins said that of the campus switching Cisco sold this quarter, “only 9% was really coming from the new portfolio.” Despite multiple quarters of strong campus growth, the installed base has barely moved to the next generation.

Two forces will push this base to accelerate an upgrade. One is agentic AI, which Robbins said is driving “modernization for bandwidth reasons” because agents generate traffic that campus networks were never designed to handle. The other is the security fallout from frontier models such as Anthropic’s Claude Mythos — the Mythos moment. “We’re beginning to hear from customers who are attributing orders to early Mythos implications,” Robbins said, noting that European service providers are upgrading managed customer premises equipment.

Robbins added that customers “got to get the architecture exactly right.” That suggests a long, deliberate redesign rather than a buying spree, which is characteristic of a multiyear cycle.

Cisco has long been criticized for building its own silicon as the industry shifted to merchant silicon. Robbins said that outside of optics, the hyperscale AI business is “100% Silicon One-based platforms.” The P200 continues to win scale-across deals, and the G300 is now in customer labs.

Asked why Cisco keeps winning those deals, Robbins kept it simple: “It’s really about performance and power. And there’s just this whole focus on diversity of silicon in the space.” The second point is the more strategic one. No hyperscaler wants a single supplier for any critical layer of its AI fabric, and Cisco is the credible second source.

The bigger long-term play is the enterprise. Silicon One is already shipping across parts of the enterprise portfolio, and Robbins said the target to convert all of it by fiscal 2029 “is still on track.” That gives Cisco a single silicon architecture from the hyperscale data center to the branch, with cost and roadmap control competitors can’t match.

The reality is that at Cisco’s volumes, it makes no sense to buy merchant silicon. Not only can it build it cheaper, but it can also optimize it specifically for its own features and capabilities.

A theme running through the call is that AI is decentralizing. “Our enterprise customers will be running AI applications in the cloud, but they’re also investing heavily in private data centers,” Robbins said. “They want to run open-weight and open-source models in their own data centers. They want to train on their own data in their own data centers.”

Sovereignty is driving in the same direction, with Cisco extending its Sovereign Critical Infrastructure portfolio from Europe to Canada and preannouncing India. Robbins noted that Cisco is “one of the few companies that has maintained a robust on-premises portfolio.” For years, analysts treated that on-premises focus as a liability. In a world where countries and regulated industries want operational control, it has become an advantage.

Equally important is what Cisco isn’t chasing. Robbins called neocloud exposure “relatively immaterial,” adding that “we’ve been very conservative relative to the credit situations.” That’s a disciplined choice. Cisco is growing into the safest parts of the AI build-out rather than financing its riskiest buyers.

Given the number of neoclouds, one could look at them as a massive pot of gold, but they often required vendor financing. If the neocloud isn’t successful, it’s the financing organization left holding the bag. This was the case with CLECs in the Internet days. Cisco was conservative then and will continue to be.

Security has been the weak spot in Cisco’s story, so this quarter’s progress matters. Robbins said core security orders, excluding Splunk, were “the best it’s been in three years,” with firewalls, Zero Trust secure access, and AI Defense all gaining customers. Patterson said Cisco is “a little bit above the expectations that we set out” and feels “good about turning the corner.”

The refresh cycle drives near-term numbers, but the strategic prize is trust for AI agents. Robbins said enterprise conversations now center on “agentic security, agentic identity, agentic observability, as well as the new security architecture needed for the AI era.” The network is where agent traffic flows, making it the natural enforcement point. Cisco owns more of that network than anyone.

Investor concerns received clear answers. On margins, Patterson said, “gross margins are pretty much right on target,” and on supply, “we’re seeing not a lot of issues at all.” Robbins added that Cisco is growing revenue “with less headcount than we had at the beginning” two years ago.

The number I’d watch most closely isn’t AI revenue, campus orders, or gross margin. It’s the growth of Cisco Cloud Control. Robbins mentioned it almost in passing, noting thousands of sign-ups and integrations with AI Canvas, Cisco IQ and Cisco Model Foundry. Most people will think of Cloud Control as a network management tool, but that badly understates its potential.

Cloud Control is now Cisco’s core product. The best analogy is VMware vCenter, the data center’s control point that turned a collection of products into a sticky platform. Cheaper, sometimes free hypervisors never made a dent in VMware’s share because the operational control gained from vCenter far outweighed the few bucks saved on hypervisor licenses. Cloud Control is broader and potentially more impactful because Cisco is positioning it as the control point for enterprise AI, not just the network through the following capabilities.

Cisco’s numerous network and security competitors have their own agentic operations platforms, and many beat Cisco to market. However, Cisco played the long game. In my conversations with Chief Product Officer Jeetu Patel, he has been emphatic about how important Cloud Control is to Cisco’s vision of shifting to a platform company. It enables customers to manage the underlying infrastructure, including third parties, through a single dashboard.

If Cloud Control becomes the enterprise IT console for managing AI-era infrastructure, Cisco stops competing on boxes and starts competing on control. Hardware cycles always ebb and flow, so always being best of breed is impossible. Whether this one becomes a transformation for Cisco depends on whether customers run their environments on Cloud Control. My advice to Cisco is to start disclosing active usage, partner integrations, and attach rates for the platform.

My advice to investors is to start asking for them. That number will tell you what Cisco is worth five years from now.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5488. Operationalizing AI Governance Gives Banks an Advantage in Scaling AI

BOSTON, Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- AI agents are entering production at most major banks, but few have a comprehensive framework to monitor and control them. A new Boston Consulting Group (BCG) benchmark of 26 global and domestic systemically important banks finds that agentic AI has reached production at most banks, but usage remains limited, and agent-specific monitoring and control capabilities are still being built out. Seventy-three percent of banks permit agents in production for select use cases. However, at 88% of banks, agents make up 10% or less of the AI portfolio, and only 8% have a comprehensive, standardized monitoring and control framework that explicitly covers agents.

These are among the findings of AI Safety and Governance in Banking 2026: Why Operationalizing Governance Gives Banks an Advantage in Scaling AI. The benchmark examines how prepared the banks are to govern AI as it becomes more autonomous, assessing their AI adoption and the maturity of their AI risk management. It also finds that banks that have their governance right are better at scaling, challenging the assumption that governance and speed are a tradeoff.

"Agentic AI has arrived, but most banks are cautious in scaling aggressively, as they are lacking the controls and especially the monitoring capabilities for increasingly autonomous agents," says Anne Kleppe, BCG's global lead for AI safety and governance, and coauthor of the report. "As AI scales and becomes more autonomous, the next challenge is clear: turning governance from a framework into an operating capability. With agents still a small share of AI portfolios at most banks, there is a window to get that right before their use expands."

Scaling AI Agents Safely Will Require Monitoring Capabilities That Few Banks Have Fully Built

Agentic AI systems can plan and execute multistep tasks, take actions, and adjust their approach without requiring human input at every step. Banks are only beginning to develop the controls needed to manage these systems.

Most banks do not yet have the capabilities to monitor and control agents comprehensively, and more than half are relying on restrictions and prohibitions to manage the risks in the meantime. Moving beyond the deployment of select use cases will require banks to build frameworks and technical capabilities to monitor and control agents in a standardized and scalable way.

Nearly half of banks (46%) reported an AI-related issue or incident in the past 12 months, while more than a quarter said AI systems were falling behind their promised business case. These findings show that AI risk is already here, and its downside can include lost value in addition to major risk events.

Governance Foundations Are Largely in Place, but Day-to-Day Control Lags

Most banks have put the basic structures of AI governance in place. Almost all (96%) manage AI risk through their existing risk frameworks, 73% have defined their appetite for AI risk (up from 57% in 2025), and 77% have a dedicated AI policy. But translating those policies into operational controls remains a challenge. Fewer than half of the banks have a centralized, tool-based AI inventory, and none have a comprehensive human-oversight framework that is consistently implemented across AI systems.

Governance and Speed Do Not Have to Be a Tradeoff

BCG's research challenges the assumption that stronger AI governance slows banks down: banks with more mature risk management are 2.5 times more likely to be advanced AI adopters. For example, banks that use standardized, previously approved patterns for lower-risk AI applications are nearly twice as likely to move those applications from idea to production in under six months. By standardizing what repeats, they can reserve deeper review for novel and higher-risk uses.

"Banks have largely built the foundations for governing AI, and the benchmark shows that governance and speed need not be a tradeoff," says Matteo Coppola, global leader of BCG's Risk and Compliance practice, and coauthor of the report. "The banks that are applying governance best in day-to-day operations are the ones scaling AI most extensively. The task now is to extend that discipline to agents before they become more deeply embedded."

#5487. Data center developers brace for new reality as election backlash sinks in

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 10, 2026 at 10:25 amNovember 11, 2026 at 7:41 am

Data center developers already knew they had a public relations problem. This month’s midterm elections showed how much of a political problem it has become.

Voters approved data center restrictions in 44 of 45 local measures across a dozen states. Candidates who support stronger regulation of the facilities won 32 of the 34 gubernatorial races called so far. And political campaigns reportedly spent more than $380 million on TV ads referencing data centers, according to the Associated Press.

The results capped a year of accelerating resistance as tech giants plan to spend hundreds of billions of dollars on new facilities.

So what comes next? More outreach, more transparency and the expectation that states and local governments will pass data center rules, said leaders in the Pacific Northwest.

“We’ve been working and adapting our approach to meet the moment,” said John Wilson, chief financial officer of Sabey Data Centers, in an interview. “There used to be a time where we would say that our track record could speak for itself, and that’s clearly no longer the case.”

Communities nationwide have raised concerns about the facilities’ effect on rising electric bills, their water use for cooling electronics and the noise they generate.

Broader fears about artificial intelligence are also stoking the pushback, including worries that it will replace workers and appropriate human-created content, and that it can provide erroneous information, foster unhealthy relationships with users, or facilitate scams or terrorist attacks.

A renewed effort to regulate data centers is expected in January in Washington state — home to the headquarters of Sabey, Microsoft and Amazon.

Earlier this year, state Rep. Beth Doglio, D-Olympia, pushed legislation that included ratepayer protections, transparency on environmental impacts and clean energy requirements. Microsoft and the national Data Center Coalition opposed the bill, which failed.

“It’s going to be a very tech-heavy session,” Doglio said.

Before voters weighed in this month, tech companies launched efforts to assuage public fears.

In January, Microsoft released its “Community First AI Infrastructure” initiative, which includes promises to pay the company’s full power costs, reject local property tax breaks, replenish more water than it uses, train local workers and fund AI education and community programs.

Last month, Amazon announced its “Built Together” program, pledging to invest $1 billion over five years in the U.S. communities where it operates data centers, including support for education and civic projects. The initiative offers similar commitments to Microsoft’s on transparency and covering its energy costs.

Wilson said Sabey also works with communities to understand and meet their needs. When a proposed campus in Indianapolis triggered significant pushback, the company brought community members to Quincy, a central Washington data center hub, to tour a Sabey facility and hear from locals about their experience.

“It requires a lot of patience. It requires a lot of transparency in our communication,” Wilson said. Sabey’s Decatur Technology Park in Indianapolis is moving ahead, and the company aims to bring it online in 2030.

But the even bigger challenge now is statewide moratoriums and data center bans — a scale of resistance that is difficult to address even when there is local support.

Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek in October directed a state agency to pause processing and issuing permits for new and expanding data centers until July 2027. Umatilla, where Sabey is developing its first Oregon campus, declared a local state of emergency over the potential loss of investment and revenue, the Oregon Capital Chronicle reported.

Even with the surge in resistance, “we’ve been able to find our way through on every project that we’ve had,” Wilson said. “I’m knocking on wood as I say that.”

Corporate commitments alone may no longer be enough to win public confidence, said Brad Smith, Microsoft vice chair and president, in a GeekWire interview. Communities increasingly want laws requiring all data center developers to build responsibly — a shift he called a “watershed” moment, “but one we anticipated.”

“[P]eople want to see everyone who builds a data center do it in a responsible way,” Smith added, “and they feel that the only way that one can obtain that result is to have some new laws that are put in place.”

Come next year, that could include Washington and impact local tech giants, Sabey and others. Baxtel, a data center industry research firm, lists 29 Microsoft facilities operating in Washington and four under construction, with Sabey operating eight facilities.

Amazon plans to build its first large-scale data centers in Washington, with proposed campuses in Walla Walla County and the Tri-Cities. Amazon did not respond to repeated requests for comment on this story.

Doglio said the next version of her bill will be more stringent. “We have to have a strong bill,” she said, adding that the public and members of her party are calling for it. Microsoft did not publicly specify which provisions triggered its opposition to the previous bill.

Wilson hopes any legislation, in Washington or elsewhere, allows flexibility and recognizes that data centers vary widely in size, impact and application. Sabey provides data center space and infrastructure for customers ranging from major cloud companies to corporations and community organizations.

“Describing all data centers as one thing is just not accurate,” Wilson said, “and it doesn’t understand the realities of the industry itself.”

Smith expressed optimism that U.S. lawmakers can find a middle ground that meets the needs of communities and tech companies.

“There’s plenty of room to draft laws that enable people to go forward and build responsible data centers without chilling the economic contributions these data centers make, especially to local communities,” he said.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.
