#5486. Flash flood watch vs. warning vs. emergency: what each alert means

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Flash flood watch vs. warning vs. emergency: what each National Weather Service alert means, how the three levels differ and what to do when one is issued

A flash flood can turn a dry creek bed or a city street into fast-moving water within about six hours of heavy rain. The National Weather Service (NWS) uses three escalating alert levels for this hazard. A watch says flash flooding is possible. A warning says it is happening or about to happen. An emergency says an ongoing or imminent flash flood poses a severe threat to human life and could cause catastrophic damage.

Each level calls for a different response. Confusing them costs time. Someone who treats a warning like a watch may still be gathering information while water is already rising. Someone who reads a flash flood emergency as a routine warning may miss that it is the rarest and most severe flash flood alert the NWS issues.

Getting flash flood watch vs. warning vs. emergency right starts with what each word describes. A watch is about conditions that favor flooding. A warning is about an event in progress or close to it. An emergency is not a separate product at all. It is enhanced wording added to a flash flood warning when the threat reaches its highest level.

The system has more layers than those three terms suggest. Flash flood alerts are distinct from ordinary flood alerts, which also cover slower rises on rivers and streams. Flash flood warnings carry damage threat tags. Those tags help decide whether a warning reaches phones through Wireless Emergency Alerts. That is why a person inside a warned area may not get a phone alert for every warning.

The physical danger is also easy to misjudge. Fast-moving water does not need to be deep to knock an adult down or float a car. Some landscapes also turn rain into rushing water faster than others.

The 10 slides that follow explain what a flash flood is and what each alert level means for people in its path. They compare flash flood alerts with standard flood alerts and break down the NWS damage threat tags. They also explain why phones sound for only some warnings, how little water it takes to move a vehicle and which kinds of terrain flood fastest.

A flash flood is a rapid rise of water that usually arrives within about six hours of heavy rain or another cause. River flooding moves more slowly, and the National Weather Service (NWS) covers it with a separate set of alerts.

Timing is what sets a flash flood apart. The definition turns on how quickly water comes up after the event that caused it. It does not depend on how deep the water gets or how big the waterway is. A small creek that overtops its banks soon after a downpour can qualify, just as a larger stream can.

Heavy rain is the one cause the definition names outright. The words "or another cause" leave room for floods that do not come from a storm directly overhead. A flood counts as a flash flood when the speed of the rise fits, whatever started it.

River flooding follows a different timeline. The water comes up gradually rather than in a sudden surge. The NWS does not fold this kind of flooding into its flash flood products.

The NWS reflects that difference in pace by keeping two families of flood alerts. One family is built around fast water and short notice. The other covers flooding that develops more gradually, including rises on rivers.

The short timeline also changes what a flood means for people in its path. When water can rise within hours of heavy rain, the gap between the first sign of trouble and dangerous conditions is narrow. A slower river rise generally leaves more room to react.

The flash flood side of the system has three alert levels: the watch, the warning and the emergency. All three deal with fast-rising water. Each one marks a different stage, from flooding that is possible to flooding that threatens lives.

Knowing whether a flood is the fast or the slow kind is the first step in reading any NWS flood alert. With a flash flood, the time to act is short.

A flash flood watch means conditions are favorable for flash flooding in or near the watch area. Flooding is possible, but it is not yet happening or confirmed. The watch is a signal to prepare and stay alert.

The National Weather Service issues flash flood watches, and its definition uses precise terms. "Favorable" describes the setup. The ingredients for a rapid rise of water are present, but the water is not yet rising. A watch is a forecast of risk, not a report of an event.

The phrase "in or near the watch area" also shapes how to read the alert. The risk is not confined to the outlined zone. A person just outside the boundary should treat the watch as relevant to them.

The main value of a watch is the time it provides. While flooding is only a possibility, there is room to plan routes, check devices and decide where to go. Those choices are harder to make once water is already rising.

Preparation during a watch comes down to three steps. The first is to know the local evacuation route. That means knowing which road leads to higher ground from home, from work and from any place a person expects to spend time during the watch.

The second step is to enable emergency alerts on a phone. A watch can escalate if flooding begins. A phone set to receive alerts is one way to learn about that change quickly.

The third step is to keep a NOAA Weather Radio as a backup. The radio offers a second path for alerts if a phone is switched off, out of battery or without signal.

A watch on its own does not tell people to move to higher ground. It calls for readiness — a known route, alerts turned on and a backup source of information — for as long as the watch remains in effect.

A flash flood warning means flash flooding is occurring or about to occur. The National Weather Service (NWS) tells anyone in the warned area to move to higher ground right away.

That instruction separates a warning from a flash flood watch. A watch describes conditions that could lead to flooding. A warning describes water that is already rising or is expected to rise very soon.

The NWS does not need to wait for water to reach homes before issuing one. The phrase "about to occur" means a warning can arrive before flooding is visible at a given spot. The guidance to seek higher ground applies either way. Waiting for visible water before acting would give up the time the warning is meant to provide.

Three kinds of evidence usually trigger a warning. Radar estimates show how much rain is falling and where the heaviest rain is concentrated. Rain gauges record the rain that has actually reached the ground. Eyewitness reports describe what is happening on streets, streams and roads.

Each source covers a gap the others leave. Weather radar scans a wide area, but it estimates rainfall indirectly from the signal that precipitation reflects back. A gauge gives a direct measurement, but only at the spot where it sits. A report from someone on the scene describes the flooding itself rather than the rain behind it.

Taken together, the three sources let forecasters check one signal against another. Heavy rain on radar, a high gauge reading and a report of water over a road point to the same conclusion from different angles.

A warning covers a defined area, not an entire state or region. The practical question for a reader is whether their home, workplace or current location falls inside it.

Higher ground means a place the rising water cannot reach. Basements, underpasses and low spots along creeks sit in the path of the water rather than above it.

A flash flood emergency is the most serious flash flood alert the National Weather Service issues. The agency reserves it for an ongoing or imminent flash flood that poses a severe threat to human life and catastrophic damage.

Both parts of that definition matter. The danger to people has to be severe. The expected damage has to reach the catastrophic level. A flash flood that falls short of that threshold still gets a flash flood warning, but without the emergency designation.

The flood does not have to be underway yet. The NWS can declare an emergency for a flash flood that is imminent as well as for one already in progress. That means the alert can come before water reaches a given street or neighborhood.

There is no separate flash flood emergency product. The NWS issues it as enhanced wording inside a flash flood warning. On a phone screen, a radio broadcast or a weather app, the alert still appears as a warning. The emergency language in its text is what marks the escalation, so anyone in a warned area should read past the headline of the alert.

The designation also lines up with the strongest NWS damage threat tag. Flash flood warnings are tagged base, considerable or catastrophic, and the catastrophic tag goes with a flash flood emergency. A warning carrying that tag can trigger a Wireless Emergency Alert on phones in the warned area.

The NWS issues flash flood emergencies rarely. Most flash flood warnings never carry the label. Its use signals that forecasters see a threat beyond routine flooding.

The required response matches the threat. A flash flood warning already tells people in its path to move to higher ground right away. An emergency adds that lives are at severe risk and catastrophic damage is expected. That move to higher ground cannot be delayed to watch how the water behaves.

A flash flood watch and a flood watch are two different National Weather Service (NWS) alerts. The flash flood watch is about sudden, fast-rising water. The flood watch covers a broader chance of flooding, including slower rises on rivers and streams.

The two names differ by one word, and that word carries the meaning. "Flash" points to speed. A flash flood watch tells people that conditions in or near the watch area could produce that kind of fast-moving event.

A flood watch casts a wider net. It is not limited to fast-rising water. It also accounts for water that climbs gradually as rivers and streams fill. Slower flooding of this kind is a separate hazard, and the NWS handles it with its own set of products.

Both alerts share the same basic status. A watch of either kind means flooding is possible but is not yet happening or confirmed. Neither one tells people in the area that water is already rising.

The practical difference is the pace of the threat each one describes. Under a flash flood watch, the concern is water that can rise quickly. Under a flood watch, the concern can also include rises that build over a longer stretch.

The alert's name is the simplest way to tell which one applies. The word "flash" is the signal to look for. Its presence means the NWS is flagging the possibility of sudden, fast-rising water rather than only the broader chance of flooding.

A flash flood warning covers rapid flooding that is happening now or is about to happen. Flooding that builds more slowly, such as a gradual rise on a river or stream, falls under separate National Weather Service flood products.

The split between the two comes down to timing. The NWS treats flash flooding as its own hazard because the water climbs fast. That leaves people little room between the first heavy rain and dangerous conditions. A flash flood warning is built for that compressed timeline.

The threat a flash flood warning describes is already underway or close at hand. Its purpose is to prompt immediate action, not to start a planning process. The guidance for anyone in the warned area is to get to higher ground right away.

River flooding moves on a slower schedule. Water on a river or stream rises gradually, and the NWS keeps that hazard out of its flash flood alerts. It tracks slower flooding through a separate set of flood products instead.

That separation matters when two alerts appear close together on a phone or a broadcast. A flood alert and a flash flood alert are not interchangeable labels for the same event. Each one describes a different kind of water behavior.

The word "flash" in an alert's name is the signal to look for. It tells the reader that the gap between rain and dangerous water may be short. An alert that leaves the word out covers the broader category of flooding the NWS handles through its other products, including slower rises on rivers and streams.

Reading the full alert name, rather than skimming for the word "flood," is the quickest way to tell which situation applies.

National Weather Service flash flood warnings carry an impact-based tag that rates the expected damage threat as base, considerable or catastrophic. The tag tells people in a warned area how severe the flooding is expected to be.

The tag sits on top of the warning's basic message. Every flash flood warning carries the same core meaning: flash flooding is occurring or about to occur in the warned area. The damage threat label adds a second layer. It describes how much harm that flooding could do, not whether it is happening.

The three labels form a scale. Base is the lowest of the three. Considerable sits in the middle. Catastrophic is the highest.

A base tag does not soften the warning itself. Flash flooding is still occurring or imminent under a base-level warning. The label only places the expected damage at the low end of the scale.

The product name alone does not separate one flash flood warning from another. Two warnings can share the same name and carry very different labels. The tag is what tells them apart.

The term "impact-based" describes what the tag rates. It looks at the expected damage threat, meaning the effect the water could have on the area it reaches. That is a different question from where or when the flooding is happening, which the warning itself already answers.

The top of the scale connects to the top of the alert system. The catastrophic tag goes with a flash flood emergency, the most severe flash flood alert level. A warning carrying that label signals the threat the NWS reserves for danger to human life and catastrophic damage.

Flash flood warnings tagged with a considerable or catastrophic damage threat can trigger Wireless Emergency Alerts on phones in the warned area. Warnings tagged at the base level generally do not set off those phone alerts.

That split explains why people see some flash flood warnings on their phones and not others. One warning can make phones across a neighborhood sound at once. A later warning for the same area may never appear on a phone at all. Both are genuine National Weather Service flash flood warnings. The difference lies in the damage threat tag the NWS attached to each one.

Those tags come in three levels: base, considerable and catastrophic. Only the upper two are linked to Wireless Emergency Alerts. A catastrophic tag accompanies a flash flood emergency.

Wireless Emergency Alerts reach devices in the warned area. The alert depends on where a phone is at the moment, not where its owner lives. That makes the alert a signal about present location rather than a home address. A driver passing through a warned area can receive one. Someone whose home lies inside the warned area but who is elsewhere when the warning goes out may not.

A silent phone does not mean no warning is in effect. A base-level flash flood warning still means flash flooding is occurring or about to occur in the warned area. The lower tag describes the expected scale of damage. It does not make the water any less dangerous for someone caught in it.

A person who relies on phone alerts alone can miss a base-level warning entirely. Nothing arrives on the device, even though the warning covers the area they are in.

The NWS guidance under any flash flood warning stays the same whether or not a phone sounds. People in the warned area should move to higher ground right away.

Six inches of fast-moving water can knock an adult off their feet, according to the National Weather Service. A foot of water can float many cars. Two feet can carry away most vehicles, including SUVs and trucks.

Those three depths form the core of the agency's safety campaign, Turn Around Don't Drown. The slogan is a plain instruction. When water covers a road or path ahead, the guidance is to turn back rather than go through it.

The first threshold applies to people on foot. Six inches of water sits well below the knee of most adults. Moving water at that depth can still take a person down. Wading across a flooded street is a hazard in its own right, separate from driving through one.

The second threshold applies to cars. A car that begins to float loses the grip of its tires on the road. The driver can no longer steer or brake. The current, not the driver, decides where the vehicle goes.

The third threshold reaches larger vehicles. The NWS places SUVs and trucks among the vehicles that two feet of moving water can carry away. Extra height and weight do not take them out of danger.

Read together, the three depths show that the danger to people and the danger to vehicles overlap. Water deep enough to float a car is already deeper than the depth that can knock an adult down. A driver whose car is lifted by the current cannot count on stepping out and walking to safety. The vehicle offers no refuge, and the water outside it offers none either.

The figures also show why depth alone is a poor guide. Every number in the campaign describes fast-moving water, not still water. The force of the current, not just the height of the water, is what moves people and vehicles. A driver who reaches a flooded road has one safe option under the campaign's guidance. Turn around, and find another route.

Flash flooding strikes fastest where rainwater cannot soak into the ground or has little room to spread out. Steep canyons, paved urban areas, low-water road crossings and recent wildfire burn scars all fit that description. Each one concentrates runoff in its own way.

Narrow canyons work like funnels. Rain that falls across a wide area of rock and steep slopes drains into a single channel. The water rises quickly because the canyon walls leave it nowhere to go but up and downstream.

The storm producing that water does not have to be overhead. Heavy rain miles upstream can send a surge through a canyon where the sky is clear. A forecast for the entire drainage area, not only the trailhead, gives a fuller picture of the risk inside a slot canyon.

Cities create a similar problem with concrete instead of rock. Roads, parking lots and rooftops shed rain rather than absorbing it. That water collects in streets, storm drains and culverts within minutes. When drains back up or fill beyond capacity, underpasses and low-lying intersections can flood quickly, even in neighborhoods far from any river.

Low-water crossings are places where a road dips through a creek bed instead of passing over it on a bridge. They are common on rural roads and in hilly regions such as central Texas. During a storm, the creek can rise over the roadway faster than a driver expects. Muddy water also hides how deep it is and whether the pavement underneath has washed away.

Wildfire burn scars change how the ground behaves for months or even years after a fire. Burned slopes lose the plants and leaf litter that normally slow and absorb rain. Intense heat can also leave some soils repelling water instead of taking it in.

As a result, a storm over a recent burn area can produce far more runoff than the same rain would on unburned land. That runoff can pick up ash, mud, rocks and fallen trees as it moves downhill. Communities below a burn scar can face fast-moving debris flows, not just rising water.

#5485. Fintech giant Plaid opening Seattle engineering office, with plans to double local headcount

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 10, 2026 at 10:28 amNovember 10, 2026 at 10:28 am

Plaid is opening an engineering office in Seattle’s Westlake neighborhood in January and plans to double its local workforce to about 80 people by next summer.

The San Francisco-based fintech company says the new 11,466-square-foot space will serve as a hub for its technical teams, with most open Seattle roles focused on machine learning, data science and engineering.

Plaid said in a blog post that it chose Seattle because much of the cloud and AI technology behind modern financial infrastructure was built in the region. The company is developing AI models trained on its network to understand patterns in how money moves.

Plaid already has about 40 employees in the Seattle area, who currently work remotely, The Seattle Times reported. “There’s just great talent in Seattle, so it’s a little bit of a no-brainer for us,” Meghan Welch, Plaid’s chief people officer, told the Times.

Plaid’s careers page lists more than 50 open roles that include Seattle as a possible location, though most are also open in San Francisco, New York or other cities. About half are in data, engineering or security, with the rest spread across sales, legal, finance and other teams.

Founded in 2013, Plaid was valued at $8 billion in an employee share sale earlier this year, down from a 2021 peak of $13.4 billion. The company says more than 150 million people have used its technology to connect their financial accounts.

Plaid is led by co-founder and CEO Zachary Perret.

The new office will have views of Lake Union, an outdoor deck and event space, along with three catered meals a day, according to the company.

#5484. After Jensen Huang is Howard Lutnick the prime target of national security inquiry?

When questioning the motives of certain public leaders, the Roman orator Cicero was said to have used as a shorthand, “cui bono?” meaning, whose interests come first? That line rings true as Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick falls under rapidly escalating bipartisan scrutiny over his role in the flow of Nvidia chips into China.

Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after reports of affairs with a direct report and with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy, yet the national security questions he leaves behind keep growing amidst escalating congressional investigations. Megaspeed, the Nvidia customer where Alice Huang was an executive, was suspected of funneling advanced chips to China for years, yet the U.S. government took little action. Many are now asking: Who knew what, and when? And why is this surfacing only now?

We have already described Nvidia directors’ exposure to shareholder lawsuits over their own failures of oversight. Now the scrutiny is shifting to Washington. How did the U.S. government look past so grave a threat to national security for so long, and let these sales go on? As the reporting accumulates, all roads lead to one person, who by multiple accounts blocked action over the objections of fellow cabinet members and leading voices in both parties in Congress: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. He is now squarely on the hot seat, and it grows hotter by the day as more information comes to light.

Megaspeed has long been a major target of U.S. government focus amidst pervasive allegations that the Singapore-based data center company helped Chinese firms evade U.S. export controls on sensitive Nvidia chips.

The Department of Commerce’s own agents began investigating Megaspeed, the Singapore firm that bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips and is suspected of diverting them to China, in 2024, under the Biden Administration. After the change of administration but amidst the ongoing probe, The New York Times reported that in 2025, Nvidia’s general counsel emailed those agents directly, citing permission from Lutnick’s export-control chief, Jeffrey Kessler, with Commerce soon pausing its work on the investigation.

That sparked many concerns even within the GOP, with respected Senate Intelligence Committee Chair Tom Cotton writing to Lutnick directly, urging Commerce to investigate Megaspeed more carefully. Still, Megaspeed never landed on the entity list, the blacklist kept by the Department of Commerce that cuts suspect firms off from American technology; even though other agencies repeatedly agreed on proposing to add Megaspeed to the list, with the Financial Times reporting that the State Department, Treasury Department, Energy Department and the Pentagon were pushing particularly aggressively to add Megaspeed to the entity list. Despite these entreaties, Lutnick’s Commerce Department was unmoved, steadfastly refusing to add a single company to the entity list for more than a year.

Then came the memo. This spring, the New York Times reports, Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of a highly classified assessment built on electronic surveillance of Alice Huang. Its conclusion was as stark as can be: China’s Ministry of State Security had recruited her to gather intelligence on Jensen Huang and on America’s AI chips, and she had grown close to the Nvidia CEO. U.S. officials assessed that Beijing’s aims may have gone further, to steering Nvidia into pressing Washington for greater Chinese access to its most advanced chips.

The memo went to a handful of senior officials before President Trump’s May trip to China, with Axios reporting that Lutnick was among those who received the memo directly. Perhaps not coincidentally, Jensen Huang was originally left off the delegation of business leaders traveling to China with Trump, before being added at the very last possible minute during an Alaska refueling stop.

That same month, Reuters reported that Commerce had cleared about 10 Chinese companies to buy H200s.

Perhaps even more alarmingly, but less widely known than the existence of the memo; Axios also reports that President Trump approved a crackdown on chip diversion to China no less than three times, in May, in August, and on Nov. 5, with even Elon Musk supportive, and that Lutnick and his deputies had resisted carrying out each order. As Maria Curi and Marc Caputo of Axios reported pithily, “One administration official has repeatedly stood in the way: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick,” noting that virtually every other Administration official was supportive of these crackdowns.

Just last week, after news of the Jensen Huang spy scandal broke, Axios reported that Bessent confronted Lutnick about why his department has resisted implementing the export controls, particularly on Megaspeed, the company at the center of the spy scandal, with virtually all other Admin officials siding with Bessent; yet Lutnick apparently continued to stall. Already, there has been speculation that the leaks over the last week that felled Huang came from sources within the Trump Administration, perhaps from within the National Security Council, who were frustrated at Lutnick pushing what they perceived to be pro-China policies, with many remarking about the suspicious timing of these leaks right after midterm elections, even though the original memo was circulated in May this year, six months ago.

What makes this scrutiny so hot is who is turning up the temperature. Lutnick’s chief antagonists on the issue of China chip controls are almost entirely his own colleagues within the administration, ranging from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and National Security Adviser and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, to U.S. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, all of whom reportedly favor a far tougher approach than Lutnick has been willing to impose.

Lutnick’s Republican detractors are plenty outside the administration as well, particularly within the GOP congressional ranks. Republican Sen. John Kennedy says Lutnick must explain himself “in front of God and country.” Rep. Bill Huizenga has attacked Lutnick’s lack of responsiveness to Congress as “frustrating,” and the Republican chairs of the House China and Foreign Affairs committees, Rep. John Moolenaar and Rep. Brian Mast, have made their unhappiness with Lutnick just as vivid.

All these intraparty critics join legions of Democratic senators who are demanding records from Lutnick, and after last week’s midterms, their party takes the committee gavels in January with detractors making clear that Lutnick is one of their top targets – for reasons extending far beyond merely his role in sensitive U.S. technology making their way to China.

Many congressional Democrats are practically salivating at the prospect of being able to issue subpoenas to examine Lutnick’s perceived business conflicts of interests, and their files are already thick with hard questions Lutnick will have to answer.

Start with rare earths as one prominent example. In January, Commerce announced a tentative $1.6 billion deal that gives the government a roughly 10% stake in USA Rare Earth. To close it, the company raised $1.5 billion in a private stock offering and chose as its lead placement agent Cantor Fitzgerald, the firm Lutnick led for decades and which his son Brandon Lutnick, 27 when he took over, now oversees as chairman. By the lawmakers’ account, the company’s CEO credited Lutnick’s personal involvement for the deal. Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Ron Wyden and Chris Van Hollen have pressed for documents since February.

Crypto brings another witches’ brew of problems for Lutnick. Cantor has been custodian of the reserves of Tether, the largest stablecoin issuer, since 2021, and holds a stake that Sen. Richard Blumenthal says has swelled from about $600 million to an estimated $10 billion since Trump returned to office. A trust for Lutnick’s children reportedly borrowed from Tether around the time he transferred his Cantor stake to them. Cantor also launched Twenty One Capital, the bitcoin treasury company known by its ticker, XXI, with Tether, with Blumenthal already raising questions about the arrangement.

That doesn’t even factor in any potential lingering issues related to Lutnick’s longtime ties to Jeffrey Epstein, his onetime next-door Manhattan neighbor. Lutnick long maintained that he cut ties with Epstein in 2005, but Justice Department files showed a 2012 family visit to Epstein’s island, a shared investment and emails as late as 2018, which many called “grossly deceptive.” Republican Rep. Thomas Massie called on him to resign in February, and his closed-door testimony to House Oversight in May left Democrats on the panel calling him evasive.

For Lutnick, each of these issues raises the exact question Megaspeed poses: Whose interests came first, and whose side was he really on?

Defenders of Lutnick point out that he is merely carrying out Trump’s wishes as part of a broader implicit trade deal with China where the U.S. continues to provide cutting-edge chips and in exchange, the Chinese continue to provide the U.S. with rare earth minerals. But this is a misleading and misguided argument on several counts.

First, the U.S. is not nearly as dependent on China for rare earth minerals as many imagine, with the U.S. possessing tremendous reserves of rare earth minerals but merely needing some sustained investment to extract and process them. Second, this implicit deal did not apparently restrain other cabinet members, such as Secretary of State Rubio and Treasury Secretary Bessent, from registering their concerns with Lutnick’s stances. Third, Trump himself has endorsed the widely admired former CEO of Apple, Tim Cook, as the next CEO of Nvidia, echoing our own earlier endorsement of Cook. Cook has scrupulously abided by national security policies while capably and successfully balancing commerce in China with protection of US national security, and there is nothing to suggest that Cook would knowingly undermine US national security by continuing the illicit flow of chips into China.

As the questions pile up, there is no easy way out for Lutnick.  As Thomas More is said to have warned King Henry VIII, “Trust is as fragile as liquid in your hands, once you separate your fingers, its forever gone.”

Jeffrey Sonnenfeld is the Lester Crown Professor in Management Practice and Senior Associate Dean at Yale School of Management.

Steven Tian is the director of research at the Yale Chief Executive Leadership Institute.

#5483. Car caught in a flash flood: what drivers should do before, during and after

Free daily briefing on global business news.

What to do if your car is caught in a flash flood, from judging water depth to escaping a sinking vehicle and dealing with the damage afterward

A car feels like shelter. It has a roof, locked doors and a heater, and it sits between the driver and the storm outside. In a flash flood, that sense of protection can be misleading. A vehicle is a hollow metal box that can float once enough water gets underneath it. Moving water can then push it off the road with the people still inside.

Flash floods differ from slow river flooding. They form fast, often after intense rain over a small area. They can turn a dry street, creek bed or underpass into a channel of fast water with little warning. Roads often follow low ground, where water collects first. That puts drivers directly in the path. A route that was clear on the way out can be underwater on the way home.

Knowing what to do if your car is caught in a flash flood comes down to a short chain of decisions. Each one depends on where you are in that chain. Before reaching the water, the choice is whether to drive in at all. If the engine stalls in still water, the question becomes how fast to get out and where to go. If the car is sinking or caught in current, the order of actions narrows to seconds. Once the water drops, a different set of choices determines whether the car can be saved and how an insurance claim proceeds.

The National Weather Service, FEMA and Ready.gov publish guidance for each of these moments. Their advice is consistent on the basics. Avoid flooded roads and take official alerts seriously. Leave a stalled vehicle when water starts rising around it. Treat floodwater as dangerous whether you are inside a car or standing in it.

The 10 steps below follow that sequence. They start with reading the road and the weather alerts. They move through escaping a stalled or sinking vehicle and finish with what to do once the flood has passed. Each step covers one situation. A driver facing a specific problem can find the relevant guidance without reading the rest first. None of it requires special training. Most of it requires deciding early, before rising water removes the easier options.

If water covers the road ahead, turn around before your tires reach it. The National Weather Service sums up that rule in its slogan, "Turn around, don't drown." Do not try to test how deep the water is.

The reason is what sits under the surface. Water flowing over a road can hide a washout, where the current has carried away the ground beneath the pavement. It can also hide a stretch where the pavement itself is gone. Once both are covered, a collapsed roadbed and an intact one look the same from the driver's seat.

Floodwater is rarely clear. It usually carries mud and silt, which block any view of the road below. Lane markings, curbs and the edge of the road disappear. A driver has no reliable way to tell whether the water is a thin layer over solid asphalt or the top of a much deeper gap.

The surface of the water gives no better clue. Smooth, calm-looking water can still be flowing across the road. A flooded stretch can look shallow when the road beneath it has dropped away.

Another vehicle crossing without trouble does not prove the road is sound. Moving water keeps eroding the roadbed. A section that held one car can give way under the next. During a flash flood, conditions can change within minutes as more rain drains into the same low ground.

That is why the NWS answer to the common question "can you drive through flood water" is no. Its guidance makes no exception for drivers who believe they can judge the depth by eye.

Turning around takes only a few steps. Stop well short of the water. Check that the road behind you is clear, then reverse or make a U-turn. Take a different route, or wait on higher ground until the water recedes and the road surface is visible again. A detour adds time. Driving into water of unknown depth puts the car and everyone inside it at risk.

About 12 inches of moving water can float many cars, and about two feet can carry away most vehicles, including SUVs and pickup trucks. Those are the depth thresholds the National Weather Service and FEMA give drivers.

Water at either depth can sit well below a typical car's windows. From the driver's seat, it can look manageable. The risk does not start when water reaches the doors. It starts lower, at the tires.

A car stays on the road because its weight presses the tires against the pavement. That contact lets a driver steer, brake and accelerate. Floodwater undermines it in two ways.

The first is buoyancy. A vehicle's tires, body and cabin hold air. Water pushes upward on anything that holds air. As the water rises, that upward force offsets more of the car's weight. The tires press down with less force, and their grip on the road weakens.

The second is current. Moving water pushes against the whole side of the vehicle. Friction between the tires and the road resists that push. Once buoyancy has lightened the car, the same push can slide it sideways. Steering and braking no longer work in any useful way. The car then moves with the water.

Depth lifts the car. Current carries it. Together they can move a vehicle that looks firmly planted.

A larger vehicle is not immune. A taller SUV or pickup truck keeps its cabin above shallow water for longer. It also presents a larger body for water to lift and push against. The NWS and FEMA place both vehicle types within the two-foot threshold.

The figures are approximate rather than exact cutoffs. How quickly a specific vehicle floats depends on its weight, its shape and the speed of the water around it. A heavier vehicle may hold the road slightly longer than a light compact car. Neither is safe once the water reaches these levels.

The takeaway from these thresholds is simple. Water does not have to look deep to move a car.

A flash flood watch means conditions could produce flash flooding. A flash flood warning means flooding is happening now or is about to, and anyone in the warned area should move to higher ground immediately.

The National Weather Service issues both alerts. The two names sound alike, but they call for very different responses from anyone behind the wheel.

A watch is an early signal. It means the ingredients for flash flooding are in place, such as heavy rain falling on saturated ground or slow-moving storms over the same area. A watch usually covers a broad region. It is often issued well before any water rises, and nothing may be flooding yet.

For drivers, a watch is the time to plan. Check the forecast before leaving. Consider delaying a trip that isn't essential, or pick a route that stays on higher ground. Keep a phone charged and weather alerts switched on. That way, an upgrade to a warning won't go unnoticed.

A warning carries more urgency. It means flooding is underway or imminent in a specific area. The NWS guidance at this stage is to move to higher ground at once. A driver already on the road should head for elevated ground rather than press on toward a destination.

Flash floods can strike where little or no rain is falling. Runoff from storms upstream can rush down creeks, dry washes and canyons far from where the rain fell. A clear sky overhead does not cancel a warning.

The NWS also issues a rarer and more serious alert, the flash flood emergency. It is reserved for cases where a flash flood poses a severe threat to human life and catastrophic damage is occurring or expected.

Alerts reach drivers through several channels. NOAA Weather Radio, local TV and radio broadcasts and smartphone weather apps all carry them. Wireless Emergency Alerts can also push urgent warnings straight to a phone with a distinctive tone.

Reading the alert correctly buys time. Under a watch, that time goes into planning a safer trip or skipping it. Under a warning, it goes into getting to higher ground.

If a car stalls and floodwater starts rising around it, the driver should get out and move to higher ground. Ready.gov advises abandoning the vehicle when the water around it is climbing but not moving, rather than waiting inside for help.

A stalled engine changes the situation. The car can no longer drive out of the water, and it cannot back up to a safer spot. At that point, the vehicle offers no way out of the rising water.

Still water is the scenario where leaving on foot is most manageable. Without a current pushing against the body, a person stepping out of the car has a better chance of staying upright and reaching dry ground. That chance shrinks as the depth increases.

The National Weather Service and FEMA put the depth at which many cars begin to float at about 12 inches. A car that floats can drift into deeper water or into a current. Water that is calm at the moment of a stall may not stay calm.

Staying inside carries its own problems. Electrical systems can fail once they are submerged. That can leave power windows unusable. Doors also become hard to push open once water presses against them from outside. Each minute spent waiting makes the exit harder.

The order of action is to leave the car first. The vehicle can be inspected and reported to an insurer once the water recedes.

Higher ground means a spot above the water line and away from the path the water is taking — a raised road shoulder, a hill or an elevated structure. Low ground near the stalled car can flood next.

This advice applies to standing water. If the water around the car is moving fast, the situation is different. Wading into swift current is dangerous, and the guidance shifts to climbing onto the roof and calling 911. Reading which kind of water surrounds the car is the first decision a stranded driver makes.

If a car goes into water and begins to sink, unbuckle, open a window and climb out right away. The window, not the door, is the exit, and the best moment to use it is the first moment the car is in the water.

Every second in the water makes escape harder. As water rises along the outside of the car, it presses against the doors. That pressure can make a door difficult or impossible to push open, even for a strong adult.

An open window avoids that problem. It gives a direct route out that does not depend on fighting the weight of the water outside. Electrical systems can fail once they are submerged. Lowering a power window while the car still has power gives it the best chance of moving.

The seat belt comes first. A buckled belt holds a driver in place, and panic can make the release harder to find by feel. Unclipping it immediately frees the body to turn toward the window.

Waiting inside does not help. Some drivers assume they should stay put until the cabin fills and the pressure on the doors evens out. That approach leaves them in a flooding space with less air, less time and less control. The safer choice is to leave early, while the car is still near the surface.

Passengers change the order of operations only slightly. Children who cannot unbuckle themselves need help with their harnesses or belts. They should go out through the window ahead of the adult. That way, no one is left behind in a cabin taking on water.

A phone call can wait. Dialing 911 from inside a sinking car uses up seconds that are better spent leaving it. The call can be made once everyone is out of the vehicle.

Once out, the priority is getting clear of the vehicle and toward safety. If the side windows will not open at all, breaking the glass becomes the fallback route.

A spring-loaded window punch or a hammer-style escape tool can break a car's side window when floodwater has knocked out the power windows. Aim it at a side window, not the windshield, which is built to resist breaking.

Power windows depend on the car's electrical system. Once that system is submerged, it can fail and leave the window switches dead. A driver who planned to lower the glass and climb out may find it stuck in place. An escape tool gives that driver another way through.

The two common designs work in different ways. A spring-loaded punch is pressed firmly against the glass. Pressure builds inside the tool until a spring drives a hardened pin against the window. It needs almost no swinging room. That helps in a cramped cabin or with water around the driver's arms.

A hammer-style tool has a pointed steel head on a short handle and is swung against the glass. Many hammer-style models also carry a recessed blade for cutting through a jammed seatbelt.

Glass type decides which window to target. Side windows are usually tempered glass. Tempered glass is heat-treated so that a sharp, concentrated impact breaks the whole pane into small, granular pieces. That is why a small pointed tip can clear a side window opening.

Windshields are laminated, with a layer of plastic bonded between two sheets of glass. When struck, laminated glass cracks but tends to stay in one piece, held together by that interlayer. Breaking through it is much harder, so it is a poor escape route.

Some vehicles also use laminated glass in their side windows, often to cut road noise. The small printed marking in the corner of each window often identifies the glass type. The owner's manual can confirm it. If the front side windows are laminated, a rear side window may be the better exit.

A tool helps only if the driver can reach it quickly. One kept in the trunk or under clutter in the glove box may be out of reach once water enters the cabin. A keychain, a door pocket or the center console keeps it within the driver's grasp. Every adult who rides in the car regularly should know where it is and how it works.

If moving floodwater traps your car, get onto the roof if you can and call 911. Do not try to wade through fast-moving water to reach dry ground.

This advice covers a different situation from a car stalled in still water. When a strong current flows around the vehicle, stepping off it puts a person directly into the flow. The roof keeps the body above the water and out of its push.

The roof is usually the highest point a stranded driver can reach. Sitting or lying flat there keeps the body lower and steadier than standing. Holding onto a roof rack, the edge of the roof or the top of the door frame helps if the car rocks or shifts.

A 911 call from the roof should start with location. Dispatchers need the road name, the direction of travel and the nearest cross street or highway exit. A nearby landmark, such as a bridge, a business sign or a mile marker, can narrow the search. Saying plainly that people are on top of a car in moving water tells the dispatcher what kind of rescue is needed. The number of people, along with the color and type of vehicle, helps responders find the right car.

Text-to-911 works in many U.S. areas, though not everywhere. Where the service is not offered, the sender should receive an automatic reply saying so.

Wading out is the step to avoid. Fast water pushes against the legs with steady force, and the ground beneath it cannot be seen. A stretch that looks shallow can drop away without warning. The current also carries branches and other debris that can strike or pin a person.

Once on the roof, the safer course is to stay put and wait for trained rescuers instead of swimming or walking out. At night, a flashlight or a lit phone screen can help crews spot the car. Keeping the phone dry and saving its battery keeps the line to dispatchers open.

Walking through floodwater exposes a person to hazards they cannot see, including submerged debris, open storm drains, contamination and downed power lines. Anyone who has left a car should head straight for higher ground and stay out of the water wherever possible.

Murky water hides what lies underneath. A path that was solid before a storm can be covered with branches, broken fencing, rocks or pieces of damaged vehicles. Any of these can trip a person or cut a foot or leg. A fall in moving water is much harder to recover from than a fall on dry pavement.

Open drains are a separate risk. Rushing water can push manhole covers and storm drain grates out of place. A pedestrian has no way to tell where the opening is. A single step can drop a leg, or a whole body, into a drain that is pulling water downward.

Current adds force to every one of these hazards. The National Weather Service and FEMA put the threshold low: about six inches of moving water can knock an adult off their feet. Water that shallow can look harmless from the edge of a road. Once a person is down, the current can carry them into debris or toward a drain.

Floodwater is also dirty. It can carry sewage, fuel, chemicals and other contamination picked up as it moves across streets, yards and industrial sites. Cuts and scrapes from hidden debris give that contamination a way into the body. Anyone who touches floodwater should wash with soap and clean water as soon as possible.

Electrical hazards are easy to miss. Storms bring down power lines, and a line lying in water can sit hidden below the surface. Water conducts electricity. A downed line can energize the water around it. Stay well away from any downed line and report it to the local utility.

The safest route is the one that avoids water entirely. After leaving a vehicle, look for the nearest high point, such as a hill, a raised embankment or an upper floor of a sturdy building. Move there without wading through current. If every way out crosses moving water, waiting on the highest available ground is safer than attempting the crossing.

Never drive around a road barricade during a flood. Low-water crossings, underpasses and dips are among the first places to fill with water in heavy rain. Darkness or a downpour makes that water much harder to see from behind the wheel.

A barricade marks a road that crews have already closed because of a hazard. Whatever made them close it may sit under the water or farther down the road, out of view. Moving a barrier or steering around it throws away the clearest warning a driver will get. It can also leave the road looking open to the drivers who arrive next.

Dips collect water because they are the lowest point on a stretch of road. Rain running off the surrounding pavement and ground drains toward them. In a heavy storm, a dip can fill with standing or moving water long before the rain stops.

Underpasses carry the same risk for a similar reason. A road that passes beneath a railway or highway sits below the ground around it. During intense rain, water can flow in from several directions faster than drains can clear it. A driver entering an underpass may not see how deep the water is until the car is already in it.

Low-water crossings are built where a road meets a creek or wash at stream level instead of on a bridge. They are designed for water to flow over them when the stream rises. In a flash flood, the creek can run across the road with force. The water feeding it may come from rain that fell well upstream, out of the driver's sight.

Night driving adds another layer of risk. Headlights show only a limited stretch of road ahead. Floodwater can look like ordinary wet pavement in the dark. Heavy rain cuts visibility further, even with wipers on their fastest setting.

Planning helps before the storm arrives. When heavy rain is in the forecast, drivers can choose routes that avoid known dips, underpasses and creek crossings. A flooded crossing or underpass can also be reported to local authorities, who decide when a road needs to be closed.

Do not restart a car that has sat in floodwater. Turning over an engine with water inside it can cause serious damage. Photograph the vehicle and contact your insurer before making any other decision about it.

A flooded car can look normal once the water drains away. The floor mats dry out and the body panels shed their mud. The engine may even seem ready to run. None of that shows what happened inside the engine or under the dashboard.

An engine is designed to compress a mix of air and fuel. Water does not compress. If water has reached the cylinders, starting the engine can force the moving parts against it. Mechanics call this hydrolock, and it can bend internal components. The ignition key, the push-button start and any jump-start attempt should all stay off-limits.

The engine is not the only system at risk. Electrical systems can fail once they have been submerged. A car that powers up normally may still have water in its wiring. Have the car towed rather than driven, even if it appears to work.

Return to the car only after the water has gone down and the area is safe to reach. Floodwater can carry contamination. Soaked seats, carpets and trim may hold more than water. Wearing gloves while handling wet items inside the cabin limits contact with whatever the flood left behind.

Photographs are the core of any damage record. Take wide shots of every side of the car, then close-ups of the seats, floor, dashboard and engine bay. Capture any line the water left on the doors or upholstery, because it shows how high the flood rose. Take these pictures before cleaning anything or having the car towed.

Then call the insurer and start a claim. Whether flood damage is covered depends on the specific policy. Do not assume the damage is either covered or excluded. Ask the insurer which part of the policy applies and what documentation it needs. Ask, too, whether an adjuster will inspect the car before any repair begins.

#5482. ‘I Just Cannot Get Ahead’: Why Americans Are Under Extreme Financial Pressure, According to a New Report

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

One 73-year-old borrower described owing nearly $40,000 across 19 credit cards.

Why does getting ahead feel so out of reach? A new analysis from the Urban Institute offers a look at the financial strain Americans are facing.

The report, which drew from U.S. Census Bureau data, revealed that 23.5% of Americans with a credit history have debt in collections. They owe a median amount of $2,913.

As grocery bills and other essentials take a bigger toll on household budgets, some Americans are relying on credit cards to bridge the gap. However, steep interest charges can turn that short-term relief into debt that is difficult to pay off, even for borrowers who are making payments.

Susan Cannon described that cycle to Business Insider earlier this year. The 73-year-old owes nearly $40,000 across 19 credit cards, with interest rates ranging from roughly 12% to 35%. She lives in a mobile home in rural Texas. Despite paying more than the minimum balance on her credit cards, she struggles to reduce her balances while continuing to charge necessities such as groceries and gas to her credit cards.

“I can’t get the balance down because I am still having to use credit cards at the end of the month to get groceries and gas,” Cannon told the publication. “I pay my bills, but because of the interest rates, it keeps going up — I feel like I’m being gouged.”

Despite Cannon’s best attempts to build a savings account, her monthly payments are all going towards interest payments on her credit cards.

“I just cannot get ahead,” Cannon told Business Insider.

Where Americans live can make a noticeable difference in how heavily overdue their bills are. For example, in rural Jim Hogg County in South Texas, more than half of residents with a credit history have debt in collections, according to the report. Nationwide, the share is 23.5%, making the county’s rate more than twice the national figure.

How quickly an unpaid bill reaches collections depends on the type of debt. Credit card accounts typically enter collections four to six months after a missed payment, while unpaid medical bills generally take three to six months. The balances also differ: The analysis put the median delinquent credit card debt at $680, compared with $1,492 for medical debt.

Student loans follow a different path, with the rules varying between federal and private lenders. Federal loans generally fall into default after 270 days without payment. Borrowers can then pursue options such as loan rehabilitation to resolve the default and restore their loans to good standing.

The New York Federal Reserve determined that Americans collectively owe $18.8 trillion in debt as of the second quarter of the year.

#5481. Microsoft awards $20K grants to 25 Seattle-area nonprofits amid state budget crunch and tax debate

by Todd Bishop on Nov 10, 2026 at 10:48 amNovember 11, 2026 at 10:27 am

The Lighthouse for the Blind is adding braille displays to its computer lab. Friends of the Issaquah Salmon Hatchery is taking its lessons to low-income schools. And Lake Washington High School’s band boosters are replacing marching capes that date to the MS-DOS era.

Those are among 25 King County nonprofits that received $20,000 apiece from Microsoft in grants announced this week. It’s the first round of the company’s Community-First Grants, a $1 million program launched in September.

Microsoft said it received 813 applications.

“Boy, I think we hit a nerve,” said Jane Broom, Microsoft’s senior director of Community Affairs, during an event Monday recognizing the nonprofits on the company’s Redmond campus, featuring Mariners catcher Cal Raleigh and the team’s mascots.

The grants are meant for immediate needs, such as replacing a broken-down van or a failed freezer, Broom explained. Nonprofits that already received or were invited to receive Microsoft corporate grants in 2026 weren’t eligible.

Funding and the tax debate: Nonprofits are dealing with rising costs and tighter budgets. As a group, their largest funding source is the state government, which is in the middle of an ongoing debate with members of the business community over taxes and economic competitiveness amid a budget crunch.

Microsoft is among the companies asserting that current and proposed taxes are hurting the business climate. It’s also the second-largest funder of the state’s nonprofits, behind only the state itself, said Brad Smith, the company’s president and vice chair.

“In my view, a healthy nonprofit community actually has aspects of support from more than one source,” Smith said in an interview after the event, noting that state grants are often at risk when a recession forces budget cuts.

Where the money goes: Demand is climbing for many of the grant recipients. At Community Lunch on Capitol Hill, which serves free hot meals, it’s up 40% this year, and the diaper bank at Byrd Barr Place has grown from 720 families in 2021 to 1,600, Microsoft said at the event.

Friends of the Issaquah Salmon Hatchery gives more than 700 tours during the salmon season. It will use its grant to bring lessons to classrooms, mainly at Title I schools, which serve large numbers of low-income students and often can’t afford a field trip to the hatchery, said Mark Clemens, the group’s executive director.

“If they can’t bring the school to the hatchery, we will go out to the school,” said Clemens, a former Scientific American art director, who was creative director of the Modernist Cuisine cookbook project before taking over the nonprofit in 2023.

One bonus for the group, which goes by the clever acronym of FISH, was the appearance of the Mariners’ salmon mascots, which joined the group onstage for a photo op when Clemens and his colleagues accepted its grant.

The Lighthouse for the Blind, a Seattle-based nonprofit that employs blind people in manufacturing, retail and other jobs, will use its grant to upgrade its computer training lab with Windows 11 PCs, braille displays and wireless keyboards, said Antonio Rozier, the nonprofit’s IT director.

The goal is to keep employees current on screen readers and other tools so they can work alongside sighted colleagues, Rozier said. The Lighthouse also has computer labs at its three manufacturing plants, and employees can use them for personal tasks, since some don’t have that equipment at home.

Rozier called the upgraded lab “a game changer for the future.”

The Lake Washington High School Band and Jazz Boosters will buy 150 uniforms for the school’s marching band, which returned in 2025 after a 40-year absence and has been performing in capes from 1981.

Microsoft’s company culture: Most of the company’s local giving is directed by its employees. Microsoft matches their donations and adds $25 for every hour they volunteer, up to a combined $15,000 a year per person, Smith said.

That program accounts for most of the $1.9 billion that Microsoft and its employees have given to about 13,000 Washington nonprofits over the past 30 years, he said.

“We let our people decide where the money goes,” Smith said.

Microsoft’s employee base is going through a period of major change. After layoffs in July and September, the company offered voluntary buyouts last month to about 60,000 people, roughly a quarter of its global workforce. Employees have described mounting pressure to use AI, stagnant pay and a growing sense of job insecurity, The New York Times reported.

Asked about the buyouts, Smith said it’s a good time for Microsoft to keep investing in the employee experience, and he described the giving program as part of that.

Silicon Valley companies may offer more free food as a perk, he said, but Microsoft matches employee donations, giving workers who often move to the region from elsewhere a way to get involved in the community.

This year’s Microsoft Give campaign in October, the company’s biggest month for employee donations, was again a success, Smith said, showing that “employee participation and employee giving is alive and well.”

Microsoft plans to open a second round of applications for the Community-First Grants in the spring of 2027.
