#5461. ‘A dark day’: Jensen Huang’s sex drive threatens to pop the AI bubble, and the industry isn’t sure what’s next

Welcome to Eye on AI. Emily Forlini here, filling in for Beatrice Nolan. In today’s issue:

Before we get to the news, can I just say, you are not going to want to miss this year’s edition of Fortune Brainstorm AI San Francisco.

We have an exceptional line-up of speakers for you: OpenAI president Greg Brockman and Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman will both be onstage. Once the closest of partners, their two companies are increasingly, competitors, so I’m eager to hear how differently they see the road ahead. AI pioneers Fei-Fei Li, now of World Labs, as well as Andrew Ng, now of LearnVector, will be discussing their view of AI’s future too. Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora will talk about AI and cybersecurity. Greylock partner Reid Hoffman, CapitalG’s Jill Chase, and Kleiner Perkins’ Mamoon Hamid and Ilya Fushman will weigh in on where the money is going. Recursive Superintelligence’s Richard Socher will talk about RSI and automating AI research.

Plus, we’ve got Nick Fox from Google. We’ve got Fireworks CEO Lin Qiao. We’ve got Cerebras’ Andrew Feldman, Vanta’s Christina Cacioppo, Unconventional AI’s Naveen Rao, Brex’s Pedro Franceschi, Maven Clinic’s Kate Ryder, Box’s Aaron Levie, Atlassian’s Mike Cannon-Brookes, New Work Foundation’s Clara Shih, Twilio’s Khozema Shipchandler, Rubrik’s Bipul Sinha, Harvey’s Winston Weinberg, Dynamic Creatures’ Marc Theermann, SendCutSend’s Jim Belosic, Apptronik’s Jeff Cardenas, Accenture Song’s Ndidiamaka Oteh, and Senra Systems’ Jordan Black. It’s going to be epic. So please join me and many of my Fortune colleagues at the St. Regis in San Francisco on December 7th and 8th. You can apply to attend here.

Jensen Huang’s abrupt resignation as Nvidia CEO may be the biggest story in AI we’ve seen since the launch of ChatGPT almost exactly four years ago. Not only because it’s a stunning, swift downfall, but also because it’s the end of the first major phase of AI development as we’ve known it. At Fortune, we’ve been following the story closely over the past two days. You can check out our coverage by following the links in the “Fortune on AI” section of this newsletter.

It turns out, one man might just be able to single-handedly pop the AI bubble by not keeping it in his pants, with not one but three affairs—at least that we know about so far. But in all seriousness, this is a sad story. It’s a visceral betrayal for Huang’s family, his wife of 41 years, Lori, and their two children, both of whom work at Nvidia.

Huang has disappointed just about everybody in his orbit, from shareholders to customers, to people who held him up as a role model. Martin Casado, an investor at the prominent firm a16z called today a “dark, dark day,” and a “horrible decision for the U.S. and the western world.”

“It’s very sad by every dimension,” Penny Herscher, a longtime executive in the semiconductor industry, told me today. “It’s sad for his family, for the employees, for the customers. Jensen’s a remarkable person, and it’s sad to see such a remarkable person in this horrible situation—self-inflicted, but horrible.”

“I am extremely sad today as I see Nvidia without Jensen Huang,” one Nvidia employee posted. Several others have made similar public remarks.

My hunch is Nvidia will prevail, given the immense amount of money and geopolitical stability hanging on the health of its GPU business. But there will likely be a period of uncertainty, both in the boardroom and in Washington. America’s position at the top of the AI industry hangs in the balance, and stricter regulation may be more likely, especially given the Democratic Party’s sweeping midterms wins. As Jeremy Kahn wrote in Tuesday’s edition of Eye on AI, Huang had been a leading voice opposing both U.S. export controls on AI technology and government regulations on open models, and now that community has lost their main champion.

“This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened. It’s a really sad day!” posted Clement Delangue, CEO of Hugging Face, the open source repository Nvidia acquired for nearly $13 billion in September. “But I want to make one thing clear: we’ll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever. This is too important to slow down now. Let’s go!”

There is much more to the story yet to unfold. Huang has agreed to appear before Congress. More investigations are likely to ensue. Meanwhile, rumors are swirling that Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei may have orchestrated Huang’s downfall. Amodei has warned that open models can serve as uncontrolled weapons that bad actors can harness to incur serious societal harm, and is in favor of industry-wide slowdowns. I’m not quick to believe that theory, mostly because there is not yet any proof, but also Anthropic had every incentive to wait until after its IPO if it was going to take down Huang. The dark cloud his ousting has cast over the AI industry threatens Anthropic’s valuation as investors enter arguably the greatest period of instability we’ve seen yet in AI.

“My expectation is a 10–15% valuation haircut, potentially approaching 20% if Nvidia’s leadership crisis raises doubts about its $10 billion anchor commitment,” Jonathan Tower, managing partner at the VC firm Catapult, tells Fortune. “Anthropic’s underlying business hasn’t changed overnight, but investor confidence has. I expect the anchor to hold, but investors will demand a greater margin of safety. The larger question is whether this marks the beginning of a broader repricing of AI risk.”

The big unknown is how the stock market will react. Nvidia shares are trading down 4% at the bell today, a modest dip.

As far as silver linings go, there will be a few winners to come out of Huang’s downfall. Nervous Nvidia customers could place bigger orders with other chipmakers, such as Google, Amazon, AMD, and Broadcom. Another winner could be Nvidia’s next CEO, who stands to score the role of a lifetime, and perhaps propel the company into a new and even more successful era. That search is already underway. But given the allegations against Huang at this time, particularly that he may be complicit in funneling chips to China via Megaspeed, the shell company helmed by his paramour Alice Huang—there could always be more executives involved.

The biggest story in AI since ChatGPT is far from over.

#5460. Rand Fishkin’s Seattle game studio serves up first trailer for ‘The Snackbar at the End of the World’

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 11, 2026 at 11:21 amNovember 11, 2026 at 11:21 am

If the eventual release of “The Snackbar at the End of the World” is a full-on meal for video game fans, news this week of the game’s first trailer should at least suffice as an appetizer.

Seattle-based Snackbar Studio, co-founded by SparkToro founder Rand Fishkin and his wife, writer Geraldine DeRuiter, unveiled its debut title and Steam page on Tuesday. The hand-drawn narrative adventure RPG puts players in the role of a chef trying to save a struggling family restaurant in a magical version of 1960s Italy.

The studio now plans to launch the game late next year, after originally targeting the second half of 2026. Snackbar raised $2.15 million from 38 angel investors two years ago, and the project began four years ago, according to Fishkin. The team includes five co-founders (Fishkin, DeRuiter, game designer Nicolas Kraj, lead programmer Miriam Cabrera and art director Francesco Mazza) plus about 10 contractors.

In the studio’s description on Steam, players forage for ingredients in the “forbidden wilds” outside town, battling explosive tomatoes, chaotic zucchini and vendetta-driven poultry. They then cook dishes back at the restaurant before a tyrannical mayor known as the Sindaco can shut it down. The game mixes combat and stealth with cooking mini-games based on real-world recipes.

The trailer is set to “’O surdato ’nnammurato,” a classic Neapolitan song performed by professional musicians recruited by the studio’s music director. Fishkin said he and DeRuiter both cried the first time they heard it.

Fishkin is best known in Seattle tech circles as co-founder of SEO software company Moz and audience research startup SparkToro, and he more recently launched Alertmouse, a tool for tracking online mentions. DeRuiter, a writer and author, is Snackbar’s head writer.

In a LinkedIn post this week, Fishkin recalled telling DeRuiter during the COVID lockdown that he wanted to fulfill a childhood dream of making a video game. Her reply: “Don’t wait. Do it now. I’ll do it with you.”

In the same post, he said the game’s themes include found family and fighting fascism “even when there’s no hope you’ll win.” He called it a love letter to DeRuiter’s small family village in the mountains outside Naples, to that era of Italy, to video games, and to the many people both of their families have lost in recent years.

Moments like hearing that song come often in the work, Fishkin said, such as when a new feature clicks or a new animation brings DeRuiter’s characters to life. He has always loved art without being good at any form of it. “I may not be able to create art, but I can enable it,” he said. “What a wonderful feeling.”

There have been lows, too. The team spent its initial 18 months on the project with a contract agency that didn’t work out, losing money with nothing to show for it. Fishkin is glad they kept going, “even when it felt financially irresponsible.”

The game is entirely human-made, and Snackbar’s no-AI stance is firm. “Geraldine hates AI with the fury of a thousand suns,” Fishkin said. He once suggested, just once, that she use Google’s AI Mode to find a synonym, and she was mad at him for the rest of a six-hour flight home from Philadelphia. Even if players, the rest of the team and the games media were fine with AI (and they’re not), DeRuiter alone would make it a no-go, he said.

Still ahead are 10 to 12 months of finishing the game’s content, playtesting, bug fixing, marketing and launch prep. Fishkin called it daunting, but said team members have done it many times before, “even though it’s our first rodeo.”

Fishkin is still juggling Snackbar with SparkToro and Alertmouse, and describes his role at the studio as mostly oversight and management. SparkToro is growing again, and Alertmouse recently hit a big milestone in annual renewals with high retention. He and his Alertmouse co-founders are putting more money into the company to fund growth.

Balancing the three roles is a challenge, he said, but only rarely completely overwhelming. “Like this week.”
